the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner jourová, allow me first of all to thank the commission, the shadow rapporteurs and the latvian and luxembourg presidencies, under which the negotiations took place, for the constructive approach they took during the course of the work. it is almost a year since i was given the mandate to negotiate following the approval by the libe committee of the text of the directive we are discussing today. the work carried out during this period was inspired by the desire to create a measure which, for the first time, took into account the specific nature of the juvenile process at a supranational level, accompanied by clear guarantees for the children involved. it took nine trilogues, sometimes very difficult, and many technical meetings before a final agreement was reached, which i very much welcome and on which i hope there will be a broad consensus in this house. with over one million children subjected to criminal proceedings in europe each year, there are still significant differences between the legal systems of the member states in the treatment of children at the various stages of the proceedings. the directive seeks to bridge these gaps by defining and identifying clear rights for children who are being investigated or accused through a body of minimum standards which, however, establish a high level of safeguards. the best interests of the child were at the centre of the case, a principle also enshrined in article 24 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which is already well known in civil and administrative matters and thus enters criminal proceedings for the first time. i believe that the added value of the directive lies in the fact that it has accompanied the proceedings of minors, in addition to the fundamental safeguards provided for criminal proceedings involving adults, also those required by the specific nature of minors who must always be the recipients of specific appropriate protection. there are many aspects of the procedure covered by the directive, but i cannot dwell on them for reasons of time. i would like to refer to article 6 of the directive, which provides for the right of the child to be assisted by a lawyer. this is the most delicate issue to be dealt with in the negotiations and i must say that i am satisfied with the compromise reached in the text which describes, in an accurate manner, the situations in which the presence of the lawyer is essential to ensure that the child receives technical assistance, that all the guarantees provided for are properly applied and that he is helped to understand the course of the proceedings in which he is involved. for this reason, while providing for reasonable possibilities for derogation, in view of the lesser gravity of the offence, the less complexity of the case and the measures that could be taken as a result, the directive requires states to ensure the presence of the lawyer from the earliest stages of the investigation and in particular when the child is questioned by the judicial police and, above all, in any case where he is deprived of personal liberty. another important provision is that which requires member states to subject the child to an assessment by qualified staff in order to support decisions on possible measures for the benefit of the child, on the adequacy of any precautionary measures and in the context of sentencing. i would like to stress once again the importance of training those involved in the proceedings, starting with the police, the judiciary and the defence counsel. the directive provides that they should have access to specific training to ensure that they are able to act in the best interests of the child. finally, in view of the specific needs of the child and his or her social reintegration after the end of the criminal experience, detention is always considered as an extreme measure to be used when alternative measures are not effectively feasible. where it is unavoidable to deprive the child of his or her personal liberty, the state must do everything possible to safeguard his or her psychophysical development and his or her re-education needs. i therefore believe that one of the most significant aspects of the directive is that it establishes for the first time at european level the principle of separate detention for minors. for all these reasons, i am convinced that the directive is moving in the right direction in defining a common model of fair trial for juveniles, and also contributing to the establishment of juvenile justice in the criminal field.
member of the commission.– madam president, i thank the honourable members for this discussion. i can only summarise that this directive is indeed another important contribution to strengthening the rights of suspects and accused persons by setting common minimum standards on fair trial rights. it is true that this arrangement on common minimum standards is something which is still missing in the member states of the european union and this is why we are coming with these harmonised rules. this proposal provides for special safeguards for the most vulnerable persons, who are children. you know that recently we adopted here the directive on the presumption of innocence and, among the three recently proposed directives on procedural safeguards, only the directive on legal aid is to be adopted. what we see as the main added value of this proposal is that it introduces measures which are in the best interest of a child. it covers cases when a young person commits an act which society punishes by means of penal law; but the same society must not deprive him or her of the opportunity to start again, and this is in the best interest of society.
the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank my colleagues for their speeches and for the many expressions of appreciation for the agreement reached, and i hope to be able to count on their support and that of their political groups. i would like to thank commissioner jourová again for her attention to the directive, for her words here today and for the technical support provided by the commission. tomorrow we will vote on a text which establishes specific rights for children who are the subject of investigations and accused in criminal proceedings, and we will vote in the knowledge that we have contributed to the creation of a european area of criminal justice. it will be a piece of legislation which, together with others already adopted, will form part of the overall architecture of procedural rights, but above all it will be a directive aimed at bridging the gaps between the legal systems of the member states, taking into account the specific nature of children and their vulnerabilities in criminal proceedings, especially if they are children in difficult situations, and stating that the rights of children must be protected in all circumstances. i would like to conclude, mr president, with a personal note. this year marks 20 years of work in the field of juvenile justice and i must therefore say that i am particularly pleased to have been rapporteur for the report on this directive, which paves the way for the establishment of a fair juvenile process in the countries of the union.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the eu-andorra agreement on the automatic exchange of financial information for tax purposes, which aims to improve cooperation and compliance with tax obligations at international level. the agreement ensures that andorra applies measures equivalent to those contained in the eu savings tax directive, in accordance with the oecd procedures for the automatic exchange of financial account information. under the new agreement, as of 2018 and for information collected as of 1 january 2017, eu member states and andorra will automatically exchange information on financial accounts held in their territories by their respective residents, to address situations where a taxpayer seeks to conceal capital consisting of income or assets that are subject to tax evasion. i would like to stress that the agreement approved today is part of the wider context of cooperation between the eu and certain third countries in the field of taxation, in line with the oecd-g20 guidelines, in which parliament is constantly working towards greater transparency and fairness.
in writing. ‒ the european union and the principality of andorra signed an agreement on the automatic exchange of financial information for tax purposes to improve cooperation and compliance with international tax obligations. this is the fourth of a package of five agreements, covering switzerland, liechtenstein, san marino, andorra and monaco. although these agreements bring improvements over the status quo, they are still far from resolving in practice most of the existing problems with all these countries. on the basis of this agreement, the eu and the principality of andorra will automatically exchange information on the financial accounts of their respective residents, in order to step up efforts to combat tax fraud, tax evasion and avoidance, which the principality is seen as one of the most sensitive countries in these respects. i think this text is unsatisfactory because a more complete and thorough agreement could and should have been sought without leaving any easily circumvented legal gaps. for all these reasons i have decided to abstain.

in writing. ‒ the proposal for a directive on procedural guarantees for minors who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings is part of the process of strengthening the rights of suspects and accused persons promoted by the council since 2009. the data confirm that over 1 million children are subjected to criminal proceedings in europe each year, with treatment varying considerably from country to country. i felt it necessary to support the chinnici report because i believe it is essential to deal effectively with the issue of safeguards in legal proceedings by providing a common european model of due process for minors. the directive adopted requires member states to guarantee the inalienable right to be assisted by a defence lawyer by identifying deprivation of liberty as an extreme measure, to be imposed for a short period of time only. the text reiterates the need to ensure that children are held separately from adults, while strengthening the right to be accompanied by parents or other appropriate adults at hearings and at the various stages of the trial. it is a good proposal in general terms and it is a significant follow-up to the good italian experience in this area.

in writing. ‒ the text voted today is an important milestone in the final adoption of a directive which is a key part of the european package on procedural guarantees in the judicial field. the report stresses the importance of harmonising existing rules and establishing common minimum standards for the safeguards of a particularly specific category, namely children involved in criminal proceedings. given the profound diversity which currently exists in this area between the member states, i welcome a text which aims to bring about greater harmonisation within the union on such a sensitive subject, acting first in the interests of the child, as required by article 24 of the charter of fundamental rights of the union. the minimum standards and norms identified in the report are aimed at standardising and extending the level of protection of children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings within the eu, including the right of the child to a lawyer, to an individual assessment of the measures and penalties involved in the proceedings, to greater protection of privacy during the proceedings and to a detention regime separate from that of adults, aimed at facilitating their reintegration into society.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this document because i am convinced that the situation of procedural guarantees for children who are suspects or accused in criminal proceedings in europe must be substantially improved. the enormous diversity of the provisions in this field in the various national legal systems and the lack of the most basic procedural guarantees in some of them make it necessary to create a system of minimum guarantees which will allow, on the one hand, greater uniformity and, on the other, greater protection for children accused.
in writing. ‒ the european commission estimates that over 1 million children are subject to criminal proceedings in the eu each year, or 12% of all people involved in criminal proceedings in the same territory. research carried out at european level shows that, at present, the rights of minors at the various stages of the procedure are not sufficiently guaranteed within the union, and there are numerous cases of condemnation of states by the european court of human rights. the european parliament must help ensure that the right to the compulsory assistance of a lawyer in the case of minor offences is automatically guaranteed. there are no offences which do not have consequences for the child which justify disregard for his or her rights of defence. it is therefore for parliament to approve the proposal for a directive on 'procedural safeguards for suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings', which is part of the roadmap for strengthening the procedural rights of suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings adopted by the council on 20 november 2009, together with some measures already adopted and others currently under discussion.
in writing. ‒ currently, only 6 member states have specialised prosecutors for minors (belgium, the czech republic, greece, italy, luxembourg and the slovak republic) and 9 countries do not even have specialised courts. in some countries, the assistance of a lawyer is not guaranteed; in others, it is only possible in court and not in police stations. in other cases, the decision is referred back to the competent court. we therefore see no attempt to undermine the sovereignty of our member state. the report needs to ensure, through common minimum standards, the effective and sufficiently uniform enjoyment of the right to a fair trial by persons under the age of 18 at all stages of the proceedings. the report reflects the general approach and inspiration of the proposal, including the following highlights: the inalienable right to be assisted by a lawyer, in close connection with the right to legal aid and the right to an individual assessment. the report had our support and mr fontana's vote in favour in the libe committee, where it was adopted by a single vote against. i vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on procedural safeguards for minors who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings because the child is in a particularly vulnerable situation when detained. particular efforts are needed to prevent the deprivation of liberty of the child, given the risks to his physical, mental and social development and to his reintegration into society. deprivation of liberty must be a last resort and must be for the shortest possible period. with this measure we introduce the obligation for all european countries to recognize legal assistance to the child at all stages of the proceedings, an individual assessment of the child which takes account of his or her background and personality, separate detention between minors and adults, medical assistance and special training for judges who work in the field of juvenile justice.

in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the hübner report on the conclusion of the interinstitutional agreement on better law-making between the european parliament, the council of the european union and the european commission. this is an important text which aims to improve the planning, transparency and quality of the legislative production process. this updates the previous agreement of 2003, which did not provide for the institutional framework established by the lisbon treaty. the new agreement provides for an impact assessment of the legislation. the commission will not only cover economic, social and environmental aspects but will also assess the impact of the laws adopted on competitiveness, particularly in relation to regional realities and smes. as regards programming, at the beginning of each term of office, the three institutions will coordinate their efforts to define multiannual priorities, which will be followed by a similar process on an annual basis.

in writing. ‒ the european institutions have a number of tools to improve and simplify european legislation. the interinstitutional agreement on better law-making commits these institutions to cooperate together to better legislate and to ensure that eu policies and rules achieve their objectives with minimum cost and administrative burden. the european parliament should support and implement the interinstitutional agreement on better law-making and thereby strengthen cooperation with the european council and the european commission in order to improve the way the european union legislates and ensure that eu legislation better serves european citizens and businesses. this agreement will make the eu legislative process more transparent, open to input from stakeholders and easier to follow. it will also contribute to the assessment of the impact of eu law on small and medium-sized enterprises, local industry and citizens. the new agreement between the eu institutions will also aim to make cooperation between them easier and clearer.
in writing. - i abstained. the new interinstitutional agreement on better law-making and the attached memorandum of understanding on delegated acts contain practical arrangements, agreed between parliament, the council and the commission, for the conduct of the ordinary legislative procedure and the ensuing delegated and implementing acts. the main innovation compared with the previous eia is the introduction of a preventive impact assessment of each legislative proposal and more in-depth and timely ex post evaluations of existing legislation, with the ultimate aim of avoiding over-regulation and unnecessary burdens, with particular reference to smes. the commission also aims to ensure a more uniform and transparent application of delegated acts. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 26 to supplement this regulation by laying down detailed rules for the application of this regulation. the content and objectives of the iia are shared, apart from the well-known considerations about the inherent democratic deficit of the eu. it should be noted, however, that in the afco report 'the need for greater flexibility in the application of the eight-week period available to national parliaments to give a reasoned opinion on the non-compliance with the principle of subsidiarity', as underlined in paragraph 12, is in open contrast to the support shown for the 'one-fits-all' approach, because '1 costs less than 28' (paragraph 7) - in other words, the malevolent idea of the 'cost of non-europe'.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of this agreement, which aims to improve the way the eu legislates and to ensure that eu legislation delivers better services to citizens and businesses. this agreement will involve smes, local industry and citizens more closely in the decision-making process, in particular through the creation of a web portal to follow initiatives and new public consultations during the evaluation of existing policies or possible new proposals. a permanent platform for stakeholder dialogue is also being set up to involve business, civil society and social partners in the effort to reduce regulatory and administrative burdens. this agreement makes cooperation between the eu institutions easier and clearer. finally, measures are agreed to improve the exchange of views and information between parliament and the council as legislators. however, i believe that more work is needed, particularly as regards mutual access to information and meetings, so that we can ensure a real balance and equal treatment between legislators throughout the legislative process, while ensuring that the principle of loyal cooperation between the institutions is respected.

in writing. ‒ the interinstitutional agreement on better law-making is yet another confirmation of the commitment of parliament, the council and the commission to a clearer and more transparent legislative process. in writing. ‒ while the idea behind the interinstitutional agreement between the council, parliament and the european commission on better lawmaking is certainly shared, we cannot unfortunately be fully satisfied with the way in which the agreement was reached. the negotiator appointed by parliament was given a general mandate by the afco committee, but no guidelines were laid down for the individual chapters and the substantive issues. this has in fact left a very wide margin of discretion to the negotiator, reducing the prerogatives of the parliamentary committee. the agreement reached, while containing some good points, is still lacking in certain respects: firstly, there is no guarantee of greater transparency in trilogues, nor in delegated and implementing acts. it is also regrettable that the question of the control of lobbyists and of contacts between them and the institutions has not been dealt with in practice. finally, the opportunity to call for greater direct involvement of citizens in the decision-making process was lost. for these reasons, and as i am not entirely satisfied with the agreement reached, i shall refrain from approving this proposal for a european parliament decision.

in writing. ‒ in july 2004, philip morris international and the eu signed an agreement to combat counterfeiting and smuggling of cigarettes. the initiative provided for extensive product traceability and traceability procedures, which enabled the competent authorities to easily identify where genuine products were being diverted from authorised sales channels. while the agreement reduced cigarette smuggling, the market and regulatory environment have changed since then and the agreement with smes should not be renewed, extended or renegotiated. the commission's commitment to ratify the protocol on the fight against tobacco is undoubtedly an important step towards strengthening the legislation on this matter. for these reasons i voted in favour, considering it essential that the eu should take action to combat the practice of smuggling in order to protect the health of its citizens.
in writing. ‒ since 2004, the commission and the member states have negotiated agreements with tobacco producers to strengthen anti-smuggling and anti-counterfeiting measures. under the agreements, the producers would have to pay a collective contribution of €2.5 billion, in return for the eu ending legal proceedings against them caused by the loss of revenue from the illegal cigarette trade estimated at over €10 billion a year. i have serious doubts about the effectiveness of the agreement and have decided today to vote in favour of the joint resolution calling on the commission not to renew the agreement on tobacco with philip morris. the eu's path must be the one indicated by the 2014 eu tobacco directive, which provides for more effective tools to combat smuggling, such as a community traceability and monitoring system for cigarettes, in force from 2019.

in writing. - abstention from the vote. the eu has signed agreements with the four multinational tobacco companies to make them actively involved in the fight against smuggling. the first of these agreements in chronological order was concluded with philip morris international (pmi) in 2004 and expires this year. in its assessment report, which was submitted to parliament with considerable delay, the commission argues that, although the agreement has helped to bring about a sharp drop in smuggling of sme products (which is questionable), the volumes of smuggling have not decreased at all. it was agreed that bilateral agreements with producers were an outdated instrument and, moreover, considered by the who to be a potential source of conflicts of interest. the anti-smoking organisations claim that the renewal, extension or renegotiation of the agreement would allow the tobacco industry to maintain control over traceability and traceability through codentify, at a time when no independent safety assessment of the system (which is an integral part of the sme agreement) has yet been carried out. but there is also the risk of rendering traceability systems already in place at national level useless, unless they are reintroduced at eu level.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the resolution tabled by s&d, greens/efa and efdd to urge the european commission not to renew the anti-smuggling and anti-counterfeiting agreement with philip morris, which expires in july 2016. i am deeply concerned that the budget of the european anti-fraud office (olaf) is partly financed by the annual payments of the tobacco industry, as indicated in the agreements themselves, as this situation could lead to a conflict of interest. i have serious doubts about the real effectiveness of the agreement with philip morris in reducing smuggling, because the increase in sales of non-brand cigarettes, the so-called 'cheap white', immediately compensated for the decrease in sales of counterfeit brand cigarettes. rather than renewing agreements with philip morris, the commission should focus on implementing the 2014 tobacco directive, which provides for more effective tools to combat smuggling, such as a community traceability and monitoring system for cigarettes, in force from 2019. member states should also ratify a protocol adopted under the world health organisation framework convention on tobacco control, which provides for a similar requirement at global level and is expected to enter into force in 2022.

in writing. ‒ i opposed the decision not to renew the agreement between philip morris international (pmi) and the eu as this agreement was created to combat the smuggling of illicit products and therefore i considered its extension necessary. i believe that the renewal would not have created an inappropriate relationship between the eu and the tobacco industry, but on the contrary, an important coalition in an attempt to combat a common enemy, smuggling, which directly affects the health of our citizens and our economy. i also believe that the continuation of this agreement would represent an important step forward in the fight against tobacco, in which the eu is a world leader, in line with the position of the italian customs and monopolies agency which stresses that in the italian case the agreement has given good results in the past, particularly in the fight against smuggling.
in writing. ‒ the illicit trade in tobacco, in addition to leading to a substantial economic loss, contributes to the financing of the activities of international organised crime. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. i therefore vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ i spoke against the renewal of the agreement concluded in 2004 between the eu and philip morris international (pmi), which provides for the latter's commitment to cooperate with the european commission, specifically with the anti-fraud office (olaf), and with the member states to prevent its products from entering the channels of smuggling in europe and the rest of the world. the agreement, which expires in june 2016, should not be renewed because, as the evaluation report submitted by the commission shows, its primary objective - the reduction of smuggled products of smes - has been achieved, with an 85% decrease in the trade of illegal cigarettes. although further efforts are still needed before a general reduction in this phenomenon can be achieved, i believe that the fight against smuggling cannot be delegated to the tobacco industry but must be conducted on the basis of the legal instruments available, such as the who framework convention on tobacco control and the protocol on the elimination of illicit trade in tobacco products and tobacco products directive 2014/40 which introduces, in particular, a legal obligation for product traceability by companies in the sector.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on tobacco in the first place because i believe that the current agreements with the tobacco industry are a flagrant example of a complete lack of transparency. these agreements were concluded because the european commission took legal action against philip morris international and other companies, accusing them of smuggling cigarettes: a large proportion of the smuggled goods came directly from the farms producing them. philip morris has paid the member states one billion euros over 12 years, but we do not know how this revenue, and the revenue from fines for seizures of original material, has been used. the resolution therefore calls for these agreements not to be renewed, and also calls for an independent traceability system to be set up: at present, the same manufacturers own the system for tracing cigarette packets, so that controllers and controlled are the same. the resolution also calls on the commission to ratify the who protocol on the elimination of illicit trade in tobacco products and to deal with the issue of 'cheap whites', i.e. cigarettes which are illegal in europe and are sold on the black market, with serious damage to the health of citizens.
in writing. the european commission signed an agreement with the us giant philip morris (pmi) in 2004 which expires in july 2016 and could therefore be renewed. the aim of the agreement, worth over one billion euros, was to help combat cigarette smuggling by using the cooperation of the multinational tobacco company. however, it was found that a large proportion of the illicit goods came directly from the producing companies, which smuggled their own product from secondary sites where more was produced than was required by the legitimate market. the classic paradox where the controller and the controlled coincide. the eu institutions and tobacco and cigarette multinationals are thus becoming increasingly intertwined. doubts are being raised as to why the european commission has repeatedly delayed the publication of the evaluation of the cartel with the tobacco giant. i could only vote in favour of the resolution which, thanks to the action of the five star movement, will commit the european commission not to renew the agreement with philip morris. we in m5s have worked to get the whole of the european parliament to stand up for some of our most important battles: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products.

in writing. thalidomide is the pharmacologically active substance developed by the chemie grünenthal company in germany in the 1950s it was marketed as a tranquilizer and anti-nausea and was erroneously declared safe for use in pregnancy. it is estimated that over two million doses were distributed in 50 countries and under 40 different trade names. it was withdrawn from the market only in 1961, when its devastating effects on fetuses became clear. unfortunately, women treated with thalidomide gave birth to babies with severe congenital malformations of the limbs, namely amyloid or various degrees of focomelia, estimated to have affected at least 20,000 children. after more than 50 years, survivors are still trying to find a solution that will allow them to cover the costs of their physical and medical condition, which has unfortunately worsened over the years. nothing can erase what has happened, but i believe that providing effective support and assistance to the victims of thalidomide and their families is the least the european union can do.

the agenda includes a debate on the question with a request for an oral answer to the commission on the zika virus epidemic, by annie schreijer-pierik, matthias groote, boleslaw g. piecha, josé inácio faria, katerina konecná, martin häusling, piernicola pedicini, joëlle mélin, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (o-000030/2016 - b8-0119/2016) (2016/2584 (((rsp)).
president of the envi committee. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the zika virus epidemic began in brazil in may 2015 and has since spread to 40 countries. the virus has infected about four million people in south america. on 1 february 2016, the international health regulations emergency committee declared that the zika virus epidemic constitutes a public health emergency of international concern. experts agree that a causal link between zika virus infection during pregnancy and microcephaly in newborns is highly likely, although this has not yet been scientifically proven. unlike ebola, which is much more dangerous and requires human contact to spread, zika is transmitted through mosquito bites. that is why we have asked for this debate and the debate in the house with the european commission. the subject of our oral question is the request for an overview of the current situation regarding the outbreak and incidence of microcephaly in the union and the actual risk of transmission of zika virus infection in the european union. in this connection, we know that the vector, the aedes aegypti mosquito, is not currently active. but we also know that in the summer, and already in the spring if we think of the countries of southern europe, it will become active. in addition, the presence of the olympics in brazil should be considered, an event that, due to the already expected movement of large numbers of people, will and could generate the proliferation of the spread of the virus. in addition, when the rio 2016 event begins, there will be, due to climatic conditions, a greater development of mosquito populations, which are precisely the vectors of the disease. in view of this, the commission, envi intends to ask the commissioner what actions are being taken to prevent the spread of the disease in the european territory and whether the necessary measures have already been prepared to deal with a possible emergency, should this also occur in europe. i ask, for example, whether the commission considers that it is advisable for the health authorities in the union to cooperate with the transport sector in order to ensure the disinfection of cargo, cargo carriers, cabins and passenger compartments of aircraft coming from areas affected by the virus. i would also like to know whether it is possible to extend the use of insecticides and whether, as has been proposed, efforts will be made to sterilize mosquitoes to prevent their production by means of the so-called sterile male technique. as regards the financial part, i would ask the commissioner whether he considers the sum of eur 10 million made available to be sufficient to meet the scientific challenge posed by the virus and its neurological complications, and the need to develop diagnostic tests, vaccines and cures for the disease. finally, we know that the ema has organized a task force of experts in vaccines and infectious diseases to provide pharmaceutical companies with scientific and regulatory input for the development of drugs or vaccines against the virus. on this subject i would like to ask the commissioner where we are with the vaccine study, whether we are making progress and whether we can expect positive results in the short to medium term. as you can see, commissioner, a number of issues are being brought to the commission's attention in order to prevent, because we know very well that prevention is the best strategy to avoid damage to the health of european citizens and, above all, to reduce the possible effects of an infection such as that of the zika virus.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the scope of this epidemic leaves many questions unanswered. there is no solid scientific basis yet to explain the connection between zika virus and microcephaly, or even between zika virus and barré syndrome. it seems clear to us that diagnostic tests are still needed to reduce the number of dengue fever misdiagnoses and it is not yet clear whether the virus can also be transmitted through sexual contact or blood transfusion. yet, with all these undeniable uncertainties, the development of the usual vaccine is proceeding, even though we know that a complete vaccine coverage would not eradicate a virus that can be transmitted, mutating from mosquito to mosquito and even though we know that the time to test it is, in any case, too long. so let's avoid further and unnecessary enrichment of these pharmaceutical companies with a vaccine that is not a response to this epidemic and instead look at alternative strategies, such as the sterile mosquito technique, that would have a real and effective effect on the spread of the virus.
member of the commission.– mr president, on behalf of the commission, i have listened very carefully to this debate. it seemed to me that there were some recurring themes, themes of urgency, of comprehensiveness, and the importance of coordination, prevention and information all playing a vitally important role. i can say, on behalf of the commission, that we will certainly take all of those into account as we continue our action to address zika in the months to come. i do believe that our experience of past epidemics and the structures that we already have in place stand us in good stead to make an effective and swift response to developments. right now, as many honourable members have stressed, we need to focus on preparing for the summer and on finding effective vaccines and medicines, both to prevent and to treat zika virus infection. so far as the question about the sum of the money that we are able to make available is concerned, one part, as i have said, is to rapporteur.– mr president, the banking union is the most important step towards a genuine emu since the introduction of the euro. a single supervision and a single resolution involves a significant transfer of responsibility from euro area member states to the european institutions. this is necessary to ensure stability and restore confidence in our banks and in order to reduce and share risks by enhancing financial integration. such a transfer or responsibility requires, however, an appropriate level of parliamentary scrutiny, of which this report represents the first concrete expression. i would like, in this regard, to thank all the shadow rapporteurs for their excellent cooperation, as well as the secretariat and all the staff for their work. i also appreciate the transparent and open dialogue we had with the single supervisory mechanism (ssm), the single resolution mechanism (srm) and the commission. the report considers the establishment of the ssm a success, both from an operational point of view and in terms of supervisory quality. at the same time we identify some problems and margins of improvement in both areas. in particular, we underline the importance of effective coordination between micro and macro-prudential policies, as the ssm is fully part of the eu macro-prudential framework, the need for stabilisation of the supervisory and regulatory framework, as well as improving the comprehension among banks of a common supervisory approach underlying the concrete individual micro-prudential measures. we stress also the need for proportionality. the markets need clarity and predictability on the setting of capital requirements; this has not been the case with the maximum distributable amount (mda) threshold. the report says that the legislation’s lack of clarity on this point should not prevent the ssm from using a margin of flexibility in order to avoid too-rigid solutions that can negatively affect the at1 bond market. for this reason, we call for a legal clarification of the mda and the function of pillar two, which is to address only ‘bank specific’ risks. we welcome the note provided yesterday by the commission in order to start the review process, and we think that the ssm should take it fully into account, in particular where it makes a distinction between pillar two capital requirements and capital guidance. we support the revision of options and national discretions in order to achieve a homogenisation of practices and standards. we make also some specific comments on some of the issues which have been put into the consultation. further steps are necessary to reinforce supervisory scrutiny of banks’ financial activity, in order to improve the capacity to look beyond credit risk to all forms of bank risks, including an in-depth analysis of financial portfolios, especially level 3 assets. the report supports the bail-in principle and its implementation. at the same time we recommend that the various choices at the disposal of the board on the basis of the eu legislation be assessed carefully, including different resolution tools as an alternative to the liquidation of the bank, and to apply always the appropriate proportionality, fairness and flexibility which is in-built in the legislative framework, keeping in mind the importance of safeguarding financial stability and maintaining confidence in the banking system. finally, the report calls for the completion of the banking union, guarantee of deposits and a common backstop. parliament welcomes the recent package from the commission, the european deposit insurance scheme (edis) proposal on the one hand and the commitment to work on risk-reduction on the other. on the former, we are working in the appropriate legislative procedure format; on the latter, it is important to emphasise that risk reduction is a broad concept which refers to a number of different possible measures. on the most controversial, related to sovereign exposures, we take note of the work of the basel committee and consider that any possible change should carefully be assessed and, in any case, should be done in the medium-terms in the framework of international bodies (basel committee on banking supervision) and should not affect the financing capacity of member states and financial stability.

member of the commission.– mr president, thank you for the debate, which i think has covered a range of issues, some of them on the banking union. i think it is worth reminding ourselves, as mr von weizsäcker did, of this question of whether the glass is half-full or half—empty. i think it is a good opportunity to remind ourselves of how far we have actually come and to think of the process, for trust, i think this lies at the heart of how we are going to be able to address the work we need to do on banking union if we are to go forward. i think that underlines the approach we have taken with the edis proposal and the associated risk reduction communication, because we are going to have to build trust and take both sides of the equation forward together. i agree with the points that were made about the importance of implementing existing legislation and honouring commitments that have already been entered into. as i said before, there is progress being made on the transposition of that regulation. we return to it regularly in the ecofin council every time we meet and the member states are nearly there with that. on the question of sovereign exposure, which was raised by mr gualtieri in his remarks, i concur with the prudent line that i think was set out in his report on possible prudential treatments of sovereign exposures. our approach should be part of a coordinated effort at the global level and that issue is currently being discussed at the economic and financial committee and in the basel committee. any future commission action would obviously be informed by those discussions. the important issue of the backstop was also raised. member states agreed on an approach for bridge financing and have agreed that there needs to be an appropriate backstop by 2024. transaction regulation came into force last year and that is a big step forward for monitoring shadow banking. the mifid legislation will also play a role. i hope that we will be able to make some more progress on the money market funds file in the council where i think we have greater prospects of progress. obviously, i will stay alert to any emerging risks that there are on the shadow banking side. finally, one of the recurring themes there has been from all sides of the house is points made about proportionality and that does lie behind the thinking for having the call for evidence and wanting to look at the effect of the legislation that we have already passed, not to bring the architecture of that legislation –architecture like the banking union – into question, but to ask ourselves, as mr hayes said, whether we have got everything right and whether the legislation is working in the most effective way to encourage investment, make it possible for businesses to lend, make it possible for capital to flow to businesses that want to invest and grow. that issue of proportionality will be looked at as part of that call for evidence. it will also be looked at as part of our crr review and i think the need that we have to balance micro- and macro-prudential requirements is one that i have very much in the forefront of my mind. i am very grateful to mr gualtieri and the shadow rapporteurs for the report and for the work they have done for this debate. i look forward to future reports and i hope that we will be able to demonstrate more of the progress that i know colleagues are keen to see and that we keep up the pace on strengthening our banking system.
the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it was a lively debate, which touched on many aspects, and which should not, of course, make us lose sight of the fact that the main feature of the report and its fundamental purpose was to analyse in a very detailed and precise way the various aspects of the actual exercise of this first year of single supervision, to identify what worked but also what worked less well and which needs to be corrected. there are many specific proposals in this respect, as sven giegold has said, and we naturally expect the commission, the ssm, the srm - and i very much appreciate what the commission has said - the need to maintain the sme support factor are perhaps less passionate topics in a debate in the house than the great ideological disputes about bail-in, bail-out, the separation of the banks and all the other issues that we should be discussing, even though this discussion should be based on reality, on facts and a little less on ideology. so we must not lose sight of the fact that the report says that the rules must be respected but that at the same time the rules fortunately also contain the possibility of taking measures which do not have a negative effect on financial stability and this flexibility, which mr balz has mentioned, is a positive one. it is good that something is happening in germany where an institution is being set up which can prevent bail-in and in some cases even provide relief to bondholders. that's a good thing. we must welcome the intelligent use of the rules we have set ourselves, because i believe that financial stability is a primary good. it is also good to recall the facts, namely that the edis (euro-area wide deposit insurance scheme) does not provide for any use of taxpayers' money, and finally i very much welcomed the fact that the commissioner appreciated the cautious approach taken by the report to the question of sovereign debts, a question which should be dealt with only in the basle framework.
