author. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner andriukaitis, today's debate provides an opportunity to debate a subject which is very important to our citizens. on behalf of the envi committee, whose position i represent here, i would like to stress the need for mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance for certain foods. following a number of food scandals across europe, there is a growing sense of urgency to ensure clear information for consumers and greater transparency and accountability in the agri-food chain, and as direct representatives of the citizens we are making these demands our own through this resolution. specifically, the measure covers types of meat other than beef, pig, sheep, goat and poultry meat, meat in processed products, milk, milk used as an ingredient in dairy products, unprocessed foods, single ingredient products and ingredients representing more than 50% of a food. in fact, as a eurobarometer survey shows, in 2013 around 90% of citizens in the european union consider that the indication of origin for these foods is necessary and it clearly shows that this is one of the factors likely to influence consumer behaviour. the envi committee therefore considers that the obligation to indicate the origin on the label is essential to ensure transparency and traceability and to reassure and rebuild the trust of european consumers who ask for the indication of origin. on 20 may 2015, the european commission published a report on the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance, accompanied by a study on milk and other meats, which shows that the costs of mandatory origin labelling for milk used as an ingredient in dairy products increase in line with the complexity of the production process. the envi committee considers that these costs are overestimated and that the same study by the european commission suggests that some member states have overestimated the impact of mandatory origin labelling on their competitive position, as no clear explanation for the high expenditure forecasts provided by them has been found. the report which is to be voted on tomorrow therefore calls for the establishment of a european commission working party to further assess the report and its impact in order to determine whether these costs can be reduced to a level acceptable to businesses, especially small and mediumsized ones. the envi committee also stresses that the overall willingness of consumers to pay for information on origin is relevant. many consumer studies on wtp show that consumers are widely willing to pay more for information on the origin of the products they buy, although the european commission has told us that it is rather modest. before concluding, i would like to reiterate that the envi committee confirms its call on parliament to support the compulsory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance and calls on the commission to implement it by drawing up legislative proposals in the areas mentioned. it also urged the commission to submit legislative proposals to make the indication of the origin of meat in processed foods compulsory, in order to ensure greater transparency throughout the food chain and to better inform european consumers in the wake of the meat scandal and other cases of fraud. commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that it is our duty to give our european consumers complete and clear information about the origin of many of the foodstuffs that are part of our diet. it is a matter of sharing the goodness of a general principle which makes it possible to establish a system capable of enabling informed and transparent purchases. i would like to conclude by asking the commission to give us its views and i would urge that the political will of this parliament be respected, if supported by the majority of members, by preparing a number of sectoral legislative proposals, which we are of course prepared to deal with and analyse on a case-by-case basis and which will have to take account of the transparency and legibility of information for consumers, while at the same time allowing european companies to operate in an economically profitable way.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the obligation to label indications of origin provides guarantees for informed consumer choices and the opportunity for european producers and processors in the agri-food sector to compete better on the markets. in this connection, we note a real paradox: the lack of transparency and the opacity of the labelling situation create unfair competition mechanisms which violate the rules of the free market, and which are then used by the very opponents of the indication of origin on the label to highlight negative aspects of the indication of origin. a genuinely free market is based on transparency, it does not hinder but rewards production with high food safety standards. a genuinely transparent market does not encourage unfair competition, based on imports of low-cost agri-food products of dubious quality and origin. the commission's reports show that the costs of ensuring transparency in the food chain may prove too high and that consumers, although interested in such information, would not be willing to support it. however, these reports are incomplete and do not sufficiently take into account the positive aspects of the indication of the origin of products, such as increased consumer confidence in the products they consume and greater awareness of the choice. i therefore call on the commission to re-evaluate its proposal in the light of more objective studies and to give due weight to the benefits to consumers of the indication of origin. i would remind you that voluntary labelling schemes have had positive results in several member states both in protecting the right to information of consumers and for producers, who have no or little impact on production costs. in the face of the absurdity of the timidity shown by the commission, parliament is called upon to respond with clarity to the demands of the citizen-consumer.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the desire of the european citizens to know the origin of agri-food products is clear and legitimate and we as legislators must ensure that our consumers are given complete, transparent and non-distorting information. we already have legislation requiring the labelling of the origin of many foodstuffs, including all fruit and vegetables and almost all meat. we must now go a step further and extend the european obligation to other areas in a progressive manner. the sensitivity and the more advanced positions of some countries, such as italy, for example, can be an incentive to arrive at a single european legislation. our citizens are asking us to be informed and we must ensure that they have transparent labelling which informs them but does not condition their choices, as in the case of the 'traffic light' labelling system adopted by some british supermarkets.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank you for giving the commission the opportunity to have an exchange on a highly important issue: hydroelectric power. first and foremost, with 40% of all renewable electricity generation, hydropower is europe’s largest renewable energy resource. hydropower will continue to play a key role within the european energy union as it will contribute to the delivery of the three priority objectives of security, sustainability and competitiveness. the commission aims to give all electricity generators equal access to hydropower concessions. the granting of equal access will have a positive impact on investments, on local communities, thanks to higher fees paid by concession holders, on the integration of hydropower in the electricity market and ultimately, on consumers. the commission is well aware of the economic, legal, social and environmental aspects of hydropower generation. member states remain, in principle, free to design their models for the exploitation of hydroelectric plants. we do not question the member states’ competence to impose relevant obligations on hydropower operators when granting hydropower concessions. in this way, member states can strike a balance between competition requirements and other legitimate interests. however, member states must respect the relevant european union law, for instance when a member state decides to exploit those plants via concessions, european union public procurement rules need to be respected. this ensures not only an adequate level of competition but also equal treatment and transparency among the economic operators. in this context, european union public procurement rules are infringed when the initial duration of a hydroelectric concession is extended to the benefit of the incumbent concession holder without due justification. the applicable european union law may be different depending on the approach chosen, but that does not necessarily exclude the operation of hydropower generation from the scope of european union law. where applicable, national hydroelectric concession regimes should respect european union energy rules, such as the electricity directive, as well. indeed, competitive procedures for hydropower concessions and fair treatment of economic operators are important for a well-functioning energy market. finally, when granting hydropower concessions, the eu member states may be subject to eu competition rules, namely antitrust and state aid. a member state that grants hydropower concessions to a dominant public company may infringe antitrust rules when this has anti-competitive consequences by creating unequal conditions of competition allowing the dominant public company to maintain or strengthen its dominant position on the relevant electricity market. the granting of hydropower concessions may qualify as state aid if several conditions are met: if state resources are involved, a selective advantage has been granted to certain companies in the relevant electricity market and there is an effect on trade and a distortion of competition. first, state resources have to be involved, for example, in the form of state revenues or fees that could be foregone. second, a selective advantage has to be granted to certain companies over their competitors in the relevant electricity market. third, there must an effect on trade and a distortion of competition, which is likely to be the case since electricity is sold across member states on competitive markets.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have two very specific points to make (the timetable forces me to be very practical and simple). in europe the commission needs to know there are many ways of awarding hydroelectric concessions: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. and then there are also countries where tenders are held regularly, so that at the end of the concession period, there is a subsequent tender. there is a legal and economic problem in these countries which the commission has apparently not taken into account properly, because if the depreciation of investments lasts longer than the concession, it is normal that there is a residual depreciation at the end of the concession. the successful tenderer will therefore have to pay the remaining depreciation to the previous concessionaire. it is a very simple economic and legal concept. the commission did not understand this and therefore intervened by punishing countries which applied this rule, which is a rule of transparency and competition. so i think it is right to support those who invest, but it is also right to support those who, through free competition, decide to guarantee investors the normal rules of the market. it is good that the commission is aware of this.

in writing. ‒ the european union has been fighting crossborder tax avoidance, tax competition and aggressive corporate tax planning for years. these are issues that have become increasingly important not only in europe but also in the world and therefore require more effective legislation, in line with the growing importance of the challenges to be addressed. the rosati report, which i supported with my vote, identifies mandatory automatic exchange of tax information as the key to curbing tax avoidance and tax competition. under the new legislation, multinational companies will be required to provide country-by-country reporting in accordance with a standardised model from 2017 onwards, if their total consolidated turnover exceeds eur 750 million. member states will be required to make this report available to the other countries of the union, through an automatic exchange procedure. a crucial role should also be played by the commission, which, with full access to the shared information, could assess whether tax practices comply with community state aid rules.
in writing. ‒ the report on the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the tax field, which i supported with my vote, is acceptable and does not present any particular criticisms.
in writing. ‒ the problems of crossborder tax avoidance and evasion, which generate harmful tax competition and distort competitiveness, have taken on considerable proportions, becoming one of the main sources of concern at the global and european level. to address this, the european parliament and the other eu institutions have repeatedly called for greater transparency and automatic exchange of information in tax matters, and for measures and mechanisms to curb this phenomenon, such as country-by-country reporting for certain multinational companies. i voted in favour of the resolution adopted today, as it calls for the strengthening of the existing instruments in this field and argues for the need to identify new mechanisms to combat unfair or aggressive tax practices and thus reduce the incidence of the phenomenon within the union.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this document because i believe that it is important to establish a mandatory automatic exchange of information in the tax field between all member states in order to combat the increasing phenomena of tax evasion, aggressive tax planning and harmful tax competition. this system has the advantage of making the control of the tax authorities more effective and the whole community will benefit from this.
in writing. ‒ it is unacceptable that some eu member states or some of their dependent territories do not share the eu's fight for tax justice and against tax evasion and corruption. the automatic sharing of information between the member states of the union is a necessary and fundamental step towards tax harmonization and justice within the union and in the fight against the evasion of large capital holders. that is why we must firmly support this decision, as well as any effort to combat tax injustice within the european union and its member states.
in writing. ‒ the challenge posed by crossborder tax avoidance, aggressive tax planning and harmful tax competition has taken on considerable proportions and has become a major concern in the union and globally. the commission proposal clarifies the country-by-country reporting arrangements for multinational enterprises and calls for the information collection centre to be included. i would stress that on the one hand, a greater role for the commission in tax matters will affect one of the last prerogatives of the member states, but on the other hand it is plausible that the monitoring of tax evasion at community level by large multinational companies will find a central coordination of the information provided by the national authorities. i also took into account the possible political significance of the vote in the light of the recent incidents involving several multinational companies in the eu, and i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the amendment to the directive on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation which defines the scope and conditions for the mandatory automatic exchange of information on country-by-country reporting. the proposal aims to put a stop to crossborder tax avoidance, aggressive tax planning and tax competition harmful to the european union by introducing a transparency obligation requiring multinational groups of companies located in the eu or with operations in the eu, whose total consolidated revenues are equal to or greater than eur 750 000 000, to report country by country. the competent authority of the member state which received the return will then communicate that return, by automatic exchange, to any other member state in which one or more constituent entities of the multinational enterprise group are resident for tax purposes or are subject to tax for activities carried out through a permanent establishment. i welcome the criteria introduced concerning the information to be exchanged and the imposition of a reporting deadline of 12 months from the last day of the reference tax period of the multinational group.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report in question because, although the final text for the plenary had some criticisms, our requests to increase the level of publicity and transparency of the data collected by the commission were subsequently accepted.
in writing. ‒ i therefore voted in favour of this report because i think it highlights the basic premises for effectively combating tax fraud, a phenomenon that is dangerously increasing.
in writing. ‒ in the face of recent news of the global proportions that fraud, tax evasion and avoidance have assumed, european solutions to tackle this problem have become a priority. that is why i voted in favour of the european parliament's resolution which strengthens the european commission's proposal on the automatic exchange of information in the tax field. i voted in favour of greater transparency in taxation throughout the european union. i believe that the automatic exchange of tax information between multinational companies and national authorities is an important step in facilitating the work of national tax administrations in monitoring the profits of multinational companies, in order to verify that taxes are paid in the country where those profits are made. to that end, it is important that the tax authorities of the member states have access to complete and relevant information and that that information is exchanged both between the tax authorities of the member states and with the european commission.

in writing. ‒ i supported this proposal as it will introduce a much needed directive to combat major tax evasion and avoidance; the proposals aim to focus on multi-national enterprises with large assets in several countries. i think this is a good and important part of the proposal as it is the multi-national enterprises that have the means and infrastructure to avoid taxes on a grand scale. it is important that we keep red-tape and bureaucracy for medium and smaller-sized companies as well as individual citizens to minimum and in this regard i welcome the proposal’s focus and restriction on the ‘country by country’ reports to major multi-national enterprises with assets over eur 750 000 000.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the ep resolution on the amendment of the proposal for a council directive on the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation, because i strongly supported, first of all, the explicit extension of the scope of the automatic exchange of information to combat not only tax fraud but also the equally important phenomenon of tax evasion. it is essential for the union that tax rules are designed in such a way as not to undermine growth or investment or to constitute a competitive disadvantage for companies in the union, nor to increase the risk of double taxation; it is also essential that such rules are designed to minimise the administrative costs and burdens for companies. in line with the important work of investigating the phenomenon of tax rulings, i supported the reference to the ep resolution of 25 november 2015 on tax rulings and other measures similar in nature or effect, to the parliament's report on the proposal for a directive on the encouragement of long-term shareholder engagement and to directive 2013/34/eu on corporate governance. member states are now able to tax the profits of large multinational groups and ensure that they are taxed where they are produced.
in writing. i support the report as it stands. the ep, referring to its econ and taxe reports, called for greater transparency on tax information to counteract aggressive tax planning, and for the introduction of country-by-country reporting (cbcr) for multinational groups of companies. the draft provides for the amendment of directive 2011/16/eu on administrative cooperation in which member states do not provide for reciprocal exchange on a country-by-country basis; the commission has also concluded that the measures provided for in this decision are in accordance with the opinion of the committee established by article 15 (1) of regulation (eu) no 182/2011.
in writing. ‒ as the world economy becomes increasingly interconnected, there is a need for more capacity to control multinational groups in the single market. so it is time for a unified system for the exchange of information in the union so that businesses and member states can work more efficiently. i have supported this report because i believe that everyone will benefit from its initiatives.
in writing. ‒ we welcome the report on the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the tax area, as it allows the union to make progress in the harmonisation of the regulatory framework necessary to achieve, in the near future, the harmonisation of tax regulation. this report focuses in particular on the tax status of multinationals and the need for greater transparency. the starting document for the parliamentary debate is the oecd beps text, which identifies the legislative procedures needed to strengthen the tax union and the exchange of tax information between eu countries. the report also encourages the use and sharing of country-by-country reporting (cbcr) for multinationals. the beps plan is a strategy that aims to reduce and in some cases even eliminate the inconsistencies in european tax systems that allow some companies to artificially shift profits to where only a small part of the company is present, which often does not generate output, simply because there are incentives that allow them to reduce their tax contribution to the european economy. the beps plan has gained worldwide relevance since it was signed by the g20 finance ministers at the shanghai conference last february.
in writing. - on the proposal of my colleague, i would like to say yes. tax planning and competition are particularly aggressive and damaging to the european union today. therefore, greater transparency in this area, through the exchange of information on the revenues, profits and capital of multinational enterprises, is seen as essential. i would therefore vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution because it is a priority for the union and its member states to act decisively in the face of the challenge posed by fraud and tax evasion, which have now reached intolerable proportions. in order to ensure the proper functioning of the internal market and to counter aggressive tax planning, greater transparency with regard to tax information is urgently needed and in this regard the automatic exchange of information is an important step. the instruments and mechanisms established by directive 2011/16/eu need to be strengthened to achieve this objective and to counter unfair tax practices in the field of business taxation: the aim is to promote a european and international standard for tax transparency. this directive on administrative cooperation in the field of taxation already provides for the mandatory automatic exchange of information in a number of areas, but its scope needs to be extended to achieve the mandatory automatic exchange of reports between member states, which is not yet provided for in the current legal framework. the commission should then have access to the information exchanged in order to ensure compliance with the relevant competition rules.
in writing. ‒ the proposal will oblige multinational companies with total consolidated revenues of eur 750 million or more to report on a country-by-country basis in the member state where the group's main parent entity is resident for tax purposes. this member state will then have to share this information with the other member states in which the company operates. the directive will also set deadlines of 12 months for reporting after the end of the fiscal year and a further three months for the automatic exchange of information. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. i believe that in order to assess whether tax practices are in conformity with community state aid rules, the commission should have full access to the information shared between the different national tax authorities. at european level we must promote virtuous tax behaviour in order to ensure equity and social justice. i therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the draft directive on which this report focuses concerns administrative cooperation and the exchange of information in tax matters within the union. i voted in favour of certain amendments to the original report which aim to make it compulsory for member states' administrations to exchange information and to promote the need not to undermine the competitiveness of union enterprises through the risk of double taxation or additional administrative costs.
in writing. ‒ we did not vote in favour of the latest draft directive presented by the european commission, as it still contains many criticisms. we asked for the data to be made public and transparent, but the majority still preferred to keep it confidential. in fact, the multinationals subject to reporting (less than 10%) will only have to submit a limited number of tax data, leaving out important information (for example where subsidiaries, public subsidies, assets, etc. are located) and distorting the taxation calculation. the key issue, the one concerning the banks, is not addressed. the banks are not mentioned in the draft resolution. there is no form of regulation for banks which are crucial in ensuring effective tax transparency. recent scandals like the panama papers and swissleaks show who the real drivers of the great tax evasion and avoidance machine are. with this proposal, it is clear that the european commission wants to protect the big tax evaders and the powerful instead of helping to create a fair and transparent tax system.
in writing. this proposal for a directive is unfortunately a timid step towards real transparency and a tough fight against tax avoidance, which the commission has promised in words after the recent tax scandals. the creation of an automatic mechanism for the exchange of information is an essential part of this, but it is clearly not enough to put an end to the opacity, inefficiency and inequality of the present system. the proposal lacks any really strong and credible measures: the problem of banks - through which all legal and illegal financial flows pass - which, as emerged from swissleaks and the panama papers, played a central role in supporting the great evasion, is not raised in the slightest, and sanctions are obviously not envisaged. in addition, the transparency rules on the information that multinational companies are required to report on their activities in each country in which they operate, so-called country-by-country-reporting, will apply only to companies with revenues exceeding eur 750 million, i.e. only 10% of all multinational companies operating in europe, and these companies will also be able to benefit from exemptions that allow certain information to remain confidential. it is scandalous, considering the scale of the phenomenon of tax evasion and the companies involved. for these reasons i could not support this report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the tax field. at present, member countries do not share information on taxes paid by multinational groups. the report suggests that each member country should be required to report on the taxes paid by multinationals. i am convinced that this report lays the foundations for a more transparent tax system and that transparency is the first weapon to combat tax evasion.
in writing. ‒ the report on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2011/16/eu as regards the mandatory automatic exchange of information in the field of taxation, known as dac4, was voted on today. the challenges posed by tax evasion and avoidance, aggressive tax planning and tax competition have called for increasing transparency of information through the introduction of country-by-country reporting for multinational companies. the previous legislative framework (directive 2011/16/eu) was revised with the entry into force of the recent directive 2015/2376/eu which introduced the automatic and mandatory exchange of information from 2017. although the final text gives the commission a greater role, there are still major shortcomings in terms of publicity and transparency. in fact, the reference to the publication of information online was not accepted by the other political groups. another critical point is that sensitive data can benefit from confidentiality. the amendment calling for the application of the public corporate tax credit to all large companies and not just to multinationals with revenues of more than eur 750 million, or only 10-15% of all multinationals operating in europe, was unfortunately not passed.

in writing. ‒ the european union is the largest market for fish products in the world, but a number of studies have confirmed that there is a very high rate of mislabeled fish, much of which is directed at the food and catering sector. the reduction of food fraud and mislabelling must be a priority, which is why i have decided today to vote in favour of the joint resolution on the traceability of fishery and aquaculture products tabled in the european parliament. clear, transparent and comprehensible information on fishery products should be provided to all consumers by activating mechanisms that allow species to be identified with certainty, including the use of methods such as dna barcodes. the commission should aim at the creation of a european-wide eco-labelling scheme, funded through the european maritime and fisheries fund, correcting the confusion caused by the current labelling obligation based on zones and sub-zones defined by fao.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this resolution today to express my serious concern about the alarming cases of mislabelling of fish which have given misleading information to european consumers. the replacement of one fish species by another, cheaper and less valuable, is nowadays not too difficult: the high number of intermediaries between catching and sale, the increasingly widespread processing of the product, an apparently flawless traceability and the fact that 65% of the fish consumed in europe is imported with less quality controls have made the trap easy. i therefore call on the commission and the member states to strengthen controls and to review both the functioning of the fisheries chain and the legislation on fish labelling. the effectiveness of the genetic barcode as a tool for tracing fishery products should also be better exploited. this innovative method allows the identification of fish species with a far higher degree of reliability than all other diagnostic methods previously used. it is therefore essential to create a european network against food fraud in the fisheries sector, proposing a wider use of dna testing to prevent any kind of fraud.

in writing. ‒ mekong pangasius, caught in some of the world's most polluted waters, is turned into herring or cod on restaurant tables, or senegalese sole, which is easily turned into soleola for the unsuspecting european consumers sitting at the table. this is what recent studies reveal, reporting numerous cases of "fish fraud": the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem. these are clear cases of mislabelling, apparently widespread in europe, caused by misleading information and an ineffective system of control over the traceability of products. now, as the resolution i fully supported underlines, a strong commitment is needed from the member states and the union to put in place a better and more effective labelling system that ensures the full traceability of fishery products from the moment they are caught to the moment they reach our citizens' tables. responsible and above all conscious consumption is a social and food choice which every european citizen has the right to exercise: the union must therefore ensure that clear, transparent and complete information is provided on the origins and species of all food products, including fishery products.
in writing. a number of worrying cases of mislabelling of fish, revealed by dna analysis of 280 fish samples by ngos, showed that about one third of the fish analysed were mislabelled. this is a very bad practice and needs to be tackled, both in the case of errors in the production chain and, obviously more strongly, in the case of outright fraud to the detriment of consumers. i voted in favour of this resolution which sets out a series of recommendations and actions to be implemented at european and member state level to achieve better control of fishery products, consumer protection and the protection of our seas, which are increasingly at risk from illegal fishing practices and over-exploitation of resources. the introduction of a union eco-label for fishery and aquaculture products could be a first step towards improving traceability and providing transparent information to consumers.

in writing. ‒ china is currently the european union's second largest economic partner. the member states have always sought to establish economic relations based on mutual respect and fair and loyal cooperation, including in the economic field. the proposal to grant china market economy status has, however, raised a number of concerns. the main doubts were related to the likely harmful consequences for the european market and, secondly, to the strong state influence on prices and products which characterises the chinese economy. for these reasons i voted in favour of the resolution in which parliament calls on the commission to take due account of the concerns expressed in this connection.
in writing. ‒ the people's republic of china and the european union are among the world's largest trading partners, with a daily trade volume of over one billion euros. the joint motion for a resolution on china's market economy status, which i voted on in parliament today, tackles the thorny issue of whether the asian country should be granted market economy status in the period after 11 december 2016. section 15 of the protocol of accession of the prc to the wto already provides for non-standard methodologies to ensure price comparability which may be applied beyond that date. parliament called on the commission not to grant china unilateral mes until it had met the five criteria adopted by the eu to define such status. the commission has already identified the major social, economic and environmental consequences of chinese overcapacity in the eu and therefore calls on the commission to develop a common strategy in the wto to prepare appropriate anti-subsidy and anti-dumping measures compatible with the international regulatory framework.
in writing. ‒ china is not a market economy: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i believe that the joint motion for a resolution, unlike the one we have tabled, lacks a clear and explicit call not to grant china market economy status, and for that reason i did not think it appropriate to support it with my vote.
in writing. ‒ the eu and china are two of the world's largest trading entities and highly relevant partners to each other, with a daily trade volume of over €1 billion. it is clear that eu-china trade relations, like all other trade relations, are of fundamental and strategic importance to both realities and we must be aware of this in every decision we take. however, we must also be realistic and say clearly that china is not currently a market economy. in view of the imminent expiry of the clause in section 15 of the protocol of accession of china to the wto, parliament, in the resolution we are adopting today, stresses the importance of taking timely and realistic decisions. state intervention in the chinese economy is still very strong and contributes to a large extent to price formation, preventing a dumping margin calculation based on the conventional methodology normally applied in market economies. it is not a question of raising protectionist barriers, but of protecting our industry from unfair competition until the conditions for truly fair and sustainable trade are created.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this document because i believe that granting china market economy status (mes) is not only extremely dangerous from an economic point of view, especially in view of the current state of the european continent's economy, but also presents several criticisms from a legal and political point of view, given that china, given the enormous state interference in the economy, is certainly not a market economy.
in writing. ‒ since 2001, the people's republic of china has been a member of the wto (world trade organisation) with the status of 'economy in transition' and therefore not yet entitled to market economy status (mes). from the point of view of trade defence, the chinese system is generally inadequate for the purpose of met. the central government, in fact, directs the economy with the intent of creating national champions. the enterprises, often under state control, have access to cheap raw materials and capital, thus altering trade flows and the competitive environment. the main demands made in the resolution, which reiterates its opposition to the granting of market economy status to china, are for greater involvement of the other institutional actors, coordination with the main trading partners and a call for a different system for the calculation of dumping.
in writing. ‒ today's vote concerns the resolutions of the political groups on china's market economy (mes) status. the question of the esm is in fact about the interpretation of the protocol on china's accession to the world trade organization. it contains a section, number 15, which is the subject of intense political and legal controversy. this document allows wto countries to consider imports from china as coming from a non-market economy country and therefore subject to much higher duties (around 30% of the value of the product). according to all observers, including trade commissioner malmström, china has not become a market economy in the meantime. despite this evidence, however, the importing countries of northern europe and multinational companies would strongly like the asian giant to be granted market economy status. this would mean that much lower duties of around 6% could be applied to chinese products. a widespread network of small and mediumsized enterprises and workers' unions is working hard, however, to avoid this tragic scenario.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution today to avoid unconditional recognition of china's market economy status. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment. for example, china's steel overproduction alone is now greater than the total steel production of the entire european industry. i ask the commission to take due account of the concerns expressed in the eu by industry, trade unions and the various stakeholders about the consequences for employment in the eu. whatever the eu decides, it will need to think of a 'plan b' which includes equivalent trade defence measures to counter unfair competition practices. the commission must strengthen the effectiveness of its anti-dumping tool in order to ensure a level playing field for the european industry with china, in full compliance with wto rules. i stress the importance of the eu's strategic partnership with china, in which trade and investment play a key role, and i therefore invite the commission to make proposals to protect europe's interests by identifying a third way of finding a solution that satisfies both sides.
in writing. ‒ china has joined the world trade organisation with a protocol that specifically regulates its status and treatment with other global trading partners. the protocol, which provided for the non-automatic recognition of china's market economy status, expired in january 2016, raising a number of concerns for single market member states. china is the european union's second largest economic partner and the member states have always sought to establish economic relations based on mutual respect and fair and loyal cooperation. however, it notes that the chinese economy is still characterised by strong governmental influence and a non-competitive situation between economic actors. for these reasons, i voted in favour of the resolution in which parliament calls on the commission to take due account of the fears expressed in this connection and not to grant china market economy status.
in writing. ‒ granting china market economy status would allow the country in question to trade more easily and therefore allow its products to circulate more freely in our european common market. i voted in favour of this report to express my disagreement with the granting of market economy status to china. i think it is too dangerous not only for europe but especially for italy, because most of the time chinese products do not meet our standards of quality and safety in production. i think that china must first ensure a better level of human rights and protection at work, and greater reciprocity with european products. my intention is to defend the italian economy from the threat of unfair competition, which is why i voted in favour of denying them that status. before allowing trade partnerships, it is essential that there be a fair trading basis in full compliance with our european standards which best protect the quality, traceability and safety of our products, which are so much envied in the world.
in writing. ‒ today, the european parliament took a strong stand on trade policy, deciding not to bow to chinese pressure and asking the commission to conduct trade negotiations with the country of the rising sun without being conditioned by deadlines (december 2016) and unilateral positions. china cannot be granted market economy status as it has not yet carried out reforms to meet the five criteria required by the european union. with the resolution we have adopted today in this house we have defended our industry which could have suffered serious economic, social and environmental repercussions, as demonstrated by the recent negative impact on the steel industry already weakened by unfair chinese competition. to revive european trade policy we need to protect our businesses through fair trade relations based on mutual respect and fair cooperation.
in writing. ‒ recognising china's market economy status would have very serious consequences for europe and its industry. one of the fundamental problems with the recognition of china's market economy (mes) status is that it opens up a negotiation "downwards" of european standards and principles. the negotiations on wto recognition will be conducted by the european commission and the final decision will have to be approved in strasbourg by the european parliament and the council (the member states). we can therefore oppose the granting of mes to china if we all put the right pressure on the various political groups and governments in the member states. steel, mechanical engineering, chemicals, ceramics, bolting, paper, footwear, textiles and furniture are some of the sectors at risk from the recognition of the sme to china. in view of the very important problems which recognition of the status of a market economy would entail, i therefore vote against. it is essential that the european parliament bases its trade relations on fair terms, in full compliance with wto rules, on mutual respect. i shall vote against the motion for a resolution.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the assumption of the recognition of the status of a market economy to china. the country continues to promote aggressive economic policies based on subsidies and dumping, which violate the rules of the free market and put our enterprises and our production system in serious difficulty. the government finances entire sectors of production, allowing products to be exported at costs far below their real costs. a practice of unfair competition which is insidious and harmful to other economies, which are flooded with goods at prices which are outside any market logic. this is putting the european fabric of production in great difficulty, and is taking its deepest roots, especially in countries such as italy, which has always based its capacity for growth on the development of manufacturing. first of all, we must ensure that china respects the essential rules of international trade and transparency in economic relations. only then will it be possible to build solid relations of cooperation which will be beneficial to our economy and to that of china.
in writing. china is not a market economy as it does not meet the five criteria set by the eu to define market economies. granting china market economy status could have devastating consequences for the european market, for employment (3.5 million jobs would be lost) and a decline in gdp of 1 to 2%. a number of manufacturing sectors would be affected, in particular steel, ceramics, textiles and technology. it is necessary to reformulate the trade defence instruments of the european union in order to ensure a level playing field for eu industry with china and other trading partners, in accordance with wto rules. one proposal would be to quantify the carbon content of products and to set it as a percentage of vat, a mechanism that could actually make european industries more competitive thanks to the lower co2 emissions of its production compared to those of the asian giant. i voted yes.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution against the recognition of china's market economy status. while agreeing with the eu's need to explore new trade opportunities, it is clear that there is no free market in china. the state intervenes heavily to determine the prices of goods, and to totally condition the market. whole sectors of the european economy, from steel to textiles to footwear, are already suffering from the arrival of huge quantities of cheap chinese products, and to grant this status at the present time would be a death blow to thousands of european companies and their workers.

in writing. ‒ the european parliament takes a strong stance against the risks of trade and social dumping that chinese competition could pose. i support the text negotiated by the political groups; it is important to make a joint effort to accompany globalisation and international trade by introducing high standards of social protection and respect for rights.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the ep's non-legislative joint resolution on eu-china relations and the status of a market economy because i strongly shared the need, which the s&d group has expressed, to open a public debate on this important and rightly so important issue for the future of the european union, european industry and workers. china is not a market economy as it currently stands, because it meets only one of the five criteria of the wto rules on international trade. in tackling this problem, the rules of international trade intersect with those of the protection of labour, of european industry, particularly manufacturing, and of consumer rights. it would be shortsighted and harmful, however, if we were to tackle the problem by considering only the needs of the latter at the expense of the workers. because then we would end up endorsing phenomena such as social and environmental dumping and unfair competition. europe needs a genuine european industrial policy more than ever, and that is the crux of the problem. it needs it not to protect itself but to re-create conditions for sustainable growth and development and to continue to play a leading role in world trade.
in writing. ‒ china is and remains an important strategic and trade partner for europe, but it is not a market economy. and it will not be until it has met the five criteria set by the eu that define market economies. we have therefore adopted this resolution almost unanimously, which, although not a legislative resolution, will serve as a guide for the commission in presenting its proposal. our aim is to protect european companies from unfair competition and from any dumping which would have repercussions not only on our economy but also on the environment and society. for this reason we have asked the commission to exclude the automatic granting of market economy status to china and to maintain the current anti-dumping measures in line with wto rules. finally, we called on the council to reach agreement with parliament quickly on the modernisation of the european union's trade defence instruments.
in writing. ‒ the trade relationship between the european union and china is very intense. china is the eu's second largest trading partner, while the eu is china's largest trading partner. the failure to consider beijing a 'market economy' does not mean that we are adopting a protectionist attitude towards this important partner; it simply means meeting the five criteria set by the eu to define market economies. for china, these criteria are far from being met, given the current level of state influence on the economy. the commission considers that the measures in question are not imputable to the state and that the commission has not found that the measures in question constitute state aid. the commission therefore concluded that the chinese imports were not causing injury to the union industry. the wto protocol is, however, ambiguous on the question of the recognition of market economy status after 15 years. action is therefore needed to protect european competition and to safeguard our companies against possible economic, social and environmental dumping. we therefore call on the commission to exclude automatic recognition in the future proposal.
in writing. ‒ regarding the question put to parliament whether or not china is a market economy, i would like to point out that, despite being a member of the world trade organisation since 2001, china still does not meet the criteria that are the basis of a competitive economy. i think that the expiry of the anti-dumping measures is one of the few instruments which can support the production of european products and prevent a loss of jobs. i therefore believe that the commission must ensure that china is committed to respecting the rules of free trade. i would therefore support the position of my group.
in writing. ‒ when china joined the wto 15 years ago, precise rules were established to prevent the economies of other wto members from being penalised by unfair competition practices by chinese producers. the forecast was that by the end of 2016, china would become a market economy. unfortunately, china is still far from having implemented all the reforms necessary to be able to call itself a market economy. the rules for the protection of industry in other countries must therefore continue to apply. the widespread and persistent social, environmental and commercial dumping practices of china would jeopardize the future of the entire european manufacturing industry. millions of jobs and a key share of european gdp are at stake. the s&d group is in favour of free trade, but this presupposes that all firms compete on an equal footing. we are not protecting ourselves, nor is this a vote against china. china, however, is not yet a market economy. i am glad to see that, despite initial reservations, all the main political groups have finally decided to join our position.
in writing. ‒ on 11 december 2016, the member countries of the world trade organization (wto) are to decide whether to grant china the so-called market economy status (mes). such recognition would give the asian giant access to all wto regulated markets. the debate requested this week, with the vote on motions for resolutions, was requested to discuss with the commission the position that the eu will have to take in that circumstance. china is not an ordinary economy and it is well known that many manufacturing sectors do not meet minimum standards for the protection of workers and the environment. moreover, china's overcapacity and the resulting low-priced exports are already having a severe social, economic and environmental impact in the eu, especially in the eu steel sector. we must protect european industry and guarantee the employment of our citizens. while not forgetting the importance of the eu-china partnership and the chinese market, which has been the main engine of profitability for a number of eu industries and brands, i voted against the motion for a resolution because i believe that the eu should not recognise china as an emu.
in writing. ‒ in the delicate debate on the recognition of china's market economy status, i voted in favour of this joint motion, which expresses the position of the epp group and the requests of the italian delegation in particular. it brings together a very large majority of parliament in a clear message to the commission: mes cannot be granted to china without taking into account the criteria established by the eu itself to define a market economy. as china does not meet these criteria, it cannot be considered as a market player in the same capacity as europe. the resolution therefore calls for the legitimate defence of european industry, not against the market but in accordance with the rules of the market. this means protecting the free market, european companies and thousands of jobs at the same time. the resolution also has the merit of presenting a realistic proposal to deal with the problem, to be implemented within the limits allowed by the protocol of accession of china to the wto; in fact, it calls on the commission to use a non-standard methodology for the determination of price comparability for chinese exports as long as china does not meet the eu criteria of a genuine market economy.

in writing. ‒ 84% of consumers believe that the origin of milk, sold as such or used as an ingredient in dairy products, should be indicated. as regards processed meat, the commission report of 17 december 2013 shows that 90% of consumers want to know the origin of the meat in processed foods. the commission nevertheless concludes that maintaining labelling on a voluntary basis may be the most desirable solution for the above products. according to the study accompanying the report on milk and non-bovine meat, the costs of mandatory origin labelling for milk and milk used as an ingredient in dairy products increase in line with the complexity of the production process. however, the commission does not distinguish between slightly processed and highly processed products. we therefore ask the commission to define 'slightly processed' food, particularly as regards dairy and meat products, as the cost of origin labelling should be significantly reduced if its scope is limited to milk for direct consumption, lightly processed dairy products such as cheese and cream, and some lightly processed meat products such as sausages and bacon.
in writing. ‒ the resolution calls on the commission to finally implement its obligations to implement the provisions of article 26 of regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 on mandatory indication of origin (food information to consumers is horizontal legislation on food labelling). in particular, considering that optional labelling schemes would only lead to confusion and opacity (see recital l and § 20), it calls for mandatory indication of origin on almost everything (§ 24-31). we must be careful that this very good text is not distorted by the epp amendments and the deletion of the parts on which the non-origin groups have asked for a separate vote. in this connection, i would draw attention to amendment no 8: finally they confess the real reason for their opposition. we should point out, as we explained to the president of federalimentare in recent days, that 'origin' cannot be reduced to a mere matter of costs for firms, but is, on the contrary, a lever for the 'value' of the primary sector and then of the processing sector. this is a tool that can help to counter the crisis in the agricultural sector caused by the free trade policies implemented by the eu, as france, for example, has understood.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the resolution calling on the commission to apply the compulsory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance to products intended for direct consumption. the eu regulation on consumer information adopted in 2011 made the labelling of origin or provenance for certain foods subject to an impact assessment. the study shows that the costs of ensuring transparency in the food chain for those products may be too high, but that assessment is incomplete and does not sufficiently take into account the fact that the costs related to traceability are not the same for all products. for these reasons i support the call on the commission to implement the obligation to label origin for those products whose traceability costs are negligible and to further its study to assess the possibility of extending the mandatory indication of the country of origin or place of provenance to other single-ingredient or predominantly ingredient food products by drawing up legislative proposals in these areas.

in writing. ‒ an indication of the country of origin for the labelling of all processed meat and milk products should be mandatory to make the food supply chain more transparent and help maintain consumer confidence in food products. according to eurobarometer data, 84% of european citizens believe it is necessary to indicate the origin of milk; 88% consider such labelling necessary for meat (excluding beef, pork, sheep, goat and poultry, which are already covered) and over 90% consider labelling important for processed foods. the compulsory indication of the country of origin is a powerful incentive for food businesses to promote products with high added value in terms of quality and working methods that respect animals and the environment. i would like to stress in particular that this motion for a resolution is in line with italian interests. that is why i voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the obligation to indicate the country of origin for all milk, milk products and meat products. i believe that mandatory origin labelling would give consumers the opportunity to be better informed and therefore to make more informed purchases. moreover, increased transparency along the entire food supply chain would bring significant economic benefits to raw material producers. i am referring, for example, to rabbit meat. in italy, rabbit farming is the fourth most important livestock sector in terms of economic importance, after cattle, pigs and chickens. the entire funnel chain is currently experiencing a profitability crisis, partly due to european regulatory uncertainty and the high volatility of prices linked to often unfair competition from the product imported from other countries. i hope that the european commission will fill this regulatory gap and present a legislative proposal to extend the mandatory indication of the country of origin to this type of meat and thus clearly indicate on the label the place of birth, rearing and slaughter of the animal. only in this way can we promote the true made in italy and promote the quality and safety of our products.

in writing. ‒ parental leave is the right of both parents to take time off from work for a certain period of time, thus allowing them to balance family and work commitments. ensuring a certain flexibility in employment contracts is particularly important, not only as a form of support for women workers, but above all in view of the 75% employment targets of the horizon 2020 programme. the aim was to develop social policies and measures to facilitate reintegration into working life and to ensure full implementation of the directive in all member states. for these reasons, i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the europe 2020 strategy includes among its objectives the achievement of a 75% employment rate for women. one theme is closely linked to that of work-life balance, which sees the issue of leave legislation as a central element in its implementation. national legislation on leave currently provides for three types of family leave: maternity, paternity and parenting; at european level, there are two directives, one on maternity leave and one, updated in 2010, on parental leave. the arena report, which i supported with my vote, calls strongly for a strengthening of the legislation on this subject, pushing for a strong guarantee for access to leave without any discrimination due to the sector of employment and the contractual characteristics of the work. parental leave should be equally granted to both parents and the push to enable fathers to take advantage of this opportunity should be strengthened. in this respect, new european legislation on paternity leave should be adopted to ensure a minimum level of leave of two weeks.

in writing. ‒ the migrant crisis facing europe has highlighted an important issue: human trafficking. this term covers a wide range of illegal activities, from sexual exploitation to forced labor, organ harvesting, begging, and forced marriage. these are human rights violations, crimes that affect the physical and psychological integrity of the victims and in 80% of cases involve women. the bearder report, which i have supported today, is concerned with tackling the problem in a global way, starting with prevention, then identification and finally assistance to victims. the text calls on the member states to ensure that victims are also provided with legal assistance in civil proceedings and in immigration and asylum procedures, while training police, judicial and medical staff to assist in the early identification and support of victims. an important step would be to guarantee victims residence permits and free access to the labour market within the member countries.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this document because i believe that human trafficking is a scourge of our time and must be eradicated as quickly as possible through cooperation between the member states of the union and between them and third countries of transit. it is a question of civilization and the union must be at the forefront of this fight against barbarism.
in writing. ‒ trafficking in human beings is a tragic phenomenon that gives rise to intolerable violations of fundamental human rights enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. directive 2011/36/eu allows, through measures such as the obligation for member states to establish mechanisms for the identification and assistance of victims or through a regulatory framework allowing for the swifter and more efficient initiation of criminal proceedings against traffickers, to combat a highly complex and brutal phenomenon affecting thousands of people, mostly women, every year. however, to make the tools available even more effective, the timeliness of recognition of victims needs to be increased, and victims need to have effective access to justice and services that are recognised by eu law. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances. finally, if we are to achieve more ambitious results, member states need to introduce stricter criminal sanctions and increase judicial and police cooperation through europol and eurojust, sharing sensitive information and extending existing training programmes for staff.
in writing. ‒ despite some commonalities, the report is too unbalanced on the pro-immigration front. i voted with an abstention.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report today because i believe that a further joint international effort is needed to prevent such inhuman and degrading situations. although the strategies adopted so far in the field of crime control, trafficking and victim assistance have been many, the results are far from reassuring. children and girls, representing 16% and 13% respectively of the total number of confirmed victims of trafficking in human beings, are certainly among the most vulnerable groups. unfortunately, statistics cannot give an accurate picture of the real situation, as there are a significant number of unidentifiable victims. human trafficking mainly affects so-called 'hidden populations'. the peculiarity of these is the low level of reporting and the low recognition rate. migrant smuggling and human trafficking, although different phenomena, often tend to overlap. a well-balanced and appropriate response could then be found by a careful analysis of the latest trends, including the influence that the current migration crisis could have on the phenomenon in question.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the own-initiative report which aims to express the european parliament's position on greater protection for victims of trafficking in human beings. the relationship between the various aspects focuses on the particular vulnerability of women, the definition of trafficking and the availability of data and statistics. it is certainly to be appreciated that particular emphasis is being placed on prevention, which is considered essential to combating trafficking. it also reiterates the call on the european commission to submit a legislative proposal to combat violence against women and tackles the crucial issue of victim identification.
in writing. ‒ i am pleased that this report has been adopted because i think it is the right political position on a problem of great importance to europe, namely human trafficking. with this policy document, the union is seeking to combat effectively this serious form of organised crime, with its various abuses of fundamental human rights and the personal integrity of the victim. the report in question aims to introduce stronger forms of control so that it is first and foremost the individual member states who make sure that they do everything possible to ensure that new people do not fall victim to it. i believe that prevention is essential if we are to tackle human trafficking in a concrete way. as a member of the european parliament, it is my duty to defend the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, and i believe that this report is intended to tackle these problems in a concrete way. the report also stresses the importance of gender equality and the fact that women and girls are too often the victims of violence because they are objectively more vulnerable. for these reasons, i am extremely pleased that this document has been adopted.
in writing. ‒ directive 2011/36/eu aims to better protect victims of trafficking in human beings. trafficking in human beings is considered one of the most serious crimes worldwide and constitutes a serious violation of human rights. this directive sets out rules that apply throughout the european union to tackle this horrific phenomenon and reduce the vulnerability of victims. the recruitment, transport, transfer, accommodation or reception of persons for the purpose of exploitation shall be punishable. 'exploitation' means exploitation of prostitution or other forms of sexual exploitation, forced labour or services, including begging, slavery, exploitation of illicit activities or organ harvesting. the directive required the commission to carry out evaluations and audits by 6 april 2015 to examine the measures taken by the member states to transpose the directive. the commission has not carried out any evaluation or examination to date. i believe that special importance should be attached to prevention in order to combat the phenomenon of trafficking in human beings and to assisting the victims. the report represents a fundamental step for the member states in the fight against trafficking in human beings, and i am voting in favour of it.
in writing. ‒ trafficking in and exploitation of human beings, in all its forms, but especially in the workplace and in the sexual sphere, is still a phenomenon in european societies. the victims of trafficking are already vulnerable groups such as young women, children, asylum seekers and migrants. i am voting in favour of the implementation of directive 2011/36/eu on the prevention and suppression of trafficking in human beings and the protection of victims, because we are dealing with a transnational phenomenon and i believe that all member states have an urgent need to fully and properly implement the directive and to act in a coordinated manner. the european parliament has also called for the establishment of a european police office, which would be able to provide information on the activities of europol and its staff. i also agree with the european parliament's interpretation of the implementation of the directive, which emphasizes two aspects which i consider to be fundamental. eu anti-trafficking legislation must necessarily be gender-sensitive in order to better protect the category of women. finally, it is important to take account of the eu's internal and external action on trafficking in human beings, as non-eu countries are often the source and transit countries for trafficking within the eu.
in writing. ‒ i voted strongly in favour of this measure, which aims to promote the implementation of the directive on the prevention and suppression of trafficking in human beings and the protection of victims. it is true that the victims of such trafficking are often criminalised and thus rendered even more vulnerable and excluded, without any protection. this report proposes that an integrated approach based on human rights be followed in the implementation of the directive, with particular emphasis on assistance and protection for victims. in order to make the standard really effective, particular attention is also paid to the gender perspective. indeed, according to eurostat data for the three-year period 2010-2012, 69% of registered victims of human trafficking were victims of sexual exploitation and 80% of victims of such trafficking are women and girls. my vote is therefore intended to give my full support to the report, for an increase in measures to support and defend victims, and for their recovery and reintegration into society. the european union cannot be coy in the face of such phenomena, but it has a duty to develop effective policies which put the protection of human rights and dignity at the centre.
in writing. ‒ trafficking in human beings, for a variety of purposes and in its many forms, is one of the most serious forms of human rights violation. women and children continue to be the privileged victims. various factors, in particular poverty and social exclusion, have led to situations of vulnerability, while the massive flows of migrants have highlighted the transnational nature of the phenomenon and the lack of appropriate instruments to combat it. in the legal framework to be implemented for the prevention and suppression of trafficking, tools for the assistance, support and protection of victims, cooperation between authorities and the sharing of information to investigate and uncover financial flows resulting from the activities of organised crime networks play a significant role.
in writing. ‒ the massive flows of migrants have led to a massive increase in human trafficking, which is one of the most deadly aberrant practices in recent years, as well as a clear violation of fundamental human rights. it is the duty of every state to prevent and combat it. i voted in favour of the report because it brings to the attention of the eu member states recommendations and useful tools to combat this international crime. the directive lays down an obligation for member states to establish mechanisms for the timely detection, identification and assistance of victims. in this respect, public awareness initiatives are essential, both in the countries of destination and in those of origin. in the latter, awareness raising can help prevent trafficking, but in destination countries it can help identify where victims and criminals are going.

in writing. ‒ human trafficking, whether for sexual exploitation, forced labour, forced marriages, domestic servitude, forced organ harvesting, illegal adoption is an unacceptable phenomenon that still plagues our society. the eu's aim in adopting this directive is to prevent and combat effectively all forms of exploitation, by putting the victims, the people, at the centre, paying due attention to gender and age differences, as well as to different religious beliefs. however, as a recent caritas report shows, human trafficking remains the third most profitable business for organized crime, after drug and arms trafficking. a business worth $32 billion a year. a business where the most affected victims are women and girls (80%), whose vulnerability can be attributed to barriers in access to education, gender violence, unequal access to employment opportunities. as highlighted in the latest migrantes report, the anonymity in which victims often find themselves and the lack of coordination between states are important obstacles. i hope, therefore, that the directive will bring attention to the individual and to the coordination between states, international organisations and ngos, both of which are necessary to defeat trafficking in human beings.
