first vice-president of the commission. – madam president, president juncker is travelling as we speak to the g7 summit in japan and has asked me to address you on his behalf, ahead of a summit that will address a number of urgent priorities. the economic backdrop is one of gradual recovery for our economy, despite a difficult global environment. eu annual growth reached 2% in 2015. our first-quarter growth this year was higher than that of the united states. unemployment is certainly still much too high in some member states but, across the board, it has fallen to its lowest in five years. today, there are five million more jobs than in 2013. confidence is gradually returning – we see it on investment, on consumer spending, on lending. but we must remain alert. our main trading partners’ slower performance is a cause for concern. last year, growth outside the eu fell to its lowest since 2009 as emerging markets performed less well. against this backdrop of uncertainty, growth will depend on the opportunities we create for ourselves. we need investment, structural reforms and responsible public finances. we need to stay the course. this parliament has played a vital role in this strategy. you made it possible to launch the investment plan for europe at record speed. in less than one year, it has triggered eur 100 billion in new investments, and delivered finance on better terms to more than 140 000 smes. it is generating structural change. until now, european investment has often been dominated by a limited number of large, expensive projects. today, we are starting to see more local projects, which are smaller and more diverse. public money is mobilising private finance, and supporting structural reforms. we see more interaction between the european investment bank and local institutions. in short, we are beginning to see the kind of investment that the market has often failed to deliver. our fund is helping to find new treatments for alzheimer’s disease; transforming old industrial sites into new offices; bringing energy efficiency into our homes and cutting our bills; and lending a hand to start-ups who were turned away by other lenders. investment is high on the agenda of the g7. and we have a good story to tell. we will also deliver better news on greece. last year, we fought hard to keep greece in the euro area. today, the economic data is better than expected. greece should return to growth in the second half of 2016. unemployment fell in 2015, and the government reached a primary surplus of 0.7% of gdp. the stability support programme agreed last summer has laid the ground for long-term stable development. above all, we have managed to secure greece’s place in the euro area. this week’s agreement on the completion of the first review of the programme only confirms that. discussions on reducing the greek debt burden have now started. this recognises the collective effort made by the people of greece. today, the greek economy can turn the corner, and we are confident that international investors will follow. within the g7, the european union has always fought for a global economy that is governed by rules, increasingly transparent, and as fair as possible. in other words, we strive to export our best practices to the global stage. at this week’s summit, we will continue these efforts. together with our g7 partners, we need to demonstrate that global trade can work for everyone – not just for every country, but for every part of our society. we know that, in the short term, globalisation produces winners and losers. this has helped to fuel populist forces around the world. and so our challenge is not only to shape the rules of the game and to ensure that they are respected, but also to argue that our long-term prosperity lies in openness and exchange. over the last year, the european union has taken the lead on tax transparency. we now have a ground-breaking agreement on tax rulings, and earlier this year we adopted a new proposal on country-by-country reporting. our message is clear: everyone must pay their fair share. we must now work with our g7 partners to ensure that this is a truly global effort. if our own member states have agreed to put in place central registers of beneficial ownership, then our partners must do the same. for those that try to evade their duty to society, there must be no place to hide. we must be equally firm on those countries that do not play by the rules. free trade must be fair trade. i can assure this house today that the european commission stands by a robust trade defence system. if somebody distorts the market, we will take action. this commission has launched a record number of trade defence measures to respond to the dumping on europe’s steel industry. at the g7, we will argue that offending countries need to produce clear and measurable plans to cut over-capacity. international monitoring must ensure that everyone complies. let me now turn to the global refugee crisis, which is rightly high on the g7 agenda. this commission has argued from the start that only global solutions will work. here, once again, this parliament has helped to deliver a european strategy that is comprehensive: saving lives at sea, providing humanitarian assistance, strengthening our borders, supporting the countries most under pressure, relocating and resettling people in need of international protection, returning irregular migrants to their home countries, and creating safe and legal routes for asylum-seekers from outside the european union. in 2015 and 2016, the eu will have devoted more than eur 10 billion to managing the crisis. this strategy has given us the breathing space to look to the future. together with our g7 partners, we must now develop a truly global response, backed by proper resources, and capable of addressing the root causes of migration. an international resettlement programme is urgent and necessary. only by giving asylum-seekers a legal route to safety will we convince them not to risk their lives. this is the best way to break the business model of the smugglers. and the best way to restore dignity to those who genuinely need our protection. let me conclude with climate and energy. this week’s summit of the g7 is the first since the paris agreement. the real work starts now: modernising our economy and changing the way we produce and consume. this in turn requires new incentives across the entire spectrum of policy. the best of our businesses have read the signal: leading european companies are changing their business models, and creating new jobs that require new skills, innovative processes and investments. the european union must have the ambition to be a world leader in renewables: the sector now employs over one million people and generates eur 130 billion in turnover each year. european companies today hold 40% of all patents for renewable technologies. but major obstacles remain. in 2013, across the world, subsidies for fossil fuels amounted to almost eur 500 billion. that is a lot of money being spent very badly. the g7 has promised to phase out those subsidies by 2025. next we must push the g20 to do the same. as we approach this week’s summit in japan, the need for political coordination at the global level is as compelling as ever. from a slowing global economy to a global refugee crisis, the countries of the g7 need to show leadership and join forces. as the european union, we will continue to make the case for a global economy that is governed by rules, and an open society that seeks prosperity and security in its exchange with others. in today’s uncertain world, our contribution really matters.
the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force. a new globalization, less indifferent to those who do not directly benefit from it, is the only answer to those who harness fears and revitalize ideas that we had hoped were out of date forever: nationalism, separatism, xenophobia and walls. the agenda for the summit in japan is very ambitious and so, we hope, will be the conclusions, from foreign policy to climate change to sustainable development. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in this connection, in line with the resolution which this parliament voted two weeks ago, we hope that a coherent way of dealing with china, a key partner, will be found, but it must also be a partner in the definition of fair and sustainable trade. this applies in particular to the question of granting market economy status, as well as to the question of overcapacity, especially in the steel sector, and to the question of compliance with common rules for market access. finally, we are pleased to note the inclusion of the item on gender equality in the agenda. the european institutions, which have always been at the forefront of promoting women's empowerment, will be able to use the g7 to support proposals to reduce all gender gaps through concrete and coordinated measures.

that we will slow down decline. so if you really want to use the opportunities that global developments are offering, you need to move towards a sustainable economy, you need to embrace the digital direction. that is the only way we can create enough economic growth which is sustainable, which does not deplete the earth but which maintains our natural resources and which will enable us to create the social environment that is wanted by the vast majority of europeans. we need growth for that, given our demographic challenge. that is what the commission will be advocating in the g7 – to use the opportunity that global trade offers without being naive about the abuse of the elements of global trade if we do not stick to the rules and if we do not have fair play. that is the essence of what we are doing. i do agree with all of those who have said that we need to have an enhanced attention towards implementing the paris agreements. again, if you follow my reasoning that we need a sustainable economy, we need to make sure that we slow down global warming and that we actually do what we promised in paris. for that, concrete measures are necessary and they need to be discussed in the g7 framework. finally, let me emphasise – and i cannot say this enough – the migration and refugee crisis is here to stay. it is not something that will end if, at last, the war in syria comes to an end. look at the huge demographic pressures we will see from africa and elsewhere. it is in our essential interest that we create sustainable growth in our neighbourhood. and when i talk about our neighbourhood, i mean the wider neighbourhood, including the whole of africa. the g7 should be talking about that as well. this is about migration, this is about opportunity, this is about decent, rule-of-law-based government and all these things have become factors on a global scale for the decisive choice europe needs to make: whether we want to export our stability and our prosperity, or whether we want to wait until we import instability and poverty from elsewhere. that, i think, should be the position of the european union in the deliberations in the g7.

privileged forum, not just to discuss these issues but also to forge partnerships and launch, i hope, collective initiatives for a more equitable burden-sharing. my second point is, of course, the global economy. i think we are constantly reminded that the global economy recovery is too slow, that it does not deliver enough jobs, that downside risks are accumulating, and therefore it is the right time for this group of g7 leaders to clearly signal that securing balanced and inclusive growth not only remains a top priority, but to recall that we have to get our own houses in order in our individual countries. but obviously there is also a collective responsibility. we have seen, i think, that those are the lessons learned by different partners in the g7; that taken in isolation, monetary, fiscal and structural policies do not suffice to boost economic activity in a sustainable way. additionally, and given recent movements in currency markets, it would also be timely to reaffirm existing exchange rate commitments and call on all to refrain from competitive devaluations and to resist protectionism. this is a risk that we are all faced with, and i think the g7 will have to take some leadership on this. that brings me to the third point: international trade. in 2015, g7 leaders underlined the importance of trade and investment as key drivers of growth, jobs and sustainable development. tomorrow’s summit will have an important role to play in strengthening the future of the multilateral trade agenda. in this context it is important that on 13 may the council confirmed the broad support for the commission’s proposals regarding the eu strategic objectives for the post-nairobi period. importantly, i think, public trust and support for the free trade agenda has decreased in the context of disappointing global trade in recent years. so we need to get the people back on board, and i think leaders should be clear about the benefits of maintaining economies open and free from protectionism, as well as the importance of multilateral and bilateral trade and investment agreements for growth and jobs. i think it is important that we ensure that we have a much more equal level playing field, and addressing the issue of industrial excess capacity would be part of the solution. besides that, we should honestly address the concerns of the public. if you in writing. data flows between the eu and the us are the most intensive in the world and represent an essential element in trade relations, especially for us multinationals. in october 2015, the european court of justice invalidated the safe harbour decision by ruling that national supervisory authorities can assess the adequacy of the level of protection provided by a third country and, if necessary, suspend the transfer of data. the commission has therefore drawn up a new decision, the so-called 'privacy shield', to ensure that the privacy and personal data of european citizens are respected. however, this decision does not ensure an adequate level of protection and safeguarding of the fundamental right to the protection of personal data. in the us, foreigners' data is nothing but a commodity that can be used as it sees fit without any respect for privacy. the european union has also been involved in the negotiations on the schengen agreement with the united states. our task is to protect citizens from any abuse and with this text we are de facto legalising any use of sensitive european data by the us.

in writing. ‒ virtual currencies, often referred to as digital money, are a new means of payment based largely on distributed ledger technology (dlt). among these virtual currencies, the most relevant is undoubtedly bitcoin, which holds, although it has not reached systemic size, 90% of the market. the von weizsäcker report, which i supported with my vote, effectively highlights the opportunities and challenges that are linked to the use of virtual currencies and dlt. their introduction has already led to a reduction in the cost of operations but could prove even more important in the future in areas where standardisation, reliability and ownership play a crucial role, such as public services, smart contracts, intellectual property transfers and supply chain management. the text also calls for the introduction of smart regulation that does not stifle the technological growth associated with dlt applications, while ensuring that the risks associated with the misuse of these means for illicit purposes, such as money laundering and terrorist financing, are avoided. to this end, the european commission should set up a task force to regulate virtual currencies

in writing. ‒ virtual currencies can contribute positively to citizens' well-being and economic development, including in the financial sector, through, for example, a reduction in both transaction costs and the cost of access to finance and a boost in the speed of payment systems. however, virtual currency systems may also entail risks, such as the high volatility of virtual currencies and the risk of speculative bubbles, user protection issues and criminal activities such as the possibility of black market transactions, money laundering, terrorist financing. the european parliament resolution, which i voted for, suggests that to address these risks and increase the reliability of virtual currencies, a balance needs to be struck between strengthening regulatory capacity and a sound legal framework that is in step with innovation, while maintaining a certain flexibility and avoiding that premature regulation, which is ill-suited to a still evolving reality, can convey a wrong message to the public about the benefits or safety of virtual currencies.

in writing. ‒ we welcome the report on virtual currencies. the european parliament has once again shown its ability to keep pace with the times by tackling a new issue which still touches our lives marginally but which could potentially change our daily lives profoundly. virtual currencies, as defined by the bank of italy, are digital representations of value, used as a medium of exchange or held for investment purposes, which can be transferred, stored and traded electronically. at present, virtual currencies are not legal tender but can be used by users to purchase goods or services, if the seller is willing to accept them. the most famous example is bitcoin, which today represents the largest share of the virtual currency market. although not yet considered to be money, virtual currency is certainly an innovative, fast, inexpensive and effective payment system. the institutions must therefore continue to monitor the phenomenon and try to introduce a system of rules that is streamlined and effective, which addresses and resolves the critical issues identified in this report.
in writing. ‒ the first and most well-known virtual currency, bitcoin, has been introduced for seven years now and it is clear that the technological innovation at its core, distributed ledger technology (dlt), is set to have a considerable impact on the financial sector and beyond. this technology allows for the decentralised, fast, resilient and fairly secure recording of any type of transaction. investment in dlt technology is increasing significantly and some applications could soon become systemic. the most obvious opportunities offered by these new technologies are primarily in the area of payments, allowing for cost reductions while ensuring security and confidentiality. on the other hand, the potential of dlt is also relevant for other areas such as smart contracts, intellectual property transfers, supply chain management and a number of public services. the most obvious risks (but others will probably emerge over time) include money laundering and the financing of criminal and terrorist activities. in such a rapidly changing environment, it is right to want, as this report calls for, smart regulation that encourages the free development of new technologies, but at the same time tackles risks before they become systemic.
in writing. ‒ this report is the first to be produced by the european parliament on virtual currencies and distributed ledger technology. the main opportunities offered by virtual currencies and dlt in the area of payments are related to the reduction of transaction costs and ease of use. furthermore, it is likely that much of the potential of dlt will develop well beyond the payments sector, for example in areas where reliability and the ability to prove the identity of ownership play a central role, i.e. so-called 'smart contracts'. i therefore voted in favour and hope that we can soon reach a clear and effective regulation of this payment system.
in writing. ‒ the growing phenomenon of virtual currencies raises new issues, in particular with regard to the economic and legal regime of their status and of the transactions connected with these sui generis monetary instruments. this report is the result of a compromise which i voted in favour of in unity with the ppe group: the need to set up a task force for a thorough and prior assessment of the issue was put before the call for immediate legislative action.
in writing. ‒ in recent times, the phenomenon of virtual currencies has developed and is becoming increasingly popular, including bitcoin. in this resolution, parliament called on the commission to set up a task force to regulate the use and spread of virtual currencies without hindering innovation and development. the task of this task force would be to monitor their development and, if necessary, to intervene in a timely manner. i hope that this task force will be set up in the near future so that it can combat the illegal use of virtual currencies as a means of money laundering or terrorist financing. i therefore decided to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ for the first time, the european parliament debated and voted on reports on virtual currencies based mainly on a distributed ledger technology. the report addresses the issue from different perspectives, attempting to analyse the cost-benefit of virtual currencies and calling for appropriate regulation. the positive aspects, generating cost reduction, and the new possible consumer applications based on distributed ledger technology are analyzed. the main risks are mainly related to the lack of clear regulation and the high volatility of these instruments. that is why we voted in favour of the call for an eu-wide regulatory framework taking into account existing legislation to avoid excessive costs. we have asked, as 5 star, for the creation of an expert task force led by the commission to provide expertise on virtual currencies. another request we made in the past was to use the resources already available within the commission, supplementing them with those of the national experts.
in writing. ‒ with this report, the european parliament has for the first time addressed virtual currencies based primarily on distributed ledger technology (dlt), given the growing importance this new form of payment is gaining in international markets. the report deals with the matter from several perspectives. it requires first a clear and unambiguous definition of 'virtual currencies' that is universally applicable. the commission shall, by means of implementing acts, lay down the rules on the application of this regulation, in particular the rules on the application of article 4 of regulation (eu) no 648/2012 of the european parliament and of the council [16]. the report also examines the risks associated with virtual currencies, which are often due to the lack of appropriate regulation and the volatility of these instruments. this is why it is called for an eu-wide regulatory framework to be established, taking into account existing legislation, to avoid excessive burdens. the commission also proposes to establish a horizontal task force, led by the commission and composed of the main actors and experts at national level, to ensure the necessary expertise in the field of virtual currencies. for all these reasons i voted in favour.

in writing. ‒ cross-border data flows between the eu and the us are the most intensive in the world, representing, among other things, an essential component in trade relations. in this regard, in a judgment of october 2015, the european court of justice ruled that the eu-us negotiations must take into account privacy safeguards, thus fulfilling the requirements of legal certainty. the protection of personal data is a fundamental right, formally recognised in the charter of fundamental rights and the tfeu. the new agreement is in clear contradiction with the court's rulings, and i voted against the motion for a resolution, considering it of paramount importance to ensure respect for privacy and the inviolability of personal data.
in writing. ‒ the european union recognises data protection as one of its fundamental rights, a right enshrined in article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights and reaffirmed in a judgment of the court of justice which defined as an adequate level of protection, in data exchanges with third countries, a level essentially equivalent to that guaranteed by the eu. the joint resolution on the transatlantic data flow, which i supported in parliament today, addresses this issue by stressing the need to conclude negotiations on the eu-us privacy shield by first ensuring legal certainty on how personal data is transferred from the eu to the us. this is an essential element in promoting not only increased consumer confidence but also the development of transatlantic business and international cooperation. the commission should continue its dialogue with the us administration to further improve the privacy shield agreement by overcoming its shortcomings, which have been accurately highlighted by the national data protection authorities. this will make it possible to further strengthen an economic link which is the largest in the world in terms of trade, while maintaining a high level of protection for citizens.

in writing. ‒ personal data entered online must be adequately protected and in any case their use for commercial purposes must be regulated. the handling of this data is of particular importance when it is transferred from the european union to the united states, where different privacy and personal data regulations apply. in this resolution, parliament welcomes the progress that the new privacy shield agreement would bring over the old safe harbour. however, it is highlighted how some remaining gaps in some sensitive areas, such as access by public authorities to data transferred, or the possibility of collecting a quantity of data that may not comply with the criteria laid down in the eu charter of fundamental rights, should be filled.

in writing. ‒ the privacy shield is certainly an improvement on the safe harbour agreement in terms of the protection of personal data, which is recognised as a fundamental right of european citizens by the charter of fundamental rights. cross-border data flows between the us and europe are the most intensive in the world and a key factor in business activities and judicial cooperation. a secure legal framework, simple and efficient compliance procedures are essential for smes, among the most dynamic and fastest growing players in the european economy, which are increasingly dependent on the free flow of data. the new agreement introduces several improvements, in particular the definition of key concepts and the establishment of mandatory and more effective mechanisms and controls. the privacy shield is a framework for the protection of personal data of individuals, including their family members, and their children. the collection of mass data and personal communications of non-us citizens is still in too many cases authorised by us law and therefore the rights of european citizens are still not sufficiently protected. i therefore share the commission's call to continue the dialogue with the us administration to achieve further improvements to the agreement.

in writing. ‒ the european parliament's report on the poverty situation of women in the countries of the european union highlights a problem that is unfortunately still persistent in european societies where, despite more than 50 years of gender equality policies, disparities in terms of employment and poverty remain very high. women, although a key force in the economic and social development of european countries, are more exposed to the risk of poverty than men. the causes are many and mainly concern the persistence of gender prejudices which are deeply rooted in the cultural fabric of the countries of the union. this contributes to relegating women to a secondary role in society and, consequently, to the feminization of poverty. member states should therefore encourage the development of policies to increase female employment, promote work-life balance and ensure support for the care and education of children in disadvantaged settings. and there is a need for greater use of the political and financial instruments already available to promote family support services so as to encourage women to enter, and remain, in the labour market. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the crisis we are experiencing, and which we are trying very hard to overcome, is, in my view, a subject on which the european parliament must give effective and concrete answers. i felt equally obliged to abstain from voting on this report because it has been used by certain political groups as a pretext for debating matters which have in fact contaminated its contents. i found it a pretext to want to discuss sensitive topics together, such as the economic crisis and gender differences, especially trying to shift the focus to the transgender and lgbt categories. it is not the place for me, nor is it the right way to do politics. every subject, especially sensitive ones, has its own space for argumentation to enable anyone to be properly informed and to be able to express his political opinion in complete freedom. it is for these reasons that i have decided to abstain, because i believe that such important and socially relevant matters must be dealt with in the right way, with full respect for those in the european union who invest their hopes, energies and resources.

in writing. ‒ the single market is an important element of the european union, a process which began some 50 years ago with the elimination of tariff barriers but which continues today, albeit hampered by the persistence of non-tariff barriers which prevent its full potential from being exploited. the dalton report, which i have supported, stresses the need to ensure better and more consistent application of existing rules, abandoning ever more protectionist measures and opening up national markets more fully. in the present context, the commission has the task of presenting a comprehensive picture of the obstacles to the single market, an analysis of the means to overcome them and, above all, an overall plan to overcome them. it is in the constant presence of disproportionate and often discriminatory regulatory interventions that all those costs must be identified which, in addition to generating disadvantages for the most competitive and innovative companies, cause inconvenience to consumers which translate into less choice and higher prices. it must be one of the union's priorities to make the most of the single market, enhancing europe's competitiveness on the world stage.

in writing. ‒ since its establishment in 1993, the european single market has been one of the main drivers of the european integration project, fostering the deepening of relations between the different member states and ensuring significant economic development capable of significantly increasing employment, while improving the well-being of european citizens. since then, despite the progress made, the presence of a number of unjustified non-tariff barriers, particularly in the services sector, has hindered the full completion of the services sector, resulting in unfair discrimination and significant economic disadvantages for businesses and consumers. i therefore call on the commission to re-launch the analysis of the existing unjustified non-tariff barriers with a view to drawing up a comprehensive strategy which will finally be able to solve these problems, and to monitor more closely the effective compliance by the member states with the existing rules in this particular area. finally, while the completion of the single market can indeed be a great opportunity for economic development, particular care must be taken not to jeopardize, in the context of the removal of existing unjustified non-tariff barriers, the rules established with a view to protecting consumers and the environment, which must be safeguarded and even strengthened.

answer each and every one of you. i shall therefore limit myself to three points which have been raised repeatedly this morning: the question of tax evasion in relation to competitiveness, tax regimes favourable to patents and, finally, the overall balance of the text as it stands before the council debate next week. i would like to make two brief political remarks at the outset: one to mr monot, who wondered whether we were legitimate in taking action on this matter. no, we are not only legitimate, we are necessary, and it is typically in this kind of subject that we see what europe is for, and the anti-europeans are wrong, because none of our member states could effectively fight tax evasion on their own. we are facing international, global problems, and the answer is at least european. and that is why we must have a europe which is willing, an example europe; it proves the futility of nationalism, of withdrawal, of excesses of any kind or any kind. i would also like to say a word to mr lamberts and the greens, because i am glad that this time we are no longer being criticised for not doing what we are doing, and i think it is very positive that there is a move towards taking account of a number of proposals which are of a high quality. i am all for moving forward together, as long as the analyses are of high quality and the aims are shared. but i'm going back to my three points. first, the issue of competitiveness and sovereignty and, in particular, the underlying issue of ccctb. our proposal, i should say, in general terms, our tax proposals are - i am convinced of this - balanced. the political will to fight tax optimisation is not a fight against business; i am proud to have fought for this from the beginning, and i say this especially to mrs joly, who may not have understood or seen it yet, but since i became commissioner, since the first day of my mandate, this has been a cause i have championed. i see in various media that there are voices which seem to claim that there is a contradiction between competitiveness and transparency. i am convinced of the contrary, in fact, that transparency is a weapon for competitiveness. we're not in an ideological battle for or against the company. our fight is a fight for tax justice, which is also something that serves the deepest interests of the company. how did you do that? by ensuring fair competition rules, particularly for the benefit of our smes, which, as everyone knows, are the engines of growth and employment in the european union. i would also add that we are committed to measures such as the common and consolidated corporate tax base and the resolution of tax disputes, which are important elements in the fight against double taxation. i would add, finally, that both what we are doing in the fight against tax evasion and the project i am pursuing - and i will continue to pursue - to take up the matter in a more intelligent and perhaps more consensual way, is a very important step towards the creation of a european tax system. the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the harmonization of taxation rates. this is a debate we had in the council, for example at the last ecofin council with minister noonan. what we want is not minimum taxation, not forced harmonization - we respect fiscal sovereignty - but effective taxation. the time when a multinational company, for example, could, because it had a well-located headquarters or strategically placed subsidiaries, no longer pay taxes or not pay substantial taxes where it creates wealth, that time must come to an end. our proposals do not, i repeat, call into question the sovereignty of the states to set the level of taxation: we do not deny tax competition, but we want it to be harmonious, member of the commission. – mr president, i am very pleased to have this opportunity to discuss these amendments to mifid ii, and i recognise there has been a huge amount of hard work done in the european parliament and in the council to get these agreed before july. i am particularly grateful to mr ferber and to the shadow rapporteurs on this file for having kept up the momentum and having dealt with it so effectively. i very much agreed with what mr ferber said, that this package is a key part of our financial reforms, increasing the transparency of markets and improving their oversight. it responded to the g20 agreement back in pittsburgh to reform derivatives and commodity markets, to make those markets work better, to make them more resilient, to make them more stable – and also of course to strengthen investor protection, not only by ensuring that investors have the right information, but also by introducing stronger rules to avoid conflicts of interest. so we are agreed on the goal, and if that is the goal, to achieve it we need this legislation to be implemented properly, in a way which gives legal certainty, and which does not disrupt markets that provide investment to the wider economy and help businesses manage their risks. this reform was always going to be an ambitious reform. it calls for data from hundreds of trading venues, from some 15 million financial instruments. given the scale of that challenge, the complexity of the it systems that were needed, the european securities and markets authority (esma) judged – rightly, in my view – that more time was needed to get it right, not to undermine the new framework but to make sure that it works properly when it kicks in. so, at their request, it is true that we proposed to extend by a year, until january 2018, the deadline for mifid ii entering into application, and i am grateful to the european parliament and to the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ) for its support in accepting what i see as being a common-sense proposal. like mr ferber, i am also glad that we have avoided revisiting the key aspects of the package that was agreed just two years ago, but that we have got some technical amendments in this package which improve the quality of the rules. further clarification of the scope of the transparency requirements on package transactions was an issue raised by esma when they submitted their regulatory technical standards (rts), and here i think that parliament’s amendment helps us get the balance right. it ensures that the pre-trade transparency regime continues to apply where it is needed, without imposing unnecessary burdens where it is not. it was also right to exempt securities financing transactions (sfts) from transparency obligations. sfts are not price forming and they will of course be regulated by the securities financing transactions regulation in the future, and so increased transparency in this area would create new burdens but serve little purpose. with the amendment on own account exemption we are acting to make sure that non-financial companies do not fall unnecessarily within the scope of mifid ii and its administrative and capital requirements. we are now working hard to get the majority of mifid ii’s large number of level 2 measures adopted in june, and i completely agree with mr ferber that we have to keep the pace up. in a handful of areas we have asked esma to look again at their proposals reflecting issues that have also been raised by the european parliament. taken together, i believe that these measures should make mifid ii more effective. member states will have to transpose the elements of mifid ii they are responsible for by 3 july 2017. the industry would need to start complying from january 2018. i believe that this is a sensible way forward to ensure the smooth implementation of this legislation and to bring more transparency, better consumer protection and more efficiency to markets in europe.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today's vote successfully concludes a crucial process for completing the regulation of the financial markets of the european union, of which mifid and mifir are the essential pillars. parliament and council reached an important agreement to provide stability and certainty to market operators, supervisory authorities and member states by accepting the commission's proposal to delay the application of the legislative package and the transposition of the directive by one year, allowing operators and authorities to adapt the it infrastructures for the collection of data needed to implement the new rules. parliament has been consistent in bringing this process to a rapid and effective conclusion. thanks to the initiative of parliament and the rapporteur, and with the support of the negotiating team, this quick fix also provided an opportunity to make timely amendments to the two texts, which will make their application more consistent with the objectives of the legislative intervention and with the overall regulatory framework. in this connection, i would ask mr lamberts to read the texts rather than to engage in polemics which i consider to be totally inappropriate if one reads the nature of the changes which have been made, which are designed to make the legislation more consistent and effective. i would also point out that securities financing transactions are already covered by the securities financing transactions regulation and are not essential for price determination. the mifid rules are a key element in the effort to harmonise the financial architecture of the union and to create the single rulebook which is a necessary precondition for the creation of a single union market for investment services and capital markets. we therefore reiterate the need for the commission to swiftly adopt the second-level legislation necessary to complete the regulatory framework and ensure its full application by january 2018.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, at the point we are at, it is inevitable that we will reach 3 january 2018 to ensure more effective and transparent data collection infrastructures for both esma and national authorities. the truth is that we have to be more cautious when introducing reforms of this scale without setting credible and certain time targets, without equipping ourselves with the appropriate tools to ensure the transition phase, for example by empowering esma with financial and human resources. we are thus helping investors, savers and consumers and making the fight to make financial markets more transparent more credible. we cannot set ambitious targets in our legislation and leave it to itself. the postponement of one year is therefore not a concession but a necessity which the various institutions must not squander.

in writing. ‒ the framework convention on tobacco control, signed in 2003, aims to reduce smoking-related diseases and deaths through a comprehensive approach. it is therefore clear that the elimination of illicit trade in tobacco products is an indispensable component of the achievement of such objectives. in short, the contracting parties are obliged to take all necessary measures to combat illegal production, counterfeiting and smuggling. in view of these considerations, i voted in favour, considering that these practices are not only harmful to the eu budget, but above all extremely harmful to the health of citizens.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the szejnfeld report approving the protocol to the world health organisation's framework convention on tobacco control. this instrument is the most important international initiative in this field and aims to stop a criminal practice that seriously threatens not only public health but also states, generating huge annual losses estimated at over eur 10 billion per year. the protocol introduces new licensing rules and a number of new obligations concerning the retention of documents, the regulation of internet sales, duty-free sales and international transit. adopted in seoul on 12 november 2012, it will need to be ratified by 40 parties to enter into force. the adoption of the text by the eu and its member states can be a real step forward towards the entry into force of this important instrument. the european union is also committed to the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment.

in writing. ‒ in today's vote i have expressed my positive opinion on the conclusion of the protocol in question under the world health organisation's framework convention on tobacco control, as it represents the most important international initiative undertaken so far in the fight against illicit trade in tobacco products. the agreement includes a complex set of measures, rules and strategies aimed at securing the supply chain of tobacco, tobacco products and manufacturing equipment through the establishment of a comprehensive traceability and traceability system. other provisions to ensure control include licensing rules, document retention requirements, regulation of internet sales, duty-free sales and international transit. new offences have also been introduced and issues relating to liability and payments in the event of confiscation, as well as the disposal of confiscated products, have been addressed. the aim is to strengthen international cooperation, including through mutual administrative assistance in customs matters. ratification by all participating countries and organisations will benefit public health and facilitate the international fight against illicit tobacco trade, tax evasion and organised crime.

in writing. ‒ enhanced cooperation is the procedure which allows at least nine member states to proceed to closer integration or cooperation in a particular area of european law. this allows the member states to move at different speeds in order to achieve objectives which are considered urgent. in this case, cooperation was sought in relation to decisions on matrimonial property regimes, with which the eastern european countries have shown some scepticism. i voted in favour of this procedure, since the conditions laid down in the treaties are met.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the cavada report on enhanced cooperation on international matrimonial property regimes. this is a procedural measure approving an earlier council decision authorising the development of enhanced cooperation in the matters concerned, as provided for in article 20 teu and articles 326 and 327 tfeu. enhanced cooperation has become necessary following the refusal of some countries to support two projects proposed by the commission in 2011. the launch of this procedure, overcoming the deadlock, will allow 23 member states to continue to integrate on issues concerning the recognition and enforcement of decisions on international couples' property regimes, matrimonial property regimes and the property effects of registered partnerships.
in writing. ‒ the report on enhanced cooperation on international couple's property regimes responds to a request from 18 member states, including italy. this is not a proposal from the top of the eu institutions, but comes directly from the states to improve cooperation in this specific area. i therefore intend to support it with my vote.
in writing. ‒ i supported the text voted on today, whereby the european parliament gave its approval to the establishment of enhanced cooperation between 18 eu member states, including italy, in the area of jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of decisions on international matrimonial property regimes, with reference to matrimonial property regimes and the property consequences of registered partnerships. the need for enhanced cooperation arises from the desire to provide a clearer and more comprehensive legal framework for many international couples who are often faced with problems arising from different, sometimes even conflicting, national property regimes. the main purpose of enhanced cooperation is therefore to treat the matrimonial property regime of couples in a consistent manner, to provide greater certainty in the identification of the competent court, while still allowing the parties to enjoy a certain degree of autonomy in the choice of the applicable law. the aim is to avoid the aggregation of parallel proceedings or the issuing of conflicting judicial decisions, by providing legal certainty, simpler procedures and greater predictability for the increasing number of international couples in the union.

in writing. ‒ mifir and mifid are the cornerstones of financial market regulation, seeking to encourage the competitiveness of financial markets through the creation of a single market for financial services and investment activities and through a high degree of harmonisation of investor protection in europe. stabilising financial markets and being transparent with consumers is a priority for us, but we must consider the timing needed to ensure that the implementation of reforms in this area is effective and realistic. i therefore support mr ferber's report, which welcomes the commission's request to delay the application of mifid ii by one year, to january 2018. this will, inter alia, set reasonable and realistic deadlines for esma and national authorities.
in writing. ‒ regulation (eu) no 600/2014 and directive 2014/65/eu regulate markets and securities brokers with a view to improving transparency and supervision of financial markets and conditions of competition in the field of trading and clearing of financial instruments. to that end, the new regulatory framework introduced requires trading venues and systematic internalisers to provide competent authorities with financial instrument reference data that describe in a uniform manner the characteristics of each financial instrument falling within the scope of the regulatory framework. for the purpose of efficient and harmonised data collection, the european securities and markets authority is developing, in cooperation with the national competent authorities, a financial instruments reference data system. given the complexity of the drafting of this instrument and in order to ensure legal certainty and avoid any market disturbance, i support the proposal to extend the time-limits for the entry into force of the regulation and the directive in question.
in writing. ‒ after careful consideration and discussion in the house, i have voted in favour of the report amending the directive in question, as i believe that the lack of data collection infrastructures has important implications for the entire scope of directive 2014/65/eu. without data it is not possible to establish precisely which financial instruments fall within the scope of the new regulatory framework. a new infrastructure is being developed for efficient and harmonised data collection. to that end, the european securities and markets authority, in cooperation with the national competent authorities, is in the process of establishing a system of financial instrument reference data. the january 2017 deadline will not be met by member states that have to apply the measures transposing the directive. it is therefore more than appropriate to extend the date of application of the entire regulatory framework, including all delegated and implementing acts, by one year. it is not necessary for me to dwell on the danger to legal certainty and to market disturbances of failure to comply with this transposition by the deadline.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the request to postpone the entry into force of the mifd and mifir from 3 january 2017 to 3 january 2018. the delay is justified solely by the inefficiency of the institutions in producing the second-level acts concerned.
in writing. ‒ i considered that i would vote in favour of the measure as regulation (eu) no 600/2014 and directive 2014/65/eu set requirements for the authorisation and exercise of investment firms, regulated markets and data reporting services providers, harmonise the regime of position limits on commodity derivatives in order to improve transparency, promote orderly conditions for price formation and prevent market abuse, and also introduce rules on high-frequency trading and improve financial market supervision through the harmonisation of administrative penalties. in addition, by developing existing rules, the new regulatory framework also strengthens investor protection by introducing strict requirements on organisation and conduct of business.
in writing. ‒ i agree with this proposal for a directive because i believe that the centrality of the financial system in the european economy justifies additional controls over those required of firms in other sectors (and often excessive ones!). businesses must be free to make their own choices and thrive on them, but only if they take full responsibility for the direct and indirect effects. since this is often not the case in the financial sector, it is good that controls are intensified for the benefit of the sector itself as well as all those downstream.
in writing. ‒ in order to improve transparency and to promote orderly pricing conditions and to prevent market abuse, regulated financial instruments are necessary. rules on high-frequency trading should be introduced and financial market supervision should be improved by harmonising administrative penalties. i voted in favour because, by improving the existing rules, the new regulatory framework would also strengthen investor protection by introducing stricter requirements.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution because the amendment of the transposition date is essential and urgent in order to enable the european authority esma and the national authorities to complete the construction of the data collection infrastructure, avoiding the risks of market disturbances and improving the competitiveness of financial markets. however, i believe that in future we should be more careful and cautious in setting the time-frame for the entry into force of the regulations, because postponing a date of transposition could have a negative impact on the guarantee of legal certainty, especially in a sensitive and closely monitored area such as the markets for financial instruments. investors and savers need to find a sound financial environment, free from uncertainties, in which to develop their potential. at the same time, member states must be able to transpose directives in a linear manner, without additional costs and procedural uncertainties. it is our task as co-legislators to ensure that this is so by putting the commission's departments in the best possible position to do their job.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report as i consider it appropriate to extend the deadline by which member states will have to apply the measures transposing directive 2014/65/eu and consequently repealing directive 2004/39/ec. this is due to the size and complexity of the data that esma and the national competent authorities are required to collect and process, which does not allow the infrastructure necessary to ensure its proper functioning to be built within the timeframe set, and therefore undermines legal certainty, creating possible market disruption.
in writing. ‒ i abstain from the report because in some sectors the supervisory instruments have proved insufficient to prevent speculation and dominant positions.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the agreement on the postponement of the entry into force of the markets in financial instruments directive (mifid ii), the related regulation (mifir) and the related secondary acts to 3 january 2018 because i believe that these two very complex and important regulatory acts are two key pillars to support the stability of financial markets, while providing certainty to the supervisory authorities of the member states and esma to ensure uniform application. the legislation lays down requirements for the authorisation and operation of investment firms, regulated financial markets and data communications service providers, harmonising existing legislation, in particular that on commodity derivatives, in order to prevent market abuse. they were sacked at the end of the last legislature in response to the financial crisis, which originated in the us in 2008 and later spread to the eu. however, the complexity of the matter and particularly the need to allow the it infrastructures responsible for the collection of data to be fully operational made the referral necessary. the european parliament and the council have therefore accepted esma's call to postpone the entry into force and to reschedule the entire implementation schedule provided for in the two legislative acts.
in writing. directive 2004/39/ec, also known as the markets in financial instruments directive (mifid), provides harmonised regulation for investment services across the eu. it lays down requirements in relation to a number of elements, such as investor protection, market integrity, enhanced competitive mechanisms, market efficiency and improved governance systems for investment firms. the mifir (markets in financial instruments regulation) on the other hand lays down, inter alia, uniform requirements in relation to the disclosure of trading data to the public, the reporting of transactions to competent authorities and the trading of derivatives on organised venues. i believe that in a very technical discipline such as this, it is a priority to establish a coherent framework for the creation of an integrated and competitive financial market by identifying uniform european rules, which is why i am voting in favour of mr ferber's report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 2014/65/eu on markets in financial instruments as regards certain dates. the delay will allow the data collection system to be ready and operational, and will also support the information and operational system. to quote the text: 'in order to ensure legal certainty and to avoid potential market disturbances, it is necessary and justified to act as a matter of urgency to extend the date of application of the entire regulatory framework, including all delegated and implementing acts. "
in writing. ‒ we welcome the report on the securities market. although it is an area in which regulation is necessarily difficult to understand because of its extreme complexity and the level of detail reached, regulation of the products which are the object of the activity of banks and investment companies. the mifid legislative package, together with the legislation necessary for its implementation, has been designed and developed by the european securities and markets authority together with the european commission over the past two years. the market in financial instruments is not yet harmonised across the eu countries, although it is one of the keys to achieving a single market. mifid is a set of rules that aims at fairness in markets in consumer protection, transparency and simplicity of financial products. the specifications of the legislative package in question also include a set of rules designed to prohibit or restrict the use of instruments that are potentially dangerous or harmful to the stability of markets.
in writing. ‒ considering that directive 2014/65/eu and regulation (eu) 600/2014 are fundamental acts for european financial regulation and promote a detailed collection of data and information on the various financial instruments, considering that the collection of such complex data makes it difficult for member states to transpose the european directive within the time limits provided for therein, considering, moreover, that the proposal of the colleague to postpone by one year the date of transposition of directive 2014/65/eu and the date of repeal of the previous one allows states to equip themselves with the necessary infrastructure for the collection of data, i considered it appropriate to vote in favour.
in writing. ‒ article 93 of directive 2014/65/eu on markets in financial instruments requires member states to apply the measures transposing that directive from 3 january 2017. however, due to the size and complexity of the data to be collected and processed, neither the national competent authorities nor esma (european securities and markets authority) are able to ensure that the necessary data collection infrastructures will be in place and operational by that date. therefore, in the light of the exceptional circumstances and in order to allow esma, the national competent authorities and stakeholders to complete the operational implementation, it is appropriate to extend by 12 months, until 3 january 2018, the date by which member states are to apply the measures transposing directive 2014/65/eu. to allow all this, i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ the report by mr ferber proposes some changes to the date of implementation of the markets in financial instruments directive. in april 2014, the european parliament had approved both mifid ii, an updated version of mifid, and mifir, the accompanying report of mifid, which was expected to be implemented by member states by january 2017. due to some difficulties encountered in the implementation of these measures, the commission proposed to postpone the implementation of mifid ii and mifir to 2018. in voting in favour of the report presented in plenary, i gave my approval to this postponement, which will make it possible to clarify certain points of the legislation and will also make it possible to build complex information systems for the application of the new package. these measures represent an important step forward in financial matters, in the sense of greater harmonisation of investment services throughout the european union. i would like to stress the importance of these packages, which are aimed at increasing competition and consumer protection in the investment services sector. i am therefore of the opinion that the implementation of those measures cannot be postponed beyond 2018.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of extending the transposition of directive 2014/65/eu on markets in financial instruments for member states by 12 months, i.e. until 3 january 2018. since neither the parties concerned nor the national authorities are able to ensure that the data collection infrastructure is operational by that date, i consider it necessary to extend the entire regulatory framework.
in writing. ‒ this is a technical report with the objective of extending the entry into force of mifid and mifir from 3 january 2017 to 3 january 2018, since esma and the european commission have not provided the regulatory technical standards and delegated acts within the deadline set by the legislation. in addition, this report provided a good opportunity to submit a further amendment to the text of the mifid/mifir. in fact, some exemptions from transparency requirements for transactions involving derivative contracts for own account have been proposed through amendments co-signed across the board by several political parties (s&d, epp and alde). firstly, we think that the one-year extension is unreasonable, since it is mainly due to the inefficiency of the eu institutions in producing second-level acts. secondly, we are strongly opposed to the inclusion of exemptions for derivative and other financial contracts as this could undermine the stability of the financial system. that is why we voted against it in the plenary.
in writing. ‒ after the financial scandals of the past and the present, europe needs tougher regulation of financial markets. the report requests an extension of the entry into force of mifid and mifir, citing a failure to provide regulatory technical standards and delegated acts within the deadline set by esma and the commission. it seems unreasonable and unjustified to postpone further legislation on this matter. in addition, certain exemptions for transactions in derivative contracts have been inserted. that is why i voted against.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the ferber report on the securities market, market abuse and securities regulation. this is a technical measure amending certain dates in regulation (eu) no 600/2014 on markets in financial instruments, regulation (eu) no 596/2014 on market abuse and regulation (eu) no 909/2014 on the improvement of the previous securities regulation in the european union and on central securities depositories. these instruments established a new regulatory framework for securities markets, securities brokers and trading venues following the outbreak of the international financial crisis. the amendment of the provisions was necessary in order to extend the date of application of the entire regulatory framework, including all the delegated and implementing acts envisaged, by one year and to complete certain parts.

in writing. ‒ the key element of these reforms is to make financial markets more stable and better monitored, in line with the commitment to strengthen the global financial system made at the g20 in pittsburgh. there are no substantial changes compared with the proposals of two years ago, but technical amendments to the package have been drawn up which improve its provision and make its application more consistent with the regulatory framework. of course, since these are highly complex provisions requiring the collection of enormous amounts of data and the use of complex technological systems, it is important that there is agreement between the commission, parliament and the council to ensure that the second-level legislation necessary to complete the regulatory framework is adopted quickly and to give operators the time necessary to adapt the it and technical infrastructures for data collection and the implementation of the new provisions. that is why i support the report.
in writing. ‒ regulation (eu) no 600/2014 and directive 2014/65/eu regulate markets and securities brokers with a view to improving transparency and supervision of financial markets and conditions of competition in the field of trading and clearing of financial instruments. to that end, the new regulatory framework introduced requires trading venues and systematic internalisers to provide competent authorities with financial instrument reference data that describe in a uniform manner the characteristics of each financial instrument falling within the scope of the regulatory framework. for the purpose of efficient and harmonised data collection, the european securities and markets authority is developing, in cooperation with the national competent authorities, a financial instruments reference data system. given the complexity of the drafting of this instrument and in order to ensure legal certainty and to avoid any market disturbance, i support the proposal to extend the time-limits for the entry into force of the regulation and the directive in question.
in writing. ‒ after careful analysis and debate in the house, i voted in favour of the report amending the regulations under consideration, as i believe that limiting positions in commodity derivatives, introducing rules on high-frequency trading and introducing strict requirements on organisation and behaviour will improve the transparency of financial markets and strengthen investor protection. investment firms often carry out, on their own initiative or on behalf of their clients, transactions in derivative contracts or activities involving several linked transactions. such a package of transactions allows investment firms and their clients to better manage risks, as the price of each element of the package of transactions reflects the overall risk profile of the package rather than the current market price of each element. the package of transactions can take various forms, from trading strategies executed on trading venues to tailor-made packages of transactions. it is important to take these specificities into account when calibrating the applicable transparency regime. it is therefore appropriate to specify the specific circumstances in which pre-trade transparency should not apply to bundles of transactions or to any single element of such transactions.
in writing. ‒ i voted against the report which contains the request, which is totally inappropriate and not in the interests of the citizens of the european union, to postpone the entry into force of the mifd and mifir by one year. my negative vote is also due to my opposition to the inclusion of the many exemptions for derivative contracts and other financial contracts which are dangerous to the stability of the financial system.
in writing. ‒ in 2014, following the financial crisis, the european union introduced a new regulatory framework to regulate securities markets, regulating financial intermediation operations. this package of rules, known as mifid ii, strengthens investor protection by introducing strict requirements. the rules were due to enter into force on 3 january 2017, but technical difficulties encountered in adapting the electronic data collection networks by linking trading venues, national regulatory authorities and the european securities and markets authority (esma) suggest that the application of this new system should be postponed. i considered that i would vote in favour of the directive as i agree that the challenges posed by the technical implementation of the reform are such that the data needed for the functioning of the system cannot be effectively collected and therefore neither the competent authorities nor the market operators would be in a position to apply the new rules on 3 january 2017. this would end up creating a situation of legal uncertainty which could be detrimental to the development of the market.

in writing. ‒ the procedure for appointing the members of the court of auditors is governed by article 286 tfeu. according to the article, those who have collaborated with supervisory institutions and who have the required guarantees of independence are eligible. the council shall adopt the list of members after consulting parliament, without binding decision. in short, it is a purely political procedure, without any real democratic control by the parliamentary body. for these reasons i voted against. i do not only think that the procedure is completely inappropriate, but above all there is a strong gender imbalance in the composition of the court, which the member states should resolve as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ the court of auditors is a major european institution which acts as the external and independent auditor of the union's accounts. established in 1977, it became a full eu institution only in 1993 and has continued to provide its support for improving the management of the community budget. it is composed of one member from each member state, each of whom is appointed by the council after consulting parliament and serves for six years. on this occasion, parliament was asked to give its opinion on the appointment of mr rimantas šadžius. i have taken note of the contents of the report of the committee on budgetary control and, following the instructions of my political group, the s&ds, i have voted in secret on the name proposed.
