in writing. ‒ the global financial crisis has led the european union, together with the g20, to address the role of international financial reporting standards on financial stability and growth, in particular with regard to loss-recognition rules in the banking system. the motion for a resolution on international financial reporting standards, which i have supported today, deals with ifrs 9 which is one of the main responses to the financial crisis by the international accounting standards board (iasb). the new instrument will improve accounting problems by introducing a new model for the classification and measurement of financial instruments, a new criterion for the valuation of expected losses and new rules for the recognition of hedging instruments. however, some concerns remain about the impact of ifrs 9 on the banking, insurance and financial markets in general and therefore the iasb needs to strengthen its capacity to analyse the impact, paying particular attention to the macroeconomic dimension.
in writing. ‒ the resolution on the international financial reporting standards ifrs 9 presents some critical issues that could create future problems for companies in our territories. that is why i have decided not to support the text with my vote.
in writing. ‒ i support the parliament's report on the adoption of international financial reporting standards (ifrs 9) and share the concerns raised about the commission's lack of clarity. in particular, the potential negative impact of ifrs9 on long-term investments in the absence of a quantitative impact assessment remains open. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover the whole of the eu. the path to recovery from the crisis and return to economic growth requires clarity on the priority to be given to increasing investment. in this connection, we must stress the need for coherence between eu actions, such as the european fund for strategic investments, and more technical provisions which risk inhibiting rather than stimulating investment itself.
in writing. ‒ ifrs 9 is one of the iasb's main responses to the financial crisis. it is an improvement on ias 39 in that the change from a 'loss sustained' to a 'loss expected' model addresses the 'too little, too late' problem in the recognition of credit losses. the key point to be borne in mind is that in the case of ifrs 9, there is no adequate quantitative assessment of the impact on financial markets and financial stability. therefore, a phased-in mechanism should be developed to mitigate the impact of the new impairment model by avoiding sudden impacts on capital ratios and bank lending. the accounting treatment of certain directly or indirectly held financial instruments in ifrs 9 is also of concern, as this could be contrary to the general objective of promoting long-term investment; it is therefore necessary to ensure that ifrs 9 is functional to the eu strategy. ifrs 9 will have to comply with the capital integrity directive and the accounting directive. the iasb will need to conduct a post-implementation review of ifrs 9 to identify and assess the undesirable effects of this principle, in particular on long-term investments.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the resolution on ifrs 9 which is one of the main responses of the international accounting standards board (iasb), the body responsible for the issuance of international accounting standards, to the financial crisis. ifrs 9 will improve the problems arising from the accounting treatment of financial instruments by introducing a new model for the classification and measurement of financial instruments, a new valuation criterion for expected losses and new accounting rules for hedging instruments. however, i think we need to understand better the impact of ifrs 9 on the banking sector, the insurance sector and the financial markets in general, but also on the financial sector as a whole. i therefore call on the iasb to strengthen its capacity for impact analysis, particularly in the macroeconomic field.
in writing. ‒ in my view, accounting rules which are often too weak or not harmonised have contributed to the expansion of the global financial crisis, especially in relation to the excessive use of fair value (as the reference value for the accounting of financial instruments), i will vote in favour of the motion for a resolution to achieve more european international accounting principles to achieve financial stability. moreover, the g20 and the de larosière report had already pointed out, before the crisis, certain specific concerns about accounting principles, including: accounting for profits and losses, underestimation of the accumulation of risks and lack of a common and transparent methodology for valuing unrealised assets. during the crisis, the delay in recognising losses on loans and other financial assets was recognised as one of the main sources of weakness in the existing principles. the change in the measurement of the loss allowance shall be carried out in accordance with the following: however, a proper assessment of the implications is needed: i therefore invite the commission and other supervisory authorities to monitor implementation and prepare an ex post impact assessment.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution because, in view of the general situation of economic uncertainty, the continuous change in markets and the need to use appropriate instruments to detect and evaluate new financial instruments, the commission should assess the potential effects of ifrs 9 on long-term investments and on the european rules already enacted in this area by further studying the impact of ifrs 9 in particular on the banking sector, the insurance sector and financial markets in general.
in writing. ‒ the role of international financial reporting standards (ifrs) in relation to financial stability and economic growth has increased in the light of the global financial crisis, which has highlighted the weaknesses and shortcomings of the system. we have therefore welcomed the reform and the introduction of new rules to limit the risks for the future. the new accounting principles were drawn up, precisely in the wake of the financial crisis, in order to ensure greater transparency. however, a number of open issues remain on which the commission and other financial authorities will need to act to present proposals, in particular on the insurance sector and the impact on long-term investment, ensuring a proper ex ante impact assessment on the effects of the new rules. the season of uncertainty about the rules, which has had such a negative impact on small savers, is now over. it is now a matter of going all the way to ensure that the system has the right transparency and the necessary resilience.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the ep resolution on the international financial reporting standards ifrs 9 because i strongly shared the call from the econ committee for greater transparency in the implementation of international accounting standards because of their importance for financial stability and growth and specifically with regard to the rules on loss recognition in the banking system. the main objective of ifrs 9, which is due to enter into force on 1 january 2018, is to ensure greater transparency with regard to credit risk by opting for an asset-based approach that should be more responsive to developments in the credit cycle. in other words, it is the main response of the international accounting standards board (iasb) to specific aspects of the financial crisis and its impact on the banking system, reducing the level of complexity that the previous accounting standard, ias 39, had. at present, there is no impact assessment and there are serious concerns about the potential effects of the application of these rules on investment, as they could foster some volatility. long-term investment must be considered as a 'public good' because of its positive effects on growth.

in writing. ‒ there are many materials that come into contact with food today: packaging, cooking utensils, dishes and so on. these materials, when they come into contact with food, can transfer their components to it. for this reason, it is clear that there is a need for greater harmonisation at eu level for non-harmonised materials. for example, specific measures based on scientific evidence could be implemented, giving priority to those materials which pose a particular risk to human health. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ annex i to the framework regulation on materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs lists 17 materials that could be subject to specific regulation. only four of these are currently listed as such: plastics (including recycled materials), ceramics, regenerated cellulose and active and intelligent materials. the resolution voted by parliament today calls on the commission to develop the necessary measures on the 13 materials not yet regulated at eu level, taking into account the evaluation carried out by the european parliament's research service and existing and developing national measures. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation. there is a broad consensus that the lack of uniform measures at community level in this area could jeopardise public health, environmental protection and the proper functioning of the internal market. the european union therefore has a duty to respond to this regulatory vacuum which can pose a risk to its citizens.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the implementation of food contact material regulation because i believe it is a solid legal basis for preventing risks to human health. moreover, this resolution strategically asks the commission to prioritise the drawing-up of specific eu measures for paper and board, varnishes and coatings, metals and alloys, printing inks and adhesives, and calls for further scientific research into the integration between different chemicals.
in writing. ‒ food contact materials (fcms), depending on their composition and properties, behave differently when they come into contact with food, transferring their components to it. under these circumstances, the chemicals released can be harmful to human health. the regulation lays down general safety requirements for all possible materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs. specific measures have been adopted at eu level for four csfs: plastics, ceramics, regenerated cellulose and active and intelligent materials. for the other csfs, member states take specific measures at national level, but having to comply with different national rules is neither efficient nor effective. in addition, this creates problems for the different national standards on product safety. it is also necessary to improve and strengthen existing legislation and enforcement for the protection and protection of the health of consumers.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the report on food contact materials (fcms), which are used daily to pack food, because we must avoid that they can release dangerous chemicals into food or alter the composition of food, seriously harming human health. food contact materials are subject to legally binding european standards, established by framework regulation (ec) no 1935/2004. the regulation lays down general safety requirements for all possible materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs and also provides for the possibility of adopting specific measures for the materials listed in annex i to the framework regulation. specific measures have been adopted to date for only four csfs: plastics, ceramics, regenerated cellulose and active and intelligent materials. the absence of specific measures within the eu for most of the food contact materials listed in annex i to regulation (ec) no 1935/2004 creates real barriers to the internal market. greater harmonization in this area, through the adoption of specific measures based on scientific data, could be a step in the right direction, an important step towards protecting the health of citizens.
in writing. ‒ food contact materials (fcms) are widely used in everyday life in the form of food packaging, cooking utensils, tableware, and so on. when coming into contact with food, and depending on their composition and properties, different materials may behave differently, transferring their constituents to food and risking harm to human health or altering the composition of food. it is good to remember that only some of these materials, such as plastics and ceramics, have been thoroughly tested for safety and public health. others such as paints, varnishes, inks and adhesives are not covered by eu standards and still need to be tested. i voted in favour of this resolution calling for stricter safety standards at eu level.
in writing. ‒ although regulation (ec) no 1935/2004 laying down general safety requirements for all materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs has been in force for more than ten years, there are still major shortcomings in the implementation and enforcement of the existing legislation, especially as regards specific measures, some of which have been defined at european level, which have so far covered only certain materials listed in annex i to the regulation, such as plastics (including recycled plastics), ceramics, regenerated cellulose and active and intelligent materials. there are still other materials, such as wood or printing inks, for which the member states have regulated themselves in the absence of specific european measures. we are faced with a clear disparity in safety standards which can only be addressed by action taken at european union level both to improve the implementation of the legislation and to avoid barriers to the internal market, and above all to protect the health of consumers. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ in the light of the needs identified for the gaps in regulation (ec) no 1935/2004 on materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs, i approve the report. it should be noted that of the 17 materials covered by the 2004 regulation, only four are harmonised at european level, while the remainder are governed by national rules, which creates problems. these difficulties result in a strong inconsistency in the application of laws and sanctions: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. unfortunately, this behaviour not only creates competitive disadvantages but also health risks. in view of the above, it is essential to define specific measures to be taken where these are lacking, while ensuring the full implementation of what is already in place. the funds available to the european food safety authority should therefore be used to develop and update information on controlled materials and to study the substances used in their production and those added unintentionally (nias). it is also necessary to clarify and assess the risk posed by the so-called cocktail effect and multiple exposures.

in writing. ‒ the current regulation on food contact materials provides for specific measures on 17 substances. to date, only 4 have been harmonised at eu level, while for all the others member states retain the possibility of adopting national provisions. this lack of harmonised measures at eu level creates different safety standards and a consequent loss of competitiveness and innovation in the internal market. on the other hand, materials not covered by specific eu measures may pose a risk to public health and lead to a loss of consumer confidence, legal uncertainty and higher compliance costs for operators. for these reasons, i consider it a priority to draw up specific community measures which can strengthen and harmonise the regulatory framework, ensuring that a level playing field is created and that better controls are carried out in the member states, so that the materials in direct contact with our food are safe.

in writing. ‒ the protection of the health of citizens is, as it should be, at the top of our concerns. the current legislation on materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs must be reviewed as soon as possible to ensure that these materials do not present health risks. particular attention should be paid to risk assessment, traceability, regulatory effectiveness and controls. these materials are widely used, every day, for food packaging, food preservation, kitchen utensils and so on. depending on their use and chemical composition, they can alter the properties of food and release toxic or endocrine-disrupting substances. it is therefore necessary to develop analytical and toxicological tests to be carried out on these materials in order to ensure the highest degree of safety for consumers and, where possible, to provide for the use of safer alternative materials. at the same time, reuse and recycling should be encouraged as part of the development of the circular economy. i therefore fully support the measures proposed in the report and hope that the commission will put them into practice as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ the rapporteur calls on the commission to review the current regulatory framework in order to facilitate the implementation of the legislation and to better achieve its objectives, namely the protection and protection of the health of consumers and the guarantee of an effective functioning of the internal market. regulation (ec) no 1935/2004 lays down the general safety requirements for all possible materials and articles intended to come into contact with foodstuffs (mca). it also provides for the possibility of adopting specific measures for the 17 materials listed in annex i to the framework regulation. this report analyses and develops the following issues in order to address urgently the current shortcomings in the implementation and application of the legislation in force: the risk assessment, traceability, enforcement and compliance checks. a further finding concerns the fact that some member states do not require companies producing or importing mca to officially register their economic activity, which is a significant obstacle to the implementation of appropriate controls. in conclusion, i believe that action at eu level is needed to address the lack of common specific measures and to close the gaps in risk assessment, traceability of compliance and controls. i voted to approve it.

in writing. food contact materials (fcms) are widely used in everyday life in the form of food packaging, cooking utensils, tableware, and so on. when coming into contact with food, and depending on their composition and properties, different materials may behave differently, transferring their components to food. we in the m5s have fought for the inclusion in the report of an amendment of our own which calls for a ban on the use of bisphenol a, an endocrine disruptor, in all materials in contact with food. there is now a large body of scientific literature which has demonstrated the health damage caused by the ingestion of such and such substances. the current regulation allows agreements on 17 substances, but only four of these are currently harmonised at eu level. the rest is the responsibility of the member states. the lack of harmonised rules causes problems for consumers, businesses and authorities. for us in m5s, this means that the single market is not a single market: some countries have high standards, some countries have low standards. food safety must have the same meaning throughout the eu and that is why i voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. ‒ the report analyses the periodic report on the application of eu rules by member states. i do not agree with what it says: i think that it does not take into account the real problem facing the eu, namely excessive regulation and the continuing attitude of censorship towards national parliaments which are transposing legislation which often has a strong and negative impact on the socioeconomic fabric of their territories. it is enough to think of the damage caused in italy by the directive on services to the seaside resorts and the travel trade. for all these reasons i voted against this text.
in writing. ‒ the commission's 2014 annual report on monitoring the application of european union law contains valuable insights. the european union is founded on the rule of law and its institutions must ensure that community policies and priorities are applied uniformly throughout europe. the report shows that the sectors of environment, transport, internal market and services were the ones where the highest number of infringements occurred in 2014. however, the number of formal infringement procedures has decreased over the last five years: this improvement is due to the introduction of the 'eu pilot' procedure, a mechanism which opens up a constructive dialogue between the commission, the 'guarantor of the treaties', and the member states found to be in breach of european rules, before a formal infringement procedure is opened. the report, which i support, stresses the need for greater transparency in the application of community law and greater involvement of the european parliament. transparency and information on infringement procedures can and must help to strengthen the trust of community citizens in the european union.
in writing. ‒ i endorsed the resolution on monitoring the application of union law because we are aware that it is the timely and correct transposition of eu law into national legislation which enables the intended benefits of eu law to be delivered to individuals. i believe that parliament can support the work of the national parliaments by sharing its expertise in the legislative decision-making process.
in writing. ‒ monitoring the application of eu law shows that there are still many cases where infringement proceedings are open concerning the effective implementation and practical application of eu law. it can therefore be said that the application of eu law is still not sufficiently transparent and that its effectiveness is systematically undermined by its unsatisfactory application by the member states and by unsatisfactory verification by the commission. many of the eu directives, particularly those in the economic and financial fields, have not been transposed by many of the member states. it is often the imposition of unrealistic deadlines for the implementation of legislation that makes it impossible for member states to meet them. financial penalties for non-compliance with union law should be effective, proportionate and dissuasive and should take into account the repetition of the failure to comply in the same area. delays in transposition constitute an obstacle to the proper functioning of the internal market and are contrary to the interests of citizens and businesses, depriving them of certain of their rights.
in writing. ‒ this year's report focuses on the effectiveness of the 'eu pilot' system, which provides for a continuous exchange of information between the commission and member states in order to prevent possible infringement procedures. the rapporteur stresses in particular that the decrease in the number of infringement procedures could be linked to the steady decrease in appeals lodged by the commission and not to the actual effectiveness of the eu pilot programme. the report also criticises the commission for failing to implement a number of proposals from the european parliament, including the development of a rule to regulate european administrative law.
in writing. ‒ effective and timely application of eu law is a prerequisite for a clear legislative framework and for strengthening the credibility of the european institutions. the report shows that the number of formal infringement procedures has decreased over the last five years, but i think it is necessary to analyse the origins of this outcome. it is difficult to assess to what extent the reduction in the number of infringement procedures actually represents greater respect for the law and better transposition of european standards or rather an increase in compromise solutions between the european commission and the member states. i believe that parliament can play a significant role in assessing the application of the law, but that its access to information on procedures is still too limited to allow it to carry out a thorough review, especially as regards the eu pilot procedure. i therefore join the rapporteur, heidi hautala, in her call for greater transparency and constructive interinstitutional dialogue in facilitating parliament's access to files on cases of breaches of union law.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this report which analyses the 2014 report on the application of eu rules by member states. the report is limited in describing the reasons that often lead member states to apply eu legislation beyond the time limits. i believe that the delay in transposing the directive is the result of excessive european legislation.
in writing. ‒ i agree with the 2014 annual report on monitoring the application of european union law. in particular, i think it is extremely important to encourage the clarification and transparency of national rules adopted through the transposition of eu law and to specify which national authorities are responsible for their proper implementation. as the rapporteur has pointed out, this is a right which belongs to the citizens of the union, since it is based on the rule of law and the certainty and predictability of the laws. i also believe that there is a need for greater clarity in the relations between parliament and the european commission as regards the eu pilot procedure. finally, i am pleased to note that, in comparison with the statistics in the report, italy's infringements are declining.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report as it provides a comprehensive picture of the actual implementation and practical application of eu law. the three sectors most affected by infringement proceedings in 2014 were the environment, transport and the internal market for services, but the last five years have seen a general decrease in proceedings, also thanks to an effective policy of dialogue with member states.
in writing. ‒ the primary responsibility for the correct implementation and application of eu law lies with the member states. however, the commission has a key role in monitoring the application of eu law and in presenting its annual report to parliament and the council. the european parliament has a decisive role in the political control of the commission's implementing measures. in this context, i believe it is essential to increase the use of certain existing instruments at european level to help improve the application and enforcement of eu law in the member states, in line with the new interinstitutional agreement on better law-making. in particular, the informal 'eu pilot' mechanism promotes closer and more consistent cooperation between the commission and the member states in order to remedy breaches of eu law at an early stage, so as to avoid having to resort to the formal infringement procedure. i believe that monitoring the effective transposition of eu law into national legislation is a way not only of preventing infringements but also of bringing the expected benefits to citizens and of giving credibility to the european legal system and its institutions.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the commission's annual report to promote the effective implementation of eu law by both candidate and non-candidate countries, as well as countries with association agreements with the eu, and to improve transparency and cooperation. i also supported the report to give parliament a more structured role in the analysis of compliance with eu law.
in writing. ‒ i am voting against the report which makes little mention of the shortcomings of eu hyper-regulation and continues to favour a censorship attitude towards national parliaments.
in writing. ‒ after the vote in the juri committee, we also adopt a report in plenary which makes an important point on the application of european union law. i appreciate the work of mrs hautala, who has highlighted in particular cases of infringements for the non-transposition of eu directives and regulations in the fields of the environment, transport and the internal market, which touch on issues crucial to the lives of so many of our citizens. i think it is useful that the report also stresses the difficulty of parliament being informed about the various infringements and calls for a thorough review of the right of access to all the various cases, it is a crucial point of transparency and democracy.
in writing. i am voting in favour of the 2014 annual report on monitoring the application of european union law. this brings us to the 32nd commission report, which once again provides useful information on the actual implementation of eu law practices. the report shows that the sectors of environment, transport, and internal market and services are the ones with the highest number of infringement procedures in 2014. at the same time, however, the report shows that there has been a decrease in the number of formal infringement procedures over the past five years. however, the report concludes that we should take into account the new proposals made by the administrative law working party in order to improve the application of eu law. it is also recommended that parliament play a more specific role in analysing the procedures for compliance with eu law in the candidate countries and those with association agreements with the union, and that it put in place support plans for the countries involved in this area.
in writing. ‒ respect for eu law must be a priority for the commission, the european institutions in general and, above all, the member states. making this as transparent as possible would increase citizens' trust in the eu, avoiding misunderstandings and manipulations that instead end up fomenting unjustified euroscepticism. the commission is responsible for monitoring the measures taken by the member states and ensuring that their legislation complies with community law. the european parliament, on the other hand, has the responsibility to monitor the commission's monitoring activity and the interest in ensuring that the legislation it produces is actually transposed by the member states. the commission's annual report on monitoring the application of european union law states that the number of formal infringement procedures has decreased over the past five years, thanks to the effectiveness of the structured dialogue between the commission and member states under the eu pilot. the eu pilot system has proved to be a good one, but it is not sufficiently transparent. i therefore share the regret expressed in the report that, despite repeated requests, the commission has still not ensured adequate access to information on the eu pilot procedure and on pending cases before the relevant parliamentary committees.
in writing. ‒ the european commission, in the proper performance of its duties, is called upon to play an active role in the development of various instruments aimed at improving the implementation, application and enforcement of union law in the member states. to this end, in a union based on the rule of law and the certainty and predictability of laws, eu citizens must be able to know in a clear, accessible, transparent and timely manner whether and which national rules have been adopted by transposing eu law and which national authorities are responsible for their correct implementation. it is therefore appropriate to give effect to financial penalties for failure to comply with community law. the rapporteur believes that the proposals made by the new working group on administrative law set up by the legal affairs committee could be a valuable source of inspiration for the commission. i think it is appropriate to highlight that the european parliament should play a more structured role in analysing how the candidate countries for accession, and the countries with association agreements with the european union, comply with eu law. i voted in favour of approving this annual report.
in writing. ‒ the text voted on is the 32nd annual report (for 2014) drawn up by the european parliament after carrying out specific checks on the application of european law between the 28 member states. the analysis carried out shows that the sectors where serious shortcomings persist are the environment, the internal market in transport and services. at the same time, however, infringement procedures have decreased, which shows that the european commission's decision to follow the line of dialogue before sanctions is working.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the 2014 annual report on monitoring the application of european union law. the report shows that the environment, transport, the internal market and services remain the three sectors with the highest number of infringement proceedings opened in 2014, despite the fact that the number of proceedings has decreased over the past five years. the commission considers that this decrease is due to a more effective dialogue with the member states in the context of the eu pilot procedure, but the report stresses that parliament still has limited access to information on this procedure and on pending cases. it is therefore difficult to see whether the reduction in the number of formal procedures really reflects a greater respect for eu law by member states and not rather an increase in compromise solutions between the commission and non-compliant countries. the aim of this report is therefore to ensure greater transparency in the application of eu law by the member states.
in writing. ‒ the commission has asked efsa to assess whether new elements have emerged that would alter the conclusions and recommendations of efsa's scientific opinions on the cultivation of the genetically modified bt11 maize. this resolution, considering that the risk assessment of cultivation carried out by efsa is incomplete and that the risk management recommendations proposed by the commission are inadequate, asks the commission to withdraw the draft implementing decision. i voted yes.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the objections to the marketing for cultivation of two types of genetically modified maize seeds, including bt11. i believe that the current regulatory framework does not allow the commission and efsa to provide adequate assessments of the impact of gmos. in the case of bt11 maize in particular, the concern is the presence of the cry1ab protein which confers resistance to pyralid from european maize and pyralid from mediterranean maize. there is a risk of harm to some species of butterflies and moths, calling into question the concept of 'acceptable local mortality' introduced by efsa for some lepidopteran species. , i therefore decided to vote in favour of the objection, reaffirming the need for the commission to draw up a comprehensive proposal on gmos as soon as possible in order to carefully assess the environmental and health impact of these technologies and to establish a new procedure for their authorization.

in writing. ‒ i supported the resolution on the decision concerning the placing on the market for cultivation of genetically modified maize bt11 seeds because in that resolution we criticise the draft by the commission and we consider its risk management recommendations inadequate. thus, with this vote i called on the commission to withdraw its draft implementing decision.
in writing. ‒ genetically modified bt11 maize expresses the cry1ab protein, which is a bt protein conferring resistance to european maize pyralid and mediterranean maize pyralid; and the pat protein which confers tolerance to the herbicide glufosinate ammonium. it should be borne in mind that glufosinate is classified as toxic for reproduction and therefore the cultivation of genetically modified bt11 maize is prohibited in the various territories. it is considered that the risk assessment of cultivation carried out by efsa is incomplete and that the risk management recommendations proposed by the commission are inadequate. furthermore, the draft commission implementing decision is not consistent with union law because it is not compatible with the objective of protecting human health and the environment when gmos are deliberately released into the environment for purposes other than placing on the market within the community and when gmos are placed on the market within the community as such or contained in products. the commission should therefore withdraw the draft implementing decision.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this objection today because i believe that the risk assessment of cultivation carried out by efsa is incomplete and that the risk management recommendations proposed by the commission are inadequate. to date, the safety of genetically modified bt11 maize seeds has not been demonstrated. there are still serious gaps in the data. the draft commission implementing decision is not consistent with union law as it is not compatible with the objective of directive 2001/18/ec which aims, while respecting the precautionary principle, at the approximation of the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the member states and at the protection of human health and the environment when genetically modified organisms are deliberately released into the environment. i therefore ask the commission to withdraw the draft implementing decision.

in writing. ‒ the genetically modified maize mon 810 expresses the cry1ab protein, derived from bacillus thuringiensis, which confers protection against certain species of lepidopteran parasites, including maize pyralid and maize nightshade. the placing on the market for cultivation of seeds of genetically modified maize mon 810 was initially authorised by commission decision. unfortunately, there are still persistent shortcomings in the implementation of post-market environmental monitoring; and efsa is forced to constantly reiterate its monitoring recommendations, in particular the need to provide more detailed information on the sampling methodology, to reduce the risk of bias in the selection of the questionnaires for farmers, as well as to ensure the identification of all relevant scientific publications. however, the risk assessment of efsa on cultivation is incomplete and the risk management recommendations proposed by the commission are inadequate. furthermore, the draft commission implementing decision is not in accordance with union law, as it is not compatible with the objective of ensuring a high level of protection of human life and health, animal health and welfare, the environment and consumer interests, while ensuring the effective functioning of the internal market.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this objection today because i believe that the risk assessment of the cultivation carried out by efsa is incomplete. in addition, the renewal of the authorisation for genetically modified maize mon810 seeds threatens the non-gm organic and conventional farming in europe. under the new eu rules on the use of gmos, once a gmo is authorised for use in europe as a food or feed, member states have the option of whether or not to allow a particular gmo to be used in their food chain (opt-out measures). unfortunately, member states that have not chosen to use opt-out measures to prohibit the cultivation of specific gmos on their territory have generally not applied effective measures to prevent contamination of non-gmo or organic maize. spain, for example, where most of the gmo maize in europe is grown, has no specific rules regarding isolation distances, buffer zones or mandatory information for authorities or adjacent growers. experience shows that it is almost impossible for organic and conventional farmers to grow maize in areas where gm mon810 maize is produced. i therefore ask the commission to withdraw the draft implementing decision.

in writing. ‒ as a signatory to the objection resolution, i voted in favour, as i believe that until democratic scrutiny of the european commission's decisions has been strengthened and correctly reflects the opinion of the majority of member states, meps and european citizens, no gmos should be authorised. in addition, for the three gm maize, there remains a lack of data and incomplete risk assessment, there are no comprehensive analyses on non-target species such as aquatic insects, risk mitigation measures are inadequate and impracticable, as demonstrated by the definition of 'refuge areas' or 'distances from protected habitats' measures which have proved ineffective, or there remains a strong threat to gmo-free or organic crops, which are threatened by possible contamination.

in writing. i voted in favour of the resolution which strongly calls on the european commission not to authorise the placing on the market of products made from genetically modified maize mon 810. since the beginning of my mandate i have always fought to make europe a gmo-free territory, without ifs and without buts. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the transgenic food and feed is not introduced into the european territory without any prior authorization. the lack of long-term studies on the nutrition and toxicity of gmos and insufficient risk assessment has led many member states to ban the cultivation of these organisms on their national territory. but if the cultivation necessarily takes place in the territory of a member state, their trade crosses borders, which means that a national ban on 'sale and use' proposed by the commission would be impossible to apply without reintroducing border controls on imports. if the authorization is renewed, millions of tonnes of gm feed will be circulating in europe, feeding our animals and indirectly feeding us. i have fought with my colleagues in the m5s for a europe free of gmos by promoting this resolution.
in writing. ‒ the legislative proposal of 22 april 2015 amending regulation (ec) no 1829/2003 was rejected by parliament on 28 october 2015 on the grounds that, while the cultivation of gmos necessarily takes place within the territory of a member state, their trade crosses borders, meaning that a national ban on 'sale and use' proposed by the commission would be impossible to apply without reintroducing border controls on imports. the resolution therefore calls for the withdrawal of the commission's draft implementing decision as it is not in line with union law, being incompatible with ensuring a high level of protection of human life and health, animal health and welfare, the environment and consumer interests in relation to genetically modified food and feed. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the objection to the placing on the market of products containing, consisting of or produced from genetically modified cotton 281-24-236 × 3006-210-23 × mon 88913. i believe that the current regulatory framework does not allow the commission and efsa to provide adequate assessments of the impact of gmos. in the case of cotton 281-24-236 × 3006-210-23 × mon 88913, in particular, the problem is the presence of the modified cp4 5-enolpiruvil-shikimate-3-phosphate synthase protein (cp4 epsps), which confers tolerance to glyphosate-based herbicides, a substance that the international agency for research on cancer has listed as a probable human carcinogen. in view of the possible health risks, i therefore voted in favour of the objection, reaffirming the need for the commission to draw up a comprehensive proposal on gmos as soon as possible in order to carefully assess the environmental and health impact of these technologies and to establish a new procedure for their authorization.

on behalf of the efdd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, what is the point of living in a community if the rules are not the same for everyone? the european union is also a customs union: there are no frontiers between countries, only external frontiers, so that goods entering the romanian customs area arrive without controls on the italian market and vice versa. it is therefore important that european customs apply similar procedures, controls and sanctions. the european parliament is about to adopt by a large majority a directive to harmonize the framework of customs sanctions. at present, those who do not comply with the rules have to pay a fine, and if this fine varies according to the country, of course, they will bring the goods in where they pay less if they are "tipped". the penalties must therefore be harmonised: the european parliament is almost unanimous on this, but some eastern european countries, led by germany and the netherlands, are blocking it because they have no intention of changing things, or rather because it is in their interest not to change. the customs issue is not just a question of sanctions, but also of controls and procedures. i will be reporting to the inta committee on a major process of reflection on the future of european customs, and i believe that the unblocking of this dossier is essential to continue. i am tired, frankly, and i think many, many citizens are tired of a europe where everyone eats, but only some pay the bill. a europe of solidarity only when it suits you: the economy, immigration, taxation and now customs. it is time to say enough to those who use the union for their own interests.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, mr vice-president, the primary objective of this directive is to harmonize at european union level the different national rules on customs infringements and the resulting penalties. the ineffectiveness of customs controls at key points of entry to the single market is now facilitating the movement of illegal goods throughout the union. for example, some major european seaports are too easy a landing for counterfeit goods. the achievement of a genuine customs union is hampered by the fragmentation and heterogeneity of rules and standards which prevent the proper functioning of the european single market and put citizens and consumers at risk. in this connection, we welcome the fact that the determination of penalties should be linked, where possible, to the principle of evasion of duty in order to ensure that they are more closely linked to the seriousness of the infringement. the future of the european economy will depend to a large extent on how our continent manages to establish trade relations with other parts of the globe. but all this requires a legal framework that is fully complementary to the principles and best practices of the wto, which on the one hand facilitates trade with third countries and on the other guarantees the repression of all those illegal activities that put our security and competitiveness at risk.

the agenda includes the report by laura ferrara, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the fight against corruption and the follow-up to the crim resolution (2015/2110(ini)) (a8-0284/2016).
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament is taking a significant step forward today. to combat the spread of corruption and organised crime effectively, a debate at european level was needed to introduce common laws and measures to combat it in all member states. this europe has been guilty of a grave crime: the fight against corruption and organised crime, including mafia-style crime, has been confined to strictly national borders. the lack of awareness of the transnational scope of this phenomenon has thus given easy play to the mafia and, more generally, to criminal organizations which, also taking advantage of corruption, have identified new businesses by infiltrating the management of migrant reception centres or by seizing tenders financed with european funds or by investing in the main financial centres, thus benefiting from the lack of recognition of the dangers of the association phenomenon in some member states. this calls for urgent and decisive regulatory action at european level to stop the spread of criminal organisations across the continent, to combat the most common crimes committed by mafias and to prevent the infiltration of criminal associations into the legal economy. the european parliament is doing its part with great commitment and conviction, amidst a thousand difficulties arising above all from cultural and legal differences, from the prejudices against the various forms of criminal organizations rooted in the member states. the way was paved during the last parliamentary term, and we are now completing it, not only to introduce a common concept of the crime of association with mafia-type criminals, but above all to adopt a shared and effective strategy to combat organised crime, corruption and money laundering. it is hoped that the other european institutions will also fully understand the real dangers of these phenomena, which are now transnational, and that they will not only focus on the fine crimes but also become aware of the dangers of membership of the association. these are phenomena which are not only affecting the legal economy but also the whole of civil society on which the european union is based. ladies and gentlemen, let me first of all thank my shadow rapporteurs for the excellent cooperation and the interesting and productive discussions that have taken place during all the meetings. let me also thank the european parliament's research centre for its study on the costs of the european union's failure to act in the fight against corruption and organised crime, which was essential in providing us with the information and objective basis for the preparation of the report. a special thanks goes to eurojust for responding to the questionnaire we sent and providing us with important information on how to improve cooperation and the exchange of information between member states. i would also like to thank europol for the many meetings that have taken place and for the valuable information it has provided, particularly on the more practical aspects of coordination between the different procedures in the individual countries and on how to overcome the difficulties encountered. the european commission is to be thanked for always being available for discussions and debates on the fight against corruption and organised crime. a special thanks goes to those citizens who contributed to the drafting of the report on the internet and in particular on the rousseau portal of the 5 star movement, thus taking an interest in first person and providing us with important suggestions. i would also like to thank all those who have tabled a number of amendments to the report, which also show that the issue is a matter of great concern at transnational level and is not a national phenomenon. i thank the rapporteurs for the opinions of the deve and cont committees and i thank, let me thank, all the staff, young and old, and all the staff who, believing in the work being done, have contributed passionately to the work of this report.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, organized crime is undoubtedly a global threat and as such it requires a joint and well-balanced response from the european union and the member states. due to the evolution of the modus operandi of criminal organisations, the complexity of this phenomenon and the danger of infiltration into the business, institutional and political fabric of the member states has not yet been fully realised. some european legislation should therefore be interpreted in such a way as to restrict the activities of whistleblowers. the latter play a major role in the fight against corruption and their work is of fundamental importance in preventing or detecting illegal acts. it is of the utmost importance that the european union insist on combating organised crime and that, as part of a genuine and comprehensive european anti-corruption strategy, efforts and resources be focused on combating money laundering, corruption and human trafficking.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with mr ferrara's report the european parliament is once again shining a spotlight on a phenomenon, corruption, which has extended its sphere of influence beyond national borders. the crim committee has helped to bring the debate on the fight against corruption to the international stage by providing clear guidance on legislative action to be taken. but the answers we expect from the union can only be obtained by starting from a common definition of organised crime, which is essential to give effect to existing and future legislative instruments. today we are operating in a heterogeneous environment, not only in terms of the definition of the phenomenon but also in terms of the provisions for combating it, which are even absent in some countries, which makes it more difficult to combat organized crime and corruption. i am convinced that this issue should be addressed in the framework of cooperation in criminal matters within the union by working on the mutual recognition of confiscation and seizure orders. and to hit the real centre of interest of organised crime, the most concrete action is the freezing and confiscation of assets from crime, although unfortunately many states have not yet transposed the relevant 2014 directive.

the agenda includes the report by ignazio corrao, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on the responsibility of companies for serious human rights violations in third countries (2015/2315(ini)) (a8-0243/2016).
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, this report calls on the european parliament to take a stand on an urgent matter and to set in motion a legislative process leading to concrete and effective responses in this area. the issue of corporate liability for serious human rights violations in third countries, which are still governed by ineffective rules, affects many of the fundamental human rights, such as the protection of health and the environment or the rights of workers, children and women. the main objective of this report is to ensure that urgent, coherent, continuous and effective action is taken at all levels, by addressing in concrete terms the legal problems arising from the multinational nature of enterprises and their activities. this dimension is one of the reasons for the frequent uncertainty about the attribution of responsibility for human rights violations, and this is precisely what all too often leads to impunity for the perpetrators of such violations. the report i am presenting in this house today, which has been my work for the last year, calls loudly for the introduction of binding rules which reiterate the duty of business to respect human rights wherever and however. it called for the introduction of rules which reiterate the obligation of states to protect, within their jurisdiction, natural persons who have suffered or may suffer human rights violations, including when committed outside their own territory. we therefore call on the member states to establish clear rules to ensure that companies domiciled in their territory, and operating within their jurisdiction, respect human rights in all their activities and in every country and context in which they operate. we strongly emphasise that where there are allegations of serious human rights violations, member states must ensure that victims have access to effective redress, as has been repeatedly called for by all the ngos and all the civil society and academic actors we have involved in the preparation of the report. we also call for the creation of minimum criminal standards defining cases and sanctions also for cases of human rights violations by companies with a transnational dimension. i would like to emphasize one of the many zero-cost but extremely effective measures proposed in the report i am signing. i am referring to the creation of a european 'abuse free' brand which could represent a major change in the corporate culture. a trademark granted to companies which voluntarily apply for it and which therefore decide to submit to effective and rigorous controls by independent bodies. this will enable consumers to make informed choices. all these issues have been the subject of a long, constructive and passionate debate between the political parties. i am proud that a report on a potentially divisive subject has been adopted almost unanimously in the committee on foreign affairs. i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs for their valuable contribution and for the willingness they have shown in recent months to help draft a good parliamentary report on such an important subject. finally, i would like to thank all the activists of the five star movement and all the citizens who have wanted to participate in the drafting of this report. thanks to the rousseau operating system, which allows its members to participate in the political life of the network, many citizens have had the opportunity to learn about this draft report and to express their views. all their comments have been carefully considered and some of them have been converted into amendments to my signature and have been incorporated into the text voted in committee. it is direct democracy, where the citizen becomes an institution and participates in the construction of a law or a report of initiative. this report will be voted on tomorrow by this house in the hope that it will be only the beginning of a real path towards an effective and concrete fight against human rights violations committed by companies in third countries.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, unfortunately, i would say periodically, cases of human rights violations in third countries by multinational companies and european groups are being discovered. this is particularly serious, because, since the european union is founded, among other things, on respect for human rights, european companies should set an example in the world in the field of corporate responsibility. i share the document. i only regret that the text has not dealt more deeply with the issue of child labour, which is still widespread in some parts of the world. for example, an amnesty international study found that 16 multinational electronics companies are customers of companies that produce batteries using cobalt from mines in the democratic republic of congo, where some 40,000 children work. it is therefore necessary that all companies, european and non-european, exercise what is known as 'due diligence' and that all countries have clear rules for respecting human rights in business activities.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in 2016 the rights of workers around the world have been weakened, not only by worsening working conditions, but also by restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. one issue, that of labour exploitation, involves the responsibilities of governments and companies, the latter often guilty of very serious violations of workers' rights. in the middle east and africa, millions of workers live in conditions of slavery. in many non-european countries, workers do not enjoy the right to strike, they face restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly and are often the victims of physical violence and threats. the european union must work to ensure that trade and human rights can both be strengthened. the business community, particularly in third countries, is obliged to respect human rights in all their forms. the union must be able to establish a trade and investment policy with third countries based not only on market requirements but also on ethical values.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption of a european union strategy on liquefied natural gas would help to achieve a rapid transition to a sustainable, secure and competitive energy system and to end dependence on external gas suppliers. however, the fact that the existing lng infrastructure in the european union is significantly under-utilized and that the demand for gas continues to be overestimated is not a secondary consideration in this assessment. ex ante impact assessments on the actual added value of the construction of new lng transport and storage infrastructure should be carried out, taking into account the potential for optimising the efficient and safe use of existing storage infrastructure, including gas storage. i believe that the european union and its member states should focus more on renewable resources and energy efficiency improvements, seeking to maximise the benefit of renewable generation capacity and limiting investment in new infrastructure for the transport and storage of lng to areas of low interconnection and to supplying the most vulnerable member states.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, effective control of fishing activities is essential to ensure the sustainable exploitation of marine biological resources and to maintain a level playing field between the fleets of the european union. unfortunately, it must be pointed out that the diversity of the fields of application of controls and the places where they are carried out in fact have discriminatory effects with regard to controls. in some member states, controls are carried out from the vessel to the table, while in others only certain links in the chain are checked, excluding, for example, the transport of catches or catering. there are too many provisions on the control of fishing activities, some of which are even contradictory, and there are too many derogations and exceptions. it would therefore be desirable to simplify and revise regulation no 1224 in order to establish a community control system to ensure compliance with the rules of the common fisheries policy and to improve the implementation of the rules in the various member states, in particular by encouraging greater harmonisation of the rules. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, isabelle thomas.
member of the commission. – mr president, we greatly appreciate the report by isabelle thomas and the work of the rapporteur, the shadows and their teams. effective fisheries control is indispensable if we want to improve the governance of the oceans and we, the european union, can only make a credible case for effective controls outside the eu if our own record is clean. therefore the commission is now evaluating the regulation on control of fisheries for assessing its implementation and the impact on the common fisheries policy five years after its entry into force. this makes the report very well timed and useful, as it complements the work carried out by the commission. the findings and recommendations of the report will feed into our own work and will be taken into consideration in conceiving the next actions needed for improving the current system of control of fisheries. the regulation on control of fisheries, which entered into force in 2010, changed significantly the previous control system, introducing the use of new technologies, a new management system and new principles and obligations. thanks to this reform, the fishery control system has improved, and this has led to an overall increase in compliance with the common fisheries policy. however, if some good results have been achieved, still more should be done. preliminary assessment of the regulation on control of fisheries shows that, while there is a good legal framework, improvements can be made, particularly on its implementation by the member states. in brief, the report stresses that the different implementation in the member states and their diverse commitment in its application hinder – as was said by a number of speakers – the level playing field among operators and therefore their confidence in the system and respect of the rules. the implementation by member states greatly differs in the sanctioning system and control procedures and methods in the management of control, the training of inspectors, technologies and tools used, it development and data sharing and exchange. all these have been noted. the principles embedded in the report go very much in the same direction as the commission’s policy. we all recognise that having a uniform and harmonised control system of fisheries contributes to ensuring a level playing field of operators across europe. this is important, not only in terms of treatment, but in the very end fundamental for ensuring sustainable fishing. compliance with the common fisheries policy (cfp) cannot be achieved without awareness and support from fishermen and, in order to achieve this, we need to have their trust and cooperation. we agree with the report on the importance of continuing to fight illegal fishing and to strengthen the quality, completeness and reliability of catch data. we also agree on the underlying need to strengthen collaboration between member states themselves and also between member states, the commission and the european fisheries control agency, including the need to share control data in real time. the contribution of the european fisheries control agency to the level playing field in the control of fisheries is critical. their activities and operational coordination, development of standards and training are greatly appreciated by all stakeholders. compliance with the rules of the common fisheries policy is improving. its enforcement relies on a comprehensive and sound control system with dissuasive, proportionate and effective sanctions applied by member states. so effective actions by member states remain essential. let me thank you once again for this report and the fruitful discussion. we look forward to further working with the parliament in a good spirit of cooperation.

in writing. ‒ the transmission of personal data may only take place after the implementation of the provisions on data protection contained in the provision of the national legislation of the territories of the member states concerned by the transmission. this provision shall not apply to member states where the transmission of personal data has already been initiated pursuant to the 2005 prüm treaty. the verification of the conditions for automated data exchange should be carried out on the basis of an evaluation report, which should include a questionnaire developed by the council working party on automated data exchange, an evaluation visit and a pilot test. denmark completed the data protection questionnaire and the dna data exchange questionnaire and successfully conducted a pilot with the netherlands. in addition, an evaluation visit took place in denmark. it is therefore agreed that the conditions allowing the council to conclude that denmark has fully implemented the general provisions on data protection have been met. parliament approves council's proposal to launch automated dna data exchange in denmark.

in writing. ‒ the eu-china agreement on the reciprocal exemption from the visa requirement for holders of diplomatic passports for short stays was signed by the eu and chinese heads of negotiation on 3 and 4 november 2015. it provides for visa-free travel for citizens of the european union holding a valid diplomatic passport or eu laissez-passer and for citizens of china holding a valid diplomatic passport who are travelling to the territory of the other party for a maximum period of 90 days in any 180-day period. the agreement takes account of the specific situation of the united kingdom and ireland, which will therefore not participate in the agreement. in addition, a joint declaration annexed to the agreement refers to norway, iceland, switzerland and lichtenstein, whose authorities are invited to conclude visa waiver agreements with china. the agreement also contains provisions concerning france and the netherlands, so that it applies only to the european territories of these two member states. the european parliament welcomes the conclusion of this agreement as it will facilitate people-to-people contacts which are essential for the development of economic, cultural, scientific and other links.

in writing. ‒ the continuation of the global economic and financial crisis that began in 2008 is weighing on national financial resources as member states pursue the necessary fiscal consolidation policies. in this context, it is particularly important, in terms of investment for growth and jobs, to ensure that programmes supported by the esi funds (european structural and investment funds) are implemented smoothly. at present, however, this is difficult to implement, both because of procedural problems and because of the liquidity problems resulting from the budgetary consolidation. this is particularly true for the member states most affected by the crisis which have received financial support through an adjustment programme. it would perhaps be helpful if a temporary mechanism were set up at european union level to allow the commission to increase reimbursements on the basis of expenditure certified under the esi funds and to recognise a higher co-financing rate for all operational programmes of countries in difficulty receiving support from the erdf and the esf.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the amendment to regulation (eu) 1303/2013 on financial management for certain member states, which allows countries in greater financial difficulty to benefit from more support from europe. in this period of severe economic crisis, it is important to ensure that they have easy access to the european structural and investment funds. the amendment to the regulation in question makes it possible to increase the so-called 'reintegration' payments to those countries which need to regain financial stability, such as cyprus, ireland, romania and portugal. at present only greece benefits from a financial assistance programme and therefore the extension of these provisions will also apply to the above countries. supporting recovery and investment efforts will allow these countries more time to balance their budgets, manage eu-guaranteed financing projects efficiently and lead to greater development of their national economies. the changes will not affect the eu budget as the temporary increase in payment appropriations will be offset by a reduction in payments towards the end of the 2014-2020 programmes.

in writing. ‒ the proposal for a report is to amend regulation (ec) no 91/2003 on rail transport statistics. the amendments concern the optimisation of the use of existing information that can be used for statistical purposes. it is therefore provided that the commission, after consulting the european statistical system committee, is to send a report to the european parliament and the council by 31 december 2020 and every four years thereafter. the commission will have to take into account all relevant information provided by the member states concerning the quality and methods used. the collection and dissemination of data will be carried out by eurostat in consultation with the commission, which will be responsible for defining the modalities by means of delegated acts. i therefore voted against the rejection amendment, in the same spirit as i supported the importance of monitoring and data collection in this important area.

in writing. ‒ on first reading, parliament decided that the scope of the regulation on rail transport statistics should be extended to infrastructure data, in particular the application of the european rail traffic management system (ertms). parliament stressed that it was extremely important to have a clear vision of the development of ertms in the union and considered it very important that european citizens have easy access to data on the implementation of eu policies. to avoid duplication of work between eurostat, the commission and the european railway agency (era), it is necessary to strengthen cooperation between these institutions and to ensure that statistical data relating to eu policies are easily accessible to citizens and stakeholders. agreement on a simplification of the regulation on rail transport statistics was possible following the signing of two memoranda of understanding between eurostat and the commission and between eurostat and afe. these memoranda of understanding are important tools for optimising the use of existing information and reducing administrative burdens and are useful for meeting the requirements for better use of rail transport statistics.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of amending the regulation in question because it improves, through a series of measures, the instruments for developing rail transport statistics. firstly, it extends the scope of transport statistics to infrastructure data and, finally, it makes practical in terms of operational the application of the european on-board railway traffic management system (ertms), which has so far proved ineffective due to delays and irregularities in its application. secondly, it allows eurostat to publish statistical data on stations without architectural barriers, in order to facilitate access for disabled persons who are not able to use the service. finally, it provides for close cooperation between eurostat and the european railway agency (era) to ensure the improvement of railway accident statistics, including those involving dangerous goods and involving level crossings.
in writing. ‒ the proposal aims to amend an earlier regulation with the aim of optimising the use of information for statistical purposes. the commission has the lead role alongside eurostat and is required to compile a report on the implementation of the regulation every four years. i had no hesitation in voting in favour.
in writing. ‒ good data collection on freight, passengers and accidents and the production of targeted statistics are necessary tools to enable timely monitoring of rail transport. only through proper monitoring can we identify the most important challenges to be addressed in the sector and achieve a common transport strategy. i believe in particular that such statistics are essential to strengthening european action on transport safety. therefore, i believe that the european commission's directorate-general for mobility and transport and the european railway agency should extend the scope of data collection to include timely information on infrastructure and in particular on the application of the european rail traffic management system (ertms). i appreciate that the report calls on eurostat to submit and make public data on railway stations providing assistance to disabled persons or persons with reduced mobility. i hope that eurostat and the european railway agency can further strengthen their collaboration to ensure consistency in the methodology for data collection and analysis.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this proposal because it is a very simple technical measure, which has been stuck for two years because of the refusal of the member states to publish rail transport statistics (rts). i believe that the availability of such specific, detailed and timely data is essential and that statistics on rail freight and passenger transport are necessary for the purpose of monitoring and developing the common transport policy. furthermore, considering that accidents have become a priority issue in the transport policy of the european union, together with the other undesirable effects of transport (such as pollution and co2 emissions), i believe it is essential to collect and disseminate data on accidents, fatalities, serious injuries and environmental damage relating to all modes of transport. i therefore support this proposal, which aims to simplify and optimise the current legal framework for european rail transport statistics and bring it into line with the new institutional framework.
