in writing. ‒ i agree with this report because, while it approves of the monetary policy of expansion pursued by the european central bank, it also stresses that the ecb alone cannot sufficiently stimulate aggregate demand, but that it must be accompanied by ambitious and socially balanced investment and structural reforms by the member states. the euro area continues to be characterised by high unemployment, too low inflation and weak productivity growth. all these are important signs of a lack of investment, of the lack of adequate structural reforms and of weak domestic demand. the report also rightly criticises the fact that the ecb's expansionary policy has had a limited effect on the real economy, because banks have used cheap credit to settle their accounts rather than to finance economic and productive activities. i therefore join the call on the ecb to be more vigilant in ensuring that the resources it puts in place are translated into financing for the real economy and, in particular, for smes.
in writing. ‒ the euro area continues to suffer from the negative effects of high unemployment and wide macroeconomic imbalances. the annual report for 2015 focuses on the core elements of the ecb's activities, namely monetary policies. it provides an assessment of the interactions between monetary policies and structural reforms implemented by the various member states. i believe that the creation of a capital markets union, as well as better cooperation between national economic policies within the eu, can be a decisive step towards improving the effectiveness of the single monetary policy, while also reducing the recurrence of damage from a financial sector shock, similar to that of 2008. i voted in favour of approving the ecb's annual report.
in writing. ‒ in the light of the data, albeit modest, on economic growth, i would like to encourage the ecb to continue to develop a programme of structural reforms in the eu member states. i also stress the importance of a strong strengthening of the powers of the single supervisory mechanism. in conjunction with the monetary policy programmes, the completion of the banking union would provide a window of opportunity for competitiveness to grow in the coming years, with a view to returning inflation to the 2% target. policies to stimulate the economy must be combined with the fight against unemployment, which must be considered an urgent matter and which continues to be one of the causes of the slow economic recovery. despite falling from 2015 levels, there are still significant disparities between european countries, with 24% unemployment in greece and 6% in germany, all the more alarming when looking at youth unemployment figures. it is crucial to address the consolidation of public deficits in a timely manner by highlighting the key role of governments, by giving impetus to policies of growth and support for disadvantaged groups, from research to integration policies.
in writing. i voted against this parliament's report on the ecb's annual report 2015 because it expresses a completely distorted and short-sighted view of reality. this is mere pro-ecb and pro-euro propaganda, which seems to ignore completely the real causes of the problems and the clear failure of monetary policy to counter the crisis. the text celebrates the success of monetary policy and blames the failure of the member states to achieve economic recovery on the failure to fully implement the absurd and unsustainable structural reforms imposed by the commission. the report is clearly unbalanced and even incomplete, as it does not express any critical remarks on the controversial role of the ecb in the troika and especially on the conflicts of interest and the strong asymmetries of the new banking supervision function. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy, and to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances.
in writing. ‒ as every year, we voted on the ecb report. this year the report is particularly controversial: the commission's proposal is based on the principle of subsidiarity and is designed to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. all the ecb's unconventional policies are labelled as successful and the complete independence of the frankfurt bank is emphasised repeatedly. on the contrary, the capacity of states to carry out structural reforms is repeatedly called into question and the failure of policies not provided for in the treaties is blamed on them. no criticism of the ecb's role in banking supervision, let alone in the troika. as i have already done in the econ committee, i voted against this report, with particular reference to the fact that the unconventional policies of the ecb have not only proved to be useless because they have not helped the real economy, but have also been harmful in that, by providing liquidity to the market, they have encouraged speculative activities by banks and increased the risk of speculative bubbles.
in writing. the report, which is submitted annually by the ecb to parliament, describes the measures and policies adopted by the ecb in monetary matters during 2015. in this document all the ecb's unconventional policies are identified as successful policies. instead, the capacity of the states to carry out structural reforms is called into question and the failure of policies not provided for by the treaties but put in place by the ecb is blamed on them. again, we find no criticism of the ecb's role in banking supervision. we in the five star group have tabled amendments which show that the unconventional policies adopted by the ecb have not only proved to be useless because they have not helped the real economy, but have also been harmful. the injection of liquidity into the market has in fact encouraged speculative activities by banks and thus increased the risk of speculative bubbles. the ecb also needs to put an end to an excessive interpretation of its founding treaty, by taking on more functions than originally envisaged, such as participation in the troika and more recently eu banking supervision (ssm). i therefore voted against this report.
in writing. ‒ the following report concerns the creation of a single european market in retail financial services. the report lacks any critical analysis of the consequences of the creation of a single european market. contrary to what is described in the report, the consequences would be very negative, especially for private investors and smes, who would find their access to the markets very restricted. i believe that the above is not a solution at all, but creates and amplifies the macroeconomic imbalances already present on a large scale in the european economy, especially to the detriment of small investors. that is why i voted against.
in writing. ‒ the retail financial services market is still underdeveloped and highly fragmented within the union, with a low number of crossborder transactions. the need to promote effective action in this area has therefore prompted the commission to present a green paper on retail financial services, which was welcomed by the ludvigsson report, which i have supported today. the text underlines the importance of a dynamic approach to policy-making, providing for continuous monitoring of policy implementation at national level and highlighting the main challenges in advancing the retail financial services agenda. the capacity to collect and analyse data at union level should be strengthened, with a greater emphasis on empirical aspects in impact assessments. the absence of unfair differences between member states joining or not joining the euro must be ensured, by supporting the maintenance of a level playing field and ensuring genuine collective financial inclusion. the future of the european retail financial services market needs to be coordinated with the agendas of the digital single market, the capital markets union and the single market strategy; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject.
in writing. ‒ i supported this resolution on the green paper on retail financial services because i shared with the rapporteur the idea of developing the retail financial services market at eu level. indeed, a genuine european internal market for retail financial services will have an important impact both on consumers and competition: the former will have more choices and the latter will lead to lower prices.
in writing. ‒ there are three main reasons why the green paper was presented at the right time. firstly, because it is necessary to ensure that the level 2 measures are fair and adequate and that the implementation is monitored at national level. in addition, little progress has been made to date in building a single market for retail financial services and, due to a large number of barriers, cross-border activity is still limited. this is not good for consumers, innovative businesses or the general functioning of the european economy. finally, if managed well, digitalisation could create the necessary momentum to start removing barriers to cross-border activity. it is necessary to advance the agenda for retail financial services by strengthening the union's capacity to collect and analyse data, by making identification work in practice and by creating and maintaining a level playing field. the needless differences between eu and non-eu member states must also be eliminated. for the single market to be truly effective, its integrity must be maintained within this essential element. finally, it is crucial to ensure that everyone is included. financial exclusion must be reduced drastically.
in writing. ‒ after careful reflection and debate in the house, i have voted in favour of the green paper on retail financial services. i believe that the reason why retail financial services at eu level are still underdeveloped is the lack of transparency of transactions, which has a negative impact on consumer confidence. it follows that i have great difficulty in imagining the development of coordination with the digital single market, firstly because of the lack of respect for the principles of cooperation and exchange of information and privacy profiles. however, i am convinced that coordination with the digital single market is a necessary and useful way forward, given the ease with which communication exchanges take place in the digital world. robo-advisory, the latest frontier of fintech, will soon be a reality.
in writing. ‒ the commission green paper report does not analyse the negative impact of the liberalisation of the retail financial services sector, either from a macroeconomic or financial stability perspective. it does not take into account that, instead of creating a real improvement in competition in the sector, the market configuration will favour the production of standardised and increasingly complex instruments, which are difficult to access for small investors and smes. the proposed solution therefore risks exacerbating the macroeconomic and financial imbalances existing within the euro area, especially in the absence of effective preventive protections for investors. this is an intervention which would not bring any benefits to the real economy and which is liable to be harmful. i therefore voted against it.
in writing. ‒ retail financial systems, in each national context, offer citizens a range of essential services. however, in the absence of a european market at present, it is difficult for consumers in one member state to buy products supplied in another member state. the creation of a single market through digitalisation would make it possible to overcome differences in price and choice within the union, facilitating cross-border transactions to the benefit of both consumers, who would benefit from a wide range of products, and businesses, who could make their products available anywhere in the union. i believe that for this ambitious project to be realised it is essential to ensure that consumers are better protected, that they are properly informed and that there is greater transparency. i therefore voted in favour of the report because i believe it is crucial that the commission, in preparing an action plan for 2017, tries to identify and remove the barriers that hinder consumers and businesses from cross-border opportunities. in this connection, i believe that it is essential to improve the use of new technologies and to strengthen the fight against fraud and tax evasion in order to achieve a fairer single market.
in writing. ‒ i vote against this report, which expresses strong support for the european commission's activities, without taking into account the criticisms it has expressed. nor is there any mention of the fact that opening up the single market for financial services could bring down the business of firms based in member states with a more fragile economic situation, such as italy.
in writing. ‒ one of the key challenges facing europe is to make its financial system as transparent and as close to savers and businesses as possible. i therefore regard the adoption of the green paper as an important piece in this unfolding mosaic of legislation. the aim is to open up the european market for retail financial services, thereby achieving better outcomes in terms of benefits and protection for consumers and businesses. the aim is to bring the users of these services progressively closer together by removing the many obstacles to the single market, which is still underdeveloped and highly fragmented. the dynamics of high concentration and low competition which characterise this market certainly do not make it attractive because of the limited choice and unsatisfactory cost-benefit ratio. the green paper will provide a solid consumer protection framework, including the extension of its scope to digitalisation and financial technology innovation, which are the producers of revolutionary and potentially valuable services, reducing transaction costs and improving product comparability. these methods will help to achieve a wider inclusion of savers, start-ups and smes, thus facilitating access to finance and opening up cross-border markets.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because it highlights one of the major issues in retail financial services, namely inclusion and financial literacy. in order to achieve the completion of the capital market union, it would be necessary to ensure equal opportunities for all consumers to access essential financial services, including through non-digital channels in order to avoid financial exclusion. moreover, in the current context of an increasingly financial market, it is necessary for the protection of consumers to ensure and promote sound and thorough financial education enabling citizens to make the best possible assessment of the investment opportunities offered. finally, in encouraging the digitalisation of financial services, it is appropriate to take into account both new benefits and new risks, which may affect both consumers and the technological infrastructures of the sector.
in writing. ‒ while supporting the commission's priority to identify the barriers faced by consumers and businesses and ways to overcome them, especially in the use of new technologies, the econ report stresses the need to ensure consumer protection through further action to enable consumers to make informed decisions, to increase the transparency of retail financial products and to remove barriers to consumption and any unjustified costs related to them or to withdrawal from a product. the socialist and democratic group's contribution to this text was decisive in strengthening consumer protection while seeking to maintain specific safeguards to facilitate cross-border transactions and the development of new services to digitalisation. i therefore consider this text to be a very important step by the institutions towards consumers in order to increase their confidence in the markets.
in writing. ‒ the green paper on retail financial services highlights the need to create an eu market where consumers are well protected, have equal opportunities and access to simple, transparent and good value for money products, in a harmonised legal framework on standardised default options for the most commonly used eu financial products. it also supports the strengthening of the international fight against tax fraud, tax evasion and tax avoidance, and money laundering, including further efforts to develop a common tax code. however, there are growing concerns about the emergence of new retail financial service providers, such as insurance, and the increasing complexity and engineering of retail financial products. citizens do not always have a clear and full understanding of the products they buy, whereas it is desirable that they are complete, simple, safe and standardised. moreover, while digitalisation will continue to create new opportunities for consumers, investors, smes and businesses in terms of competition, cross-border activity and innovation, it will not solve problems related to the safety and protection of consumers and their investments. for these reasons, i am voting against.

in writing. i voted against this own-initiative report which supports the commission's strategy to create a single market for retail financial services and remove the remaining obstacles to the expansion of cross-border financial activities. i naturally share the objectives of facilitating competition and transparency in the sector, but i believe that the only way to achieve these objectives is through stronger financial regulation and supervision, not through liberalisation, which would have harmful and counterproductive effects, especially in a banking and financial system which has not yet been secured and which is also heavily distorted by the single currency. experience shows the catastrophic consequences of financial liberalisation in an economic area characterised by severe distortions and imbalances. we have seen this with greece, which has become a hostage of the german and french banks, which had fuelled its excessive accumulation of private external debt with soft loans. it is not difficult to foresee that the single market in retail financial services will not increase competition and the protection of retail investors, as the report hopes, but will encourage the concentration and oligopoly of the big too-big-to-fail banking groups and will amplify the already unsustainable financial imbalances in the euro area. i've seen that story before.

today we are wondering how we are responding to the 82% of european citizens who are rightly afraid and who believe that the fight against terrorism is a common european priority. the time has come to choose the direction europe must take. we have already tried cooperation, sometimes strengthened, sometimes not, which does not work. if the future, after brexit, is to be more union, then we need to support a common defence policy, which does not mean having an army to wage war. we must be very careful about the messages we send to our citizens, but rather intervene in hot spots to do prevention above all. after every tragic attack in europe, everyone has pointed out the lack of effective intelligence and cooperation between the member states, a lack which has unfortunately cost us dearly. europe has shown itself unprepared in the face of an enemy that must be sought within and beyond europe's borders, and we can only do this if we aim at a common defence policy, because if the threat is to europe, the response must be european.
in writing. ‒ the report highlights the need to create a 'defence union' to ensure security throughout the european union. the report also stresses some controversial aspects, such as investing part of the multiannual financial framework funds in defence research, allocating 2% of member states' gdp to defence expenditure or supporting nato initiatives. in order to express my concern at the inadequacy of the measures in the report on european defence, i have decided to vote against.
in writing. ‒ while a large number of member states have decided to continue to cut defence spending over the past 30 years, global challenges have increased due to the rise of phenomena such as international terrorism, hybrid threats, cyber and energy insecurity and organised crime. i strongly supported the paet report on european defence union because i believe that it is essential at this historic moment to intensify efforts in this direction. finally, multinational forces must be set up within the framework of permanent structured cooperation and made available to the common security and defence policy. all the duplication, overcapacity and obstacles which lead to an estimated waste of eur 26.4 billion in public procurement today must be reduced by jointly purchasing resources and pooling non-lethal materials such as transport vehicles and aircraft. the creation of a headquarters for planning, command and control of joint operations, together with a complete overhaul of the csdp, are key steps in ensuring that the european union plays a leading role on the global stage, operating in synergy with nato and also taking into account the new political spaces.
in writing. ‒ given the eu's obvious inability to defend its borders, especially the southern ones, which thousands of illegal immigrants enter daily, it seems absurd to me that the disastrous recipe of 'more europe' should also be imposed in the field of defence. i think that further ceding of our national sovereignty is unacceptable, especially in a sensitive and strategic area for every member state, such as defence. for these reasons i did not intend to vote in favour of this text.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution on the european defence union because i strongly believe that the widespread perception of insecurity by european citizens makes the european defence union a matter of urgency. in particular, considering the increase in conflicts at the eu’s borders i believe further integration with regard to defence policies at eu level is needed.
in writing. ‒ due to duplication of administrative staff, overcapacity and obstacles in the area of public procurement in the security and defence sectors, the cost of non-europe is estimated at eur 26.4 billion per year. strategic and military analysts have concluded that if the european union were to truly integrate its defence functions, it would double its defence capability in the event of an attack and save money for its citizens. today, with the us gradually disengaging from the european and mediterranean scenario and with the increase of threats in eastern europe and north africa, the need for an autonomous defence of the european space and the need to develop a rapid response system that is resilient and effective in the face of the hybrid threats of the 21st century is becoming relevant again. the white paper on common defence must be a concrete act for the revival of european defence, it cannot be reduced to a manifesto of good intentions but the first step towards the creation of common armed forces.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of this report today because i believe that a more ambitious security research programme and a ready strategy are needed to proceed with the implementation of the european defence union. in recent years, the security situation in europe and the world has deteriorated dramatically. the threats of terrorism, organised crime and climate change are common fears to the entire world population. the eu therefore has a duty to work to ensure the safety of people and to place this issue among the most important challenges of the immediate future. the commission needs to be effective with its european defence action plan (edap) and make it a key strategic instrument to foster industrial cooperation for the development of defence capability programmes. close cooperation between the commission and the european defence agency (eda) is appropriate to strengthen the industrial and technological base of the defence sector.
in writing. ‒ european security must be guaranteed in the long term. in the report we are discussing we stress the need for political will and determination based on strong and modern military capabilities. we need to define a new model of a council of defence ministers to provide lasting political guidance. the council of the european union will have to set up a permanent meeting of the defence ministers of the member states committed to better synergy between the states. the way forward is through enhanced cooperation in the field of european defence, which will mean greater effectiveness, unity and efficiency. the report rightly emphasizes the priority of defining a preparatory action for a future european defence research programme, and we hope that it will be launched as soon as possible.
in writing. ‒ the multiple armed conflicts and tragic terrorist acts of recent years require concrete actions and new defence strategies from the european union. individual member states cannot respond to these growing threats on their own; eu countries must therefore join forces to ensure security within and beyond their borders. the eu is called upon to play a greater role as a provider of security, promoting european values in full respect of the treaties and human rights. in this respect, i believe that the member states must exploit the full potential of the lisbon treaty in relation to the european defence and security policy (edps) and continue the path towards structured cooperation. appropriate common defence policies at union level and the provision of the necessary resources to ensure their implementation are therefore necessary. i hope that the report will positively encourage the member states to move in this direction and to make a real effort to achieve the objectives set out in the csdp. for these reasons i have decided to support the report.

in writing. ‒ according to the eurobarometer 85.1 of june 2016, around two thirds of eu citizens would like to see the eu become more involved in security and defence policy issues. in addition, the cost of non-europe in the field of defence and security is estimated at eur 26.4 billion per year, due to duplication, overcapacity and obstacles in the field of defence procurement. this resolution seeks to respond to the need to implement a european defence union, building on the unused instruments already provided for in the lisbon treaty. the treaty provides that member states are to make available adequate capabilities for military and civilian missions and operations under the common security and defence policy, through instruments such as permanent structured cooperation and tactical groups. i voted in favour of this resolution because i believe that the full benefits of european cooperation must be exploited to respond to the context of crises and interconnected challenges facing europe. in particular, i believe that we must focus on key elements such as constructive cooperation between the eu and nato, the extension of the athena mechanism, joint work between the commission and the european defence agency in favour of the strategic autonomy and competitiveness of the european defence industry.

in writing. ‒ the international geopolitical situation calls for a common defence policy. the fragmentation of eu defence systems costs almost €26 billion each year. the changing landscape in the east and the south calls for thinking about integrated defence mechanisms, complementary to nato. horizontal coordination between member states is essential to avoid wasting resources and to ensure better results. we need to increase investment in defence, reaching the nato target of 2% of gdp, if we are to have a stronger european position in the atlantic context. at the same time, part of the european budget could be allocated to defence cooperation, including specific requirements in the multiannual financial framework. the creation of a kind of defence schengen is intended to prevent eu policy from being dependent on only a few member states, or from not being a major player in nato's choices. a european defence commissioner, more regular meetings of european defence ministers, structured cooperation mechanisms including the deployment of multinational forces, a framework for technological research in the defence sector which ensures strategic autonomy and enhances european excellence in the sector: these are the final steps towards creating a genuine common european defence.

vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, honourable members, last month you adopted a resolution on syria clearly asking the european union – which means in this case me personally – to play a more pronounced role as a european union. so collectively, all our institutions together, all our member states together – the institutions together means also parliament – were called on to play a more pronounced role in mediating a peace deal for syria. i remember very well, during the state of the union speech in september, not only president juncker but many of you called for a pronounced work of the european union on the future of syria. this is why it is quite surprising for me to hear some of you say that we should not focus on the future of syria. i would invite some coherence here in what we ask ourselves to do. i heard very clearly the first two interventions here, by mr preda and mr boştinaru, prioritising the two key elements of our work: first, delivering humanitarian aid and making sure this can happen; second, using all the diplomatic tools we have to find, or rather to build, a political solution to put an end to the war in syria. this is exactly the work we are doing: providing humanitarian aid, together with the un, together with international agencies, together with international ngos, with our people on the ground, still. you cannot imagining how difficult the conditions are, or maybe you can, and talking to all relevant players in the region to try and open ways for the political solution to the crisis. so if we are the ones, not some of them, but the ones financing humanitarian aid and making sure it can be delivered –obviously this does not depend only on us – but if we were not there, for sure there would be no humanitarian aid at all in the country. secondly, if we are the ones today still keeping open the talks, the dialogue, in a situation that otherwise is rather stalled, then i am sorry: i do not share the views of the few of you who have said that europe should be ashamed. i believe we are not the ones who should be ashamed about syria. we are doing our job, finally, maybe, but we are. the point is, this is not enough. we need the unity of the international community, so this is also part of our work. six years of war; five years of polarisation in the international community. you remember that very well. this year for the first time, thanks in part to our work in the international support group, we managed to have unity in the security council for the first time ever – even though we are not a member of the security council. you know that very well, but we managed to facilitate consensus in the security council twice, and those were the only weeks where aid was delivered, syrians were getting out into the streets, trying to live a normal life again. these are the efforts we have to make in order to continue to build the unity of the international community. otherwise, our efforts alone will be necessary and indispensable. we will continue to do that, but doing so alone would not be enough. we have to be a key player, but we cannot pretend we will be the only player. we have to build alliances, starting with those we have worked with well these past months. we have our role to play, and we are now playing it fully. this was maybe not necessarily the case in past years in the first years of the conflict, but here, now, the european union is there, politically and from a humanitarian perspective – not from a military perspective. this is not because we do not have a european army, but because of a clear political decision that was taken and i am sincerely proud that we are not a military player on the ground. we are not part of the war in syria. having said that, why focus on post-conflict? some of you asked this and some others explained why, but let me say a few words on that. firstly, many conflicts in the past were solved exactly when the parties started to see the endgame shaping up. sometimes it works, sometimes it does not, but we are facing a war and a crisis that does not allow us to leave any of the possibilities untried. when you start shaping the endgame, the parties would feel more confident engaging in direct talks, so this is a contribution we can make to the un efforts to restart direct talks and find common ground. secondly, we need to be ready for the construction – the reconstruction – of syria. at a certain moment, it will come; it will cost an enormous amount of money. how many conflicts in our region have faced the problem of nothing following the end of the conflict and have thus fallen back into conflict after maybe a few months or a few years? working on post-conflict reconstruction today is fundamental so as to be ready at the moment when arms are finally laid down. thirdly, to give hope to the syrians – not only to the refugees, but also to the internally displaced people and those that are still living in syria in their own communities; to offer positive incentives; to offer the dividends for peace that make it possible for the parties to engage. last but not least, you mentioned empowering the local players that can still be a force for good in their country – the women, the small experiences of civil society that are still struggling, the churches, the communities that are taking care of their own everyday lives, the children, and the women. this is work that the european union does, but does not expect any of the big military players to do on the ground. we can be – and we are – a force for good in syria. others are not, true – definitely true! we cannot delete this issue, but we can maybe compensate, maybe engage, or maybe encourage a more positive dynamic on the ground and diplomatically. this is the work we are doing. i thank you for the support in this effort. it will be needed, because it will not be something that we will solve in one week or one month. i am sure that we are now on the right track as regards what the european union can and should do, and what it finally is doing.

in writing. to reduce the number of low-skilled adults in europe, the commission has proposed the introduction of a 'skills guarantee'. the initiative should help low-skilled adults to acquire a minimum level of literacy, mathematics and digital skills. i think that there are some gaps in this proposal which should be filled. the commission calls on the member states to draw up an action plan for the implementation of this 'skills guarantee' without providing for a mechanism or body to support the member states in drawing up and monitoring this plan. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission refers to the use of several eu funds, for example the european social fund and the erasmus+ programme, but without defining appropriate procedures that allow the combination of these different funding without creating bureaucratic burdens. another gap in the proposal that should be filled is the strategy that the commission should adopt to involve the member states in this non-legally binding initiative. without a clear strategy to help make the skills guarantee operational, the potential benefits risk being undermined.
member of the commission. – madam president, the challenges of the deaf and hard of hearing community do not yet get enough attention in the european union, and i am therefore grateful to members of the european parliament, helga stevens and ádám kósa for constantly reminding us of what still needs to be done in order to ensure that all european citizens can participate actively in society. commissioner tibor navracsics recently took part in a conference on sign languages and human rights, organised by helga stevens, which showcased the challenges faced by the deaf and the hard of hearing on a daily basis. the commission was impressed by the professional competence of the sign language interpreters, who were conveying the speeches in more than 30 sign languages. the commission welcomes the political groups’ initiatives for a motion for a resolution, because we believe that more should be done to show respect for the deaf and hard of hearing community and its languages. the charter of fundamental rights of the european union explicitly excludes any form of discrimination, and the disability strategy 2010-2020 stresses the principle of social inclusion. the commission believes in, and promotes, inclusive education. whenever possible, schools should open their doors to deaf children, ensuring that the conditions are met for their successful inclusion in the classroom. sign language interpretation should be provided whenever possible for public services. education and language policy falls under the exclusive competence of the member states. however, the commission supports them through facilitating cooperation and exchange of best practices. the erasmus+ programme already funds a number of partnerships and mobility projects that develop open educational resources and train sign language teachers and interpreters. for example, the research project developing and documenting sign bilingual best practice in schools maps the situation of sign bilingual education in 39 european countries. the european forum of sign language interpreters provides opportunities for meetings, conferences and exchange of experiences. we also have the toolkit signs for handshakes, deaf—youth—meets—employers, and the european language label. more support for sign languages is provided through the research programme horizon 2020, and there again we have many examples: information technology is used for the early detection of and compensation for hearing impairment, and also to develop applications supporting the use of sign languages, for example. another example is that a digital archive presenting the life narratives of elderly signers has developed. remote communication between signing and speaking people through applications that translate text into sign languages is made possible, and another example under horizon 2020 is an interactive digital atlas of the linguistic structures of the world’s sign languages. as regards the commission, the directorate general for interpretation regularly provides sign language interpretation for eu—level meetings. to support the full participation of those using sign languages, interpreters tailor their services by discussing with participants whether international sign language is appropriate or whether a national sign language is needed. as you can see, the commission has come a long way since this house adopted its last resolution on sign language recognition in 1998, but we know we can and should do more to ensure our societies not only tolerate diversity, but also cherish and promote it. the commission therefore welcomes this resolution, and will continue supporting sign languages, their users and their interpreters.
the s&d group is therefore calling for the introduction of a european standard for the interpretation of sign language, which is a fundamental requirement for the development of the european union. this is an inalienable right of over one million european deaf sign language users and 51 million deaf citizens. we talk about the possibility of leading independent lives, of receiving inclusive and quality education, of increasing employability, of being guaranteed the right to health, of having equal access to justice. we are talking about the possibility of active participation in political and democratic processes, as well as the creation and exchange of culture. the eu's motto is 'united in diversity' and that is why we have always been committed to promoting linguistic richness and pluralism. it 's time to take it to the next level . today we call on the eu and the member states to recognise national and regional sign languages, to recognise the professional status of sign language interpreters and to provide quality training and supervision for this profession.

a writer. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, trade and the environment are closely linked. the relationship between the two areas, however, is not clear. one could argue that the expansion of international trade and growth is one of the causes of global warming. however, it is important to acknowledge that globalisation has contributed to the spread of technologies with a low environmental impact and better standards. that is why we think the green goods agreement, which is being negotiated by 17 parties, including the united states and china, as well as the european union, is so important. the negotiations, which, as we know, have had successive phases of speed and success, but which could be concluded in december, have some critical elements. we have therefore put this question to clarify the commission's strategy and the union's offensive and defensive interests in the field of environmental goods. there are two concerns at the heart of our request. the first, conceptual, concerns the nature of the agreement itself and, in particular, the objective of contributing to the fight against climate change. we fear that the agreement may betray the results of the paris conference, because of the lack of a definition of 'environmental goods'. we wonder how the environmental credibility of the agreement can be safeguarded by including some products which can hardly be classified as environmentally friendly or energy-efficient. equally worrying is the choice to disregard the impact of production and the potential for dual use of selected items. increased imports from countries with less stringent regulations could lead to an increase in emissions. i would remind you that when we talk about dumping we are not referring only to the economic dimension but also to the social and environmental consequences. the liberalization of certain products such as bicycles, whose manufacturing process in europe meets the most stringent standards, could paradoxically have a negative ecological impact. a ton of co2 emitted in a country with less stringent regulations is not only equally harmful, it is also cheaper. we are thinking of articles such as pipes, and we ask the commission how it intends to regulate any dual use of such articles. one tube could be used for a water recycling plant or for the construction of an oil pipeline. the second concern is economic. europe is a leader in environmental goods. we are aware of the continuing growth of the sector and the associated fall in employment, and we wonder whether the offensive european interests are actually reflected in the agreement. in fact, apart from duties, the main obstacles faced by our companies are non-tariff barriers. we fear that their exclusion could harm our interests. europe cannot afford to increase its exposure to competition without gaining equal access to foreign markets. another important exclusion concerns services. for example, maintenance and repair of a wind farm can reach 40% of the total value of the sale: we therefore ask the commission how the negotiations are proceeding to include both of these aspects. in conclusion, the current state of the environment requires us to take concrete action against climate change. at the same time, this agreement could offer great economic potential for a fast-growing sector. we cannot afford to lose this opportunity to demonstrate that trade is also a tool for sustainable development and can therefore contribute to improving the lives of people and the planet.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the agreement reached with the council on the reduction of national emissions of certain air pollutants will make it possible to halve by 2030 the number of premature deaths caused by toxic pollution. at present, there are more than 400 000 per year in europe alone. but the limits identified by the directive are far from the recommendations made by the world health organization, which parliament has tried to defend in every way during the trilogue phase. the short-sighted attitude of some member states will result in about 10 000 additional premature deaths each year. the flexibility criteria introduced are also unsatisfactory, which will make the limits more difficult to apply. the authorization given to member states to regulate emissions according to seasonal temperatures or to compensate for the reduction in emissions in one sector by the higher emissions produced in another sector raises a number of concerns. the hope is that the member states will change the short-sighted attitude they have shown during the negotiations. breathing clean air is a right of citizens and the european union must raise the bar of ambition. we must do this for ourselves and for the new generations.

the agenda includes the debate on the statement by the council and the commission on the outcome of cop22 in marrakech (2016/2995 ((rsp)).
president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, one year after the paris agreement, the conference in marrakech last week clearly marked a new phase in global climate governance. at the outset, let me highlight that the european union has shown its strong commitment to climate action by ratifying the paris agreement on 5 october 2016. following the consent given by parliament, the ratification of the agreement by the eu, together with seven member states, triggered its entry into force on 4 november 2016 and confirmed the key role of the european union in the multilateral process. this was clearly recognised in marrakech. overall, 112 parties ratified the paris agreement by 18 november. the european union can be satisfied with the result of the marrakech conference. we witnessed the unprecedented quick entry into force of the paris agreement, the progress made on the development of its rules and the major demonstration of activities by non-state actors. this all confirmed the determination of the international community to continue moving forward, with a transition towards a low emission and climate-resilient future. the european union’s main objective at the marrakech conference was to put on track the swift preparation for the effective and comprehensive implementation of all the elements of the paris agreement. marrakech demonstrated progress and enabled action in the following areas: first, the subsidiary bodies outlined the work to establish the paris rulebook, including the progress on the features of nationally determined contributions, the transparency framework, the adaptation mechanism and the adaptation registry. other elements to be mentioned are the global stock take, the sustainable development mechanism concerning markets, non-market approaches and the compliance mechanism. the cop also mandated the current and incoming presidencies to start preparations for the 2018 facilitative dialogues. secondly, progress was made on enhancing action and transparency before 2020, including on the predictability of climate finance flows to developing countries; on loss and damage, namely the review of the warsaw international mechanism; on technology development and transfer, capacity-building mechanisms, methodological issues, response measures, as well as on measures concerning gender and indigenous peoples. thirdly, the global climate action agenda was another key part of marrakech. the action agenda builds on the growing momentum from stakeholders to mobilise global action in the water sector and in the areas of oceans, disaster risk reduction, agriculture, forestry, transport, energy and human settlements. all these initiatives by non-state actors support the convention and the aims of the paris agreement. amongst many other issues, i would like to highlight the second round of the multilateral assessment process, which took place in marrakech. nineteen eu member states and the european union successfully completed the process of reviewing the progress made in the implementation of emission reductions and removals related to their quantified economy-wide emission reduction targets. the remaining member states will follow next year. and finally, the conference made a high-level political statement, the marrakech action proclamation, which reflects the continuous political commitment towards the implementation of the paris agreement and reaffirms the willingness of all participants to fight against climate change and to support sustainable development.

background of the early ratification and entry into force of the paris agreement. first, i want to thank the european parliament’s delegation to cop for their very strong support throughout the paris; and we will implement paris. the marrakech action proclamation reflects the spirit of cop22. it is a statement of global unity, confirming that the parties remain committed to climate action post—paris and the transition to a global low—carbon economy. important progress was also achieved under the paris work programme. the parties agreed a clear way forward to ensure that the rule book implementation of the paris agreement. now that we have returned from marrakech, the hard work does not stop. in the current uncertain geopolitical setting the european union must, more than ever, remain steady on its course to a low—carbon, energy-efficient future. marrakech showed us we are not alone. the momentum keeps growing in many of our g20 partners, including china, that are more also work closely with the german g20 presidency to make sure we exploit the positive opening under the g20 to follow up on the paris implementation. in addition to strengthening our strategic opportunity to modernise our economy and create jobs and growth. it is a central element in achieving broad and sustainable development goals as well as the european union priorities on investment, competitiveness, circular economy research, innovation and energy transition. therefore, we will also shortly come forward with a package under the title smart and clean energy for all europeans – a package of proposals which will put energy efficiency first, will reinvigorate our global leadership in renewables and deliver a fair deal for european consumers and citizens, as well as business and industry. together with existing proposals on the table, this package will ensure a comprehensive and coherent climate and energy policy framework up to 2030. it will deliver on our contribution to the paris agreement and will make bigger steps forward towards our overall vision for an energy union. in conclusion, honourable members, we have achieved marked progress this year on global climate action. less than twelve months ago, we adopted the paris agreement, and through commitment and hard work ensured its entry into force earlier this month. we still have much work to do to implement our commitments on the ground and i count on your continued support to turn our commitments into reality.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the marrakesh summit should have dealt with the implementation of the paris agreement on climate change. it wasn't like that. still many promises and few facts. but climate change is not slowing down, as the world meteorological organization has announced that 2016 is set to be the warmest year since 1880. at this point, the paris agreement, even if it is implemented, despite donald trump's claims, will not be enough to keep us within two degrees of global warming. climate finance with funds like the green climate fund is expected to mobilize $100 billion a year in funding starting in 2020, but so far it has raised only $81 million for climate adaptation, and 91 percent of that is from europe. resources for climate change mitigation need to be rebalanced with those for adaptation policies. if we do not solve this problem, we risk dividing the international community.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, one of the most alarming consequences of man-made climate change is the migration caused by environmental disasters. according to the international organization for migration, by 2050, at least 200-250 million people will be displaced by climate change; that's one person in every 45 in the world, an average of 6 million women and men forced to leave their homes every year. these are frightening numbers that could even reach, if the most dramatic of the scenarios imagined by the un agency were to come true, the staggering figure of one billion environmental refugees. unfortunately, the commitments made at cop22 still appear weak in this respect. while we await the states' implementation of the commitments they solemnly made in marrakesh, i hope that the european parliament will seize the opportunity offered by the reform of asylum legislation to provide adequate recognition and protection for environmental refugees.
member of the commission. madam president, i would like to thank all the members who have taken part in this debate and who have shown the house's interest in climate change policies. the commission has clearly played a very active role. we did it in paris, setting in motion the ambition of the grand coalition; in marrakesh, in negotiations that are different, much more technical, but moving forward on the road map. and we will have to continue in future cop's, future cop's which will be very different, they will not have that element of political negotiation so accentuated that paris had, but they will be cop's which are technically important to provide the paris agreement with the necessary instruments for its implementation and, on the other hand, they will be cop's of implementation, of developing our policies. at this cop, we saw that non-governmental actors were very present: municipalities, regions, autonomous communities, ngos, civil society, energy companies, renewable energy companies, energy efficiency companies, economic actors, social actors. it was a cop, as future cop's will be, to see best practices. i was asked what the commission's attitude is towards non-governmental actors: maximum collaboration and openness. we have worked very closely with the covenant of mayors, because we understood that cities are a crucible of very powerful climate change experiences, and we will continue to work with the rest of the non-governmental actors, with the committee of the regions and with all of these actors, because the fight against climate change is bottom up, it's not up bottom, and therefore we have to do it in a very participatory way. i want to say that 2016 has been a very positive year for climate change. 2015 had the emblematic paris agreement, but in 2016 we have ratified it - the european union and many of its member states, currently 16 member states, have already ratified it - it has entered into force thanks to european ratification, and we have developed cop 22 in accordance with the expectations that were on the table and even with the marrakesh action plan, which is the commitment of all parties to keep action at a significant level and to implement our policies. mr. helmer said paris was dead. well, "the dead you kill are in good health", because paris is alive and well, which is said in spanish, in spanish, and, if i saw something in marrakech it was the desire of everyone to move on. and the problem of china has been raised. in the face of uncertainty, it is clear that china and the european union must come together to maintain that permanent leadership in the fight against climate change by developing our policies. and the european union can be proud and come to these negotiations with very important assets that justify its participation in world leadership. because we have the most ambitious emission reduction target, at least 40 percent, with domestic action, not international credits. second, we are the only party that, at this point, has launched (or will launch next week) all the legislation necessary to meet its climate goals, through legislation, not through presidential decisions. and that is a differentiating factor, because, regardless of the different electoral results that may exist in the 28 member states, the policies remain constant, and that is a value that we europeans can boast of. and finally, we have international financial solidarity, the respect of developing countries. we can orchestrate large coalitions with developing countries because we are financially solidary; because we are the ones who put the most climate finance on the table, and also, in coordination with our development policies. commissioner mimica and i work together. we are the largest contributor to climate finance; we are the one who finances 50 percent of the green climate fund; we are the one who finances 90 percent of the adaptation fund, and we are respected by developing countries. it is not the work of this commissioner, it is the work of very consistent policies, which justify the european union's being able to speak out loud and seek alliances that will be complex in the future. and we will have to extend our partnerships to india, as mr eickhout has said: it is essential to have india, a country which has an impressive demography and equally impressive co2 emissions, as its demography. we'll have to make approaches to the big emitters, to free up the reduction of them. so the challenges ahead are important. mr turmes, you know that i strive to have the most ambitious package possible, and you know me well. therefore, in this endeavor we will be together. i will launch a major package and then, as mrs van brempt has said here, parliament will also have its responsibilities, starting with the european system of emission allowances, which is fundamental for the industrial sectors; then moving on to the diffuse sectors - agriculture, buildings, transport - and finally developing the technological innovation that will enable us to lead the world in energy efficiency and renewable energy. i know that i am counting on this parliament for all this. it is very pleasant to work in a policy which, at a time of division in the european union, is a policy which brings unity. there was unity in the environment council, under the slovak presidency, to launch the ratification process; there was unity in this parliament to give its consent to that ratification; there was unity in the national parliaments, as 16 agreement. but the first act of the government of the country i know best, after the inauguration, was to launch the ratification process. this shows that across the european union climate change policies are united, ambitious and hopeful.

in writing. ‒ if the proposed canada-european union economic and trade agreement (ceta) were to enter into force, we know full well that it would have catastrophic effects in many of the member states. it is also structured in such a way that it operates outside the judicial system of the member states and gives even more power to multinational companies, which already have too much power. for these reasons, i, my colleagues from the five star movement and other members have asked the court of justice for an opinion, which is the body responsible for assessing whether the treaties of the european union are being respected. to show that agreements like ceta are illegal, i voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution, rejected by parliament, which called for an opinion from the court of justice on the compatibility of ceta with the treaties. the comprehensive economic and trade agreement between canada and the eu is undoubtedly an important achievement of the commission: however, it also contains some provisions which, in my view, could create situations of interference with the prerogative of the community institutions and governments to legislate on such central issues as the protection of health or the environment. the main concerns relate to sections d and f of chapter 8 of the agreement, which deal with investment protection and the settlement of investment disputes between investors and states. the establishment of supranational private courts for the arbitration of conflicts between states and multinational companies is, in my view, a particularly sensitive subject which would deserve to be examined by the court.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the resolution calling on the court of justice to rule on the compatibility with the treaties of the agreement between canada and the european union on a comprehensive economic and trade agreement (ceta). this europe is concluding an agreement with canada which will be against the economies of our territories, against our agriculture, against a venetian and italian market model based on the quality of our excellences which is in danger of being wiped out by the canadian multinationals who want to appropriate our know-how. ceta must be stopped now, before it destroys our economy and our agri-food sector, with the consequent loss of thousands of jobs in our regions.
in writing. ‒ i voted against this resolution because there is no need to seek an opinion from the court of justice on the comprehensive economic and trade agreement between the eu and canada if the one issued by the legal service of the parliament already provide enough safety and the confirmation that the ceta is not against european law.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of this report to seek the opinion of the court of justice on the compatibility of the canada-eu comprehensive economic and trade agreement (ceta) with the treaties. there are many concerns about ceta: the negotiations have been conducted in complete secrecy and the conclusions could have very negative effects on our democratic processes and risk severely affecting public services and workers' rights. unfortunately, parliament has voted by a majority against accepting the request. if it had been accepted, the court could have ruled on issues related to the investment court system (ics), which will guarantee foreign investors the possibility of suing states if they issue regulations or regulations that jeopardise their business expectations. in fact, the establishment of supranational private courts to arbitrate conflicts between states and multinationals seems to be in contradiction with the eu treaties because it essentially denies national sovereignty and bypasses ordinary justice. i find it paradoxical that, in the face of all these doubts about its legitimacy, there is a desire to push for the immediate implementation of ceta.
in writing. ‒ requiring the compatibility of a treaty concluded by the eu with a third country is one of parliament's prerogatives. in particular, the eu-canada agreement raises a number of issues of primary importance to european citizens, which we have repeatedly denounced. i therefore voted in favour of the request for an opinion to the court of justice without the slightest hesitation.
in writing. ‒ of the many dissatisfactions that an agreement of the size of ceta can arouse, the legal one is certainly not to be counted. the confirmation of this assumption is not only found in the already complete and exhaustive legal verification completed on 29 february, but also in the absence of incompatibility with the treaties of the proposed comprehensive economic and trade agreement between canada and the european union and especially with the aforementioned articles 49, 54, 56 267 and 340 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. in fact, ceta cannot be regarded as contrary to the freedom of establishment provided for in article 49, which facilitates access to and pursuit of selfemployed activities. it is also established that the status of companies incorporated under the laws of a member state and having their registered office, central administration or principal place of business in the eu is equivalent to that of natural persons having european citizenship. similarly, there is nothing contrary to the principle laid down in article 340 according to which the contractual liability of the union is governed by the law applicable to the contract in question. in line with this, i reject the proposal and hope that where ceta may present gaps or well-founded doubts, there will be effective intervention.
in writing. ‒ the ceta agreement between canada and the european union is illegal, as it threatens the establishment of a supranational court at the expense of the judicial system of the various member states, benefiting multinationals. we have asked the european court of justice for an opinion on this, so that the agreement can be declared illegal, but our proposal was rejected in the parliamentary vote. in any case, i have voted against the ceta agreement, and it is clearly negative.
in writing. ‒ ceta is an agreement that would have a huge impact on the lives of european citizens. public services would be provided at all times at the "highest level of liberalization" in accordance with the logic of competitiveness, the market and the pursuit of profit by companies. the interests of the citizens, the quality of the services themselves and the benefits to society would be marginal or non-existent. more than 3 million european citizens took action last year with a european citizens' initiative to stop ttip and ceta and it is the duty of the european parliament to give them a voice, taking due account of their concerns and their will. transparency, democracy, public services and the environment are as important as trade. the latter cannot prevail at the expense of protecting the rights and health of over half a billion europeans. for this reason and in view of the opinion of the court of justice on the compatibility of ceta with the european treaties, i am voting in favour.
in writing. ‒ i voted unanimously against the resolution on the request for an opinion of the court of justice on the compatibility with the treaties of the comprehensive economic and trade agreement between canada and the european union (ceta). i consider this resolution to be purely instrumental, presented with the sole aim of delaying the ratification of the ceta agreement by the european parliament and thus delaying its provisional application. the request in question relates in particular to the compatibility of the provisions on investment dispute settlement or the new ics mechanism, which belgium has already officially stated that it wishes to verify before the final entry into force of the agreement. i would also like to point out that the provisions in question have been clearly excluded from provisional application and that the council and the commission have reaffirmed their commitment to continue the technical work to improve the ics system in the direction requested by parliament. we need more clarity and transparency in trade policy and the decision-making processes that go with it, especially in the face of an increasingly interested and attentive public. in this regard, it will be necessary to reinvigorate the role of the european parliament as the guarantor of democratic elections and to work towards building an increasingly regulated, inclusive and equitable globalisation.

in writing. ‒ the eu-canada ceta negotiations started in may 2009 and concluded in september 2014. the legal review of the treaty was completed in 2016 with a favourable verdict from parliament's legal services. we recall in particular how this parliament, on the initiative of the socialist and democratic group in particular, called for and obtained the abolition of the controversial isds system, replaced by a model of international court to settle disputes between investors and states, providing in particular for facilitation measures for smes, to make the system more accessible. ceta also recognizes geographical indications to protect consumers and typical foods from our country, as well as the agreements on standards of the international labour organization. this agreement is - as many have said - a progressive trade agreement. nevertheless, citizens have expressed concerns about certain aspects, and i believe that the amendments that have been made have taken this into account. the demand for this resolution, which i did not support, would have further slowed down a process which will provide europe, smes and workers with many opportunities for growth and employment.

in writing. ‒ a majority in the european parliament has rejected an attempt to seek the opinion of the european court of justice on ceta, the treaty with canada. there are serious doubts about its compatibility with european law, especially since it contains the ics clause which allows investors to turn to private courts to sue the state in the event of public measures contrary to their interests. this is why 89 meps from various parties including all of us from m5s have asked to seek the opinion of the european court of justice: it was only a question of checking the legality of the treaty outside the pro- and anti-positions. but the power houses are afraid that ceta will be analyzed: the more we talk about it, the more it is revealed that it contains a torpedo aimed against the precautionary principle, it weakens food security, it is killing our agriculture, it sets very wide margins for private intervention in services such as water, education and health, it sets the criteria for the issuing of permits and licences for all economic activities.
in writing. i strongly supported the request to refer the matter to the court of justice to rule on the compatibility of ceta with eu law. we need to be clear about this, because we believe that this agreement undermines the uniformity of european law and jeopardises the protection of the fundamental rights of european citizens. ceta creates a supranational para-judicial tribunal which would allow multinational companies to sue states outside the normal court system for damages for any harm suffered as a result of laws and regulations protecting citizens, health and the environment. how can this legal monster be compatible with the rights and values enshrined in the treaties? we would have liked to have heard the final opinion on this matter from the european courts. unfortunately, by 419 votes to 258, parliament rejected this request and therefore refused to open the debate. they are probably afraid that the european courts will give us the answer and not the multinationals.
in writing. ceta, the free trade agreement between europe and canada, is illegal because it creates a supranational court for the use and consumption of multinational companies, which will be able to sue states outside the normal judicial system. we of the five star movement have lodged an appeal with the european court of justice for a final opinion: we want to know whether ceta is compatible with the european treaties. the court of justice of the european union is the only body which ensures that the treaties establishing the european union are observed and enforced. ceta undermines the uniformity of european law and with it the rights of citizens. the supranational court created by ceta could be called upon to interpret eu law. and how will a court designed to defend the rights of multinational corporations deal with the rights of citizens? all this without the european court of justice, the body responsible for interpreting eu law, having any say in the matter. we must have the courage to defend the rights of european citizens in a strong way, and that is why i voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. ‒ air pollution, neglected for years by policy, is now a strategic priority as a major public health concern. poor air quality causes premature death, sickness absence from work, high health care costs, lost productivity, reduced crop yields and damage to buildings. in europe, the total external health costs to society from air pollution are estimated to be between eur 330 and 940 billion per year. in addition, a growing body of evidence is available that the deposition of nitrogen in the atmosphere causes changes in the natural environment, including reduced diversity of soil vegetation, reduced plant growth and nutrient imbalances due to eutrophication and acidification. despite significant improvements, many member states are still far from the agreed standards for reducing pollutant emissions. the new 2030 targets contained in the proposal under discussion aim to achieve approximately 70% of the reductions recommended by the who parameters: the commission has already taken a number of important steps in this direction, and we must not take a step backwards.
in writing. ‒ air pollution kills around 400 000 people in the european union every year and costs the health systems of the member states an estimated €300-900 billion annually. in order to reduce the impact of air pollution on public health, i thought i would vote in favour of updating the directive on the reduction of national emissions of certain pollutants. i believe that each member state, within its means, must reduce its emissions of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, ammonia and volatile organic compounds other than methane in order to protect the environment and the well-being of its citizens. to this end, member states should transmit to the commission every two years national pollution control programmes for all economic sectors with particular reference to industrial activities and transport. i welcome the fact that the updating of the directive commits the member states to also assess the impacts of air pollution on aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. finally, i am pleased that the directive now includes specific provisions to protect vulnerable groups, and in particular children (for example, the prohibition of the consumption of solid fuels in residential areas).
in writing. ‒ over the past 20 years, the union has made considerable progress in air quality and anthropogenic atmospheric emissions, in particular through the adoption of specific policies. i therefore welcome the setting of maximum limits for some of the most harmful gases in line with the long-term objectives of an atmosphere free from adverse effects on health and the environment. the approved measure aims to reduce levels and deposits of acidifying and eutrophicating air pollutants and other pollutants, including ozone. in addition, the urgency of synergies between the future directive and the european climate and energy programmes is confirmed. the request to member states to minimise their annual anthropogenic emissions in accordance with the national commitments applicable from 2020 is followed by a request to monitor and update the commission on their progress. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. finally, member states must ensure that the public concerned is consulted at an early stage of the development and adoption of national pollution control programmes and at any stage of such activities prior to their actual completion.

in writing. ‒ air pollution is the main environmental risk factor not only for human health but also for animal and plant biodiversity. its negative impact on ecosystems, buildings, materials and the climate causes incalculable damage. it is responsible for an excessive number of premature deaths, illnesses and hospitalizations across the european continent. the who and the oecd estimate that the economic cost of the health impact of air pollution in europe is about eur 1.4 trillion. the deterioration of air quality will not be contained by unrealistic targets, and we cannot but welcome regulations which end up protecting the business of a few at the expense of the protection of the environment and health.
