in writing. ‒ on 9 may 1950, robert schuman delivered the famous speech which would lead to the creation of the ecsc (european coal and steel community) the following year. since then, europe has supported research in this field, the sharing of resources and the exchange of knowledge. the ecsc assets and related interests, which were terminated in 2002, were placed in a sector-specific research fund which produces funding of around eur 50 million each year with a breakdown of 72.8% for steel and 27.2% for coal. it brings together partners from academia, industry, smes and public institutions. we must now find the most appropriate legal formula to enable the fund to continue its activities, supporting research in this field and directing it in a fair and effective way.

in writing. ‒ agricultural activity depends on biological processes such as climatic conditions and animal and plant diseases, i.e. factors outside the farmer's control. income uncertainty is particularly damaging to investment and innovation. in addition, changes in agricultural production generate an inherent tendency for agricultural markets to be volatile. the cap was originally characterised by strict market regulation. at its heart was price-guarantee. they gave farmers a minimum price for their produce in case of crisis. over time, the cap has been reformed and now proposes a number of new risk management measures under the second pillar. in this context, member states may or may not include them in their rural development programmes. however, it is considered that the cap risk management instruments are inadequate to limit the effects of price volatility on farmers' income. the eu should provide solutions to this through the cap, focusing on three key points: strengthening the organisation of supply chains and contracting, improving the protection of farmers' income through risk management tools adapted to price volatility and enhancing market transparency.

in writing. price volatility in agricultural markets has increased in recent years due to a number of factors, including extreme weather events and the impact of climate change on human activities. these events have also had a serious impact on food security and farmers' incomes. i believe it is the task of the european institutions to mitigate the causes of this volatility by reforming their common agricultural policy. in particular, i believe that the bargaining power of small producers should be strengthened by means of standard collectively negotiated contracts. such instruments could allow farmers to defend themselves against commercial practices that could harm them or otherwise reduce their capacity to invest and innovate. i appreciate that the report, for which i voted in favour, recommends the creation of specific european agricultural price observatories which will analyse the entire production chain, from the cost of production to the final selling price. in this regard, greater transparency of agricultural markets should be ensured so that price information is accessible in real time to all interested parties, including consumers. i am convinced, however, that price crises must be prevented by countercyclical measures such as direct aid to farmers which can compensate for large price cuts.

in writing. ‒ the mere reflection we are about to make on the year that is drawing to a close includes the many environmental disasters that have characterised europe. in fact, since the floods, natural impacts are only one of many external variables that impact agricultural production and related markets. in view of this axiom, i share this report with the full knowledge that the instruments of the common agricultural policy adopted so far have proved ineffective or inadequate in the face of the rampant volatility of commodity prices. it is difficult to limit change, and it is impossible to think that we can control it completely, but there are certain measures that can be taken to prevent or avoid its harmful effects. among these, two contextual measures are proposed. the first is to strengthen the organization of the supply chains and the contracting system in order to ensure income for farmers. to complete this, it is necessary to introduce contractual relations by adapting competition legislation. the latter must, however, be fully guaranteed and will therefore be monitored by means of effective instruments. since the agricultural sector, by its very nature, does not have an immediate adjustment, tools for risk and crisis management are needed.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report, which aims to strengthen the organisation of supply chains and contracting, to better protect farmers' incomes by providing specific risk management instruments adapted to price volatility and to strengthen market transparency by setting up price observatories.
in writing. ‒ the volatility of agricultural product prices is one of the main factors in the dire situation in which many european farmers find themselves today. on the one hand, income uncertainty, due to the difficulty of forecasting production, is particularly damaging to investment and innovation and can put the economic viability of farms in question. on the other hand, changes in agricultural production imply that agricultural markets have an inherent tendency to be volatile. the current cap, while proposing different instruments for income stabilisation, has failed to address the high volatility of prices on agricultural markets and has instead placed an excessive burden on the producer. i therefore believe that the next cap reform should seek new ways of combating price volatility and stabilising farmers' incomes in response to market imbalances.
in writing. ‒ the cap has proved largely inadequate to counter the effects of price volatility in relation to farmers' incomes. the international context, globalisation and the fictionalisation of the real economy have hit the primary sector hard: in the five-year period 2005-2010 alone, 2.4 million farms disappeared. extreme weather events have brought several regions of europe to their knees. in addition, the unchallenged dominance of the processing and retail industries has imposed high prices on farmers, who have had to cope with rising energy and production costs. the eu's policy choice of the russian embargo and the consequent retaliation on the agricultural side have contributed to price volatility and income instability. the answer cannot be to resort to higher risk financial instruments or even more expensive insurance products. the destruction of local markets by subsidies for dumping surpluses cannot continue. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i shall therefore abstain.
in writing. ‒ i am abstaining because of the lack of impact and the low value of the contribution made at the beginning of a very important phase of the future review of the cap.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the european parliament resolution on the cap instruments to reduce price volatility on agricultural markets because i believe that the instability and volatility of prices of agricultural raw materials and, consequently, of agricultural products in general, which has been accentuated by the economic and financial crisis, has always characterised agricultural markets and has become a structural element of agriculture globally in recent years, due to the rapid succession of demand, supply and price shocks. price volatility is likely to increase due to a variety of causes, such as the instability and imperfection of agricultural markets, globalisation and the sophistication of agricultural markets, increasing supply variability due to climate instability, increased health risks and the fragile balance of the food chain. agriculture as an activity and as a vital economic sector for the eu therefore faces very important challenges in terms of innovation and process rationalisation. it will be necessary to consider both new risk and crisis management tools and a strengthening of the current second pillar measures, with the aim of enhancing the competitiveness of european agriculture by actively involving producer organisations in the implementation process.
in writing. as we know, farming activities are highly dependent on natural factors, including climatic conditions and plant and animal diseases, factors which are unfortunately beyond the farmer's control. these factors only increase the volatility of food prices, making the agricultural sector more uncertain than others. uncertainties that damage investment and innovation and put the economic viability of farms at risk. following the increase in agricultural prices between 2007 and 2008 and the consequences for global food security, this problem has received international attention. this focus on risk management is reflected in agricultural policies and in particular in the cap 2014-2020. the report by parliament, which i supported in the house, focuses on three main issues in order to ensure efficient food production. the committee therefore calls for the organisation of supply chains and contracting to be strengthened, for farmers' income to be better protected by risk management instruments adapted to price volatility and for the markets to be made more transparent by introducing measures to combat unfair trading practices along the supply chain.
in writing. ‒ i supported the report on cap instruments to reduce price volatility on agricultural markets, recognising the importance of this sector, which not only provides food but also contributes significantly to the development of rural areas. the delicate balance of the food chain is now threatened by the instability of agricultural markets, which are also affected by globalisation and climate change. on this basis, coordinated action at national and european level can be effective in ensuring productivity in the agricultural sector but also in protecting farmers who are most exposed to price volatility.
in writing. ‒ ladies and gentlemen, i voted in favour of my colleagues' proposal because i believe that excessive price volatility on the agricultural market would harm producers and consumers. i therefore voted in favour.
in writing. ‒ farmers are the most important, but also the weakest link in the food production chain and are the most affected by high price volatility. the eu must develop effective measures to protect them and consumers from unfair trading practices. the current system is too slow to respond to shocks and market imbalances, such as the russian embargo or weak international demand for agricultural products, and is unable to combat unfair trading practices, excessive price volatility and to stabilise farmers' incomes. this report is a good starting point for tackling these problems. the commission is proposing a number of improvements to the common agricultural policy, such as the inclusion of new instruments for the prevention and management of crises in the short term and the provision of counter-cyclical measures in the long term. equally important will be the strengthening of farmers' bargaining power through the introduction of standard, transparent, balanced and collectively negotiated contracts. price volatility and market imbalances are a threat not only to farmers and consumers, but also to the eu's own food independence in the long term. it is therefore extremely necessary and urgent to act and that is why i have supported this resolution.
in writing. this paper seems to assume that price volatility in agricultural markets is inevitable. i am convinced that as a result of the intense weather fluctuations, increased by climate change, and the variability in the supply of agricultural products, the market is and will always be exposed to the risk of volatility. however, there are many actions we can take to regulate and contain overexposure. i am referring in particular to measures to limit speculation in foodstuffs and to manage real supply and demand, even by making them coincide. the current policy of over-reliance on third-party markets has caused major problems, as has happened in the dairy and fruit and vegetable sectors. the text also expresses shared concepts but is more a statement of the situation than a proposal for concrete measures or policies. price instability and volatility are now considered to be a structural feature of both european and world agriculture, but this is not the case. we must do more, much more, to protect a sector as important as agriculture, and it is in the light of these considerations that i have voted against this report.

statement, and our last recommendation to gradually apply the dublin rules in greece. let me first point out that, while these are two important elements in our comprehensive migration approach, they are not the only ones. secondly, all our policies are interconnected, and the progress we have achieved so far – and all our reports from last week demonstrate this – is precisely because we have made progress on many fronts, not just one. from relocation and resettlement to returns, to improving reception conditions, to fighting smuggling, and indeed to cooperating with all important partner persons per day – and fewer people have lost their lives trying to do so. in parallel, more than 2 600 syria refugees have been resettled from turkey to the european union since the entry into force member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank parliament for having raised the question of the important issue of the recognition, between member states, of the civil status of eu citizens. people in the union are increasingly mobile, and now more than ever, they live or raise a family in another member state. 14 million citizens reside in a member state other than their own, and 13% of all marriages in the union are international. in order to facilitate the free movement of citizens, the union has already adopted a number of legislative instruments. several of these instruments are in the area of family law, and they enable citizens to have a judgment that is easily recognised in another member state on such varied matters such as divorce, legal separation, child custody, children’s visiting rights, parental child abduction, maintenance obligations and succession. earlier this year, parliament played a key role in making possible the swift adoption of provisions on the property regimes of marriages and registered partnerships, which will also facilitate recognition in another member state of judgments on these matters. parliament was also instrumental in reaching, last summer, a balanced compromise with the council on a regulation to simplify the circulation of certain public documents within the union. under the regulation, public documents on civil status issued in one member state will be free of postal requirements when presented to authorities in another member state, and the rules governing certified copies and translations of such public documents will be simpler and avoid language barriers. the commission is aware that, despite existing instruments, citizens may encounter difficulties in having their civil status recognised when they travel or move to another member state. where recognition of civil status is governed by member state law, the union must ensure that citizens can enjoy their right to move freely within the union. in this respect, the court plays a very important role. with regard to a person’s name, the court has already ruled that non-discrimination on grounds of nationality and proportionality must guide member states in their decisions on whether or not to recognise a person’s name. as a result of the court’s ruling, the member states concerned have adopted their legislation or administrative practices on the recognition of names. as for same-sex unions, an important development in the court’s case law is expected. the romanian constitutional court announced in november that it will seek clarification on whether a same-sex couple, a romanian and a united states citizen married in belgium, can be recognised as spouses under romanian law, pursuant to the union provisions on family reunification. the commission, like the court, must ensure that member states apply correctly the union provisions that facilitate the free movement of citizens. in parallel to ensuring the correct application of existing law, the commission has started a reflection process on how to address issues such as the expansion of the scope beyond what is currently covered by the public documents regulation and on the recognition of civil status between member states. in this reflection process, the commission must consider the relevant case law developments in member states’ frameworks and coherence with european union policies. the commission is also ready to continue the exchange with parliament and engage in a dialogue with member states and other relevant actors. the commission contracted in 2012 a study on the recognition of civil status in the union. since then, substantial legal developments have taken place in member states regarding same-sex marriage and registered partnerships. any eventual legislative action would need to be based on updated data and the commission will look into ensuring the availability of the evidence base needed for eventual decisions. the commission will keep parliament and member states informed on its reflection process and views gathered during it.

in writing. thalidomide is a drug invented by the german pharmaceutical company chemie grünenthal, which was marketed from 1957 as a sedative, anti-nausea and hypnotic, particularly aimed at pregnant women. it was withdrawn from the market because women treated with thalidomide gave birth to babies with severe congenital limb developmental abnormalities, namely amelia or varying degrees of focomelia. it is estimated that at least 20 000 children were born with severe physical deformities. i believe that full recognition of the claims of surviving thalidomide victims in europe is essential in order to guarantee them autonomy, access to medical care and an adequate quality of life.

companies can no longer ignore paediatric development. it put an end to the dogma that children should be protected from clinical research. instead, children merit the same evidence—based therapies as other age groups. it increased paediatric discharge also in the most vulnerable population of neonates. we now see an increasing number of new products for children entering the market. indeed, more than 900 paediatric development programmes have been agreed under the regulation, and more than 100 have been completed in recent years. but there are also, of course, limitations to what the regulation can achieve. as there is an obligation for it not to regard the development of adult medicines, the additional paediatric research may not address pressing paediatric needs, especially in diseases that occur only in children, such as many paediatric cancers. we are looking closely as this issue in the context of drawing up the second report. at the same time, we are analysing economic impacts with a particular focus on the rewards and incentives. last month, the commission launched a public consultation which will run until february 2017. this exercise is important as it gives everybody an opportunity for their voice to be heard before finalisation of the report. the commission cannot therefore draw conclusions at this stage. we first needed to compare for you the data and gather experiences. the commission is committed to presenting, in the course of 2017, a detailed report on the paediatric regulation. it is our obligation, and on the basis of its findings we will be better placed to continue informed discussions on the best way forward. we are working on common discussions on those issues.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the paediatric medicines regulation has helped to improve the overall situation, bringing tangible benefits for a number of childhood diseases, but many areas have not made significant progress, in particular paediatric oncology and neonatology. the legal requirement to pursue the development of medicinal products for paediatric use is often not observed, as the medicinal products have been developed in pathological conditions typical of adults, which do not occur in children. there are therefore delays in starting clinical trials of childhood cancer medicines because the drug is expected to show promise in adult cancer patients. a legislative revision of this regulation is needed, taking due account of the need to base paediatric development plans on an action mechanism, not just on the type of tumour, and to ensure that paediatric investigation plans are more timely and feasible. finally, particular attention should be paid to the incentive system envisaged in order to stimulate research more and respond more effectively to the needs of the paediatric population, while ensuring the transparency of the research and development process.

in writing. ‒ visa policy is a key issue for the european union and has implications for both external action and internal security. it is because of its importance that it is clearly regulated as an area of shared competence between the co-legislators by the ordinary procedure. while the demand for greater security by european citizens is understandable and correct, the increased flexibility in visa suspension procedures must nevertheless be accompanied by a robust set of guarantees and measures to protect human rights, as well as by reports and statistics provided by european agencies and competent law enforcement authorities. this is the only way to guarantee the rights of third country nationals and to safeguard the principles of eu visa policy.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the amendment to the regulation in question which will make the visa suspension mechanism faster and more flexible. visa policy is a key issue for the european union in terms of its impact on both external action and internal security. the current level of migration, in particular in the light of subsequent visa liberalisation processes, required a review of the suspension mechanism. the adopted regulation will provide the european union with sound tools to deal with various circumstances, such as unfounded asylum applications, refusal of readmission applications or large and sudden increases in the number of irregular immigrants on european territory. but the increased flexibility will be accompanied by a robust set of safeguards and measures to protect human rights, as well as reports and statistics provided by european agencies and competent law enforcement authorities. this is the only way to guarantee the rights of third country nationals and safeguard the principles of the union's visa policy.

in writing. ‒ i voted today in favour of the objection to the draft implementing directive amending annexes i to v to the directive on protective measures against the introduction into the community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the community. the draft directive in question is contrary to the objectives of regulation (eu) 2016/2031 as it infringes the requirements for the introduction into the union of certain fruits susceptible to harmful organisms and is incompatible with the objective of regulation (eu) 2016/2031 to determine the plant health risks posed by any species, strain or biotype of pathogenic agents, animal or plant pests harmful to plants or plant products and measures to reduce those risks to an acceptable level. the objection is that the directive in question should be re-submitted to parliament once it has been amended as suggested.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the objection under rule 106 protection measures against the introduction into the community of organisms harmful to plants or plant products and against their spread within the community concerning community measures to help prevent the introduction into the eu of new pests attacking citrus fruit because the existing legislation is not sufficient to protect european producers. i believe that stricter rules and controls are needed to prevent the spread of pests such as citrus black spot and falsa cydia. the draft commission implementing directive does not reduce the risk of harmful organisms being imported into the eu to an acceptable level and therefore stricter rules are needed. for this reason i have argued that fruit originating in third countries should be visually inspected at the point of entry into the eu and that such inspections should be carried out on samples of at least 200 fruits per 30 tonne consignment. i also shared the european parliament's call for citrus fruit to be subjected to cold treatment or to an alternative, sustainable, effective and equivalent treatment before being imported into the eu, and for measures to improve the traceability of imported citrus fruit.

in writing. a resolution was adopted today in strasbourg which contains corrections to the european commission's draft amendment containing a series of protective measures against the introduction and spread of organisms harmful to plants or plant products on our territory. these are measures which we in parliament want to correct and improve, also in order to bring them into line with the entry into force of the new regulation introducing the so-called plant passport. the proposal provides that fruit from third countries must be accompanied by a phytosanitary certificate authorizing its entry, and that a declaration must be made that the fruit originates from a production area which has undergone appropriate treatment against citrus black spot, a pest which can destroy our citrus trees. the damage caused to our agriculture by plant diseases caused by viruses introduced by the importation of products from third countries is enormous. i have been fighting for some time to protect our ornamental heritage from pathogens from third countries, and i believe that supporting this request will have a positive effect.
in writing. ‒ thalidomide is a drug invented by the german pharmaceutical company chemie grünenthal and marketed from 1957 as an anti-nausea sedative and hypnotic, particularly for pregnant women. it was withdrawn from the market because women treated with thalidomide gave birth to babies with severe congenital limb developmental abnormalities, namely amelia or varying degrees of focomelia. it is estimated that at least 20 000 children with severe physical deformities were born. i voted in favour of the report, considering it essential that the claims of surviving thalidomide victims in europe be fully recognised, so that they can be granted autonomy, access to medical care and a decent quality of life.

in writing. ‒ from the late 1950s to 1961, thalidomide, a drug used at the time to reduce morning sickness in pregnant women, caused 20,000 disabled children and 100,000 people with permanent disabilities. thalidomide survivors are still waiting for adequate compensation, some form of community assistance, public recognition of their plight. we call on the german government to remedy a tragic mistake made 60 years ago, to find a just solution to the difficulties faced by people like him. thalidomide was introduced to the market in west germany in 1957 as an over-the-counter medicine to promote sleep and relieve symptoms of nausea in pregnant women. according to the company that makes it, chemie grünenthal, it's non-addictive and completely safe, even in pregnancy. by 1960 it was being sold with great success in 46 countries. in 1961 australian gynecologist william mcbride and german pediatrician widukind lenz demonstrated the correlation between malformations in newborns and the use of the drug during pregnancy. thalidomide was consequently withdrawn from the market. the european parliament has called on the commission to adopt a formal recognition for victims in the light of scientific and legal research confirming the responsibility of thalidomide.

in writing. ‒ the paediatric medicines regulation has had a significant impact on the development of medicines for infants and children, as many pharmaceutical companies consider paediatric development as an integral part of the overall development of a medicinal product. the number of paediatric research projects has increased significantly and more high-quality information on approved medicines is available. in addition, the relative number of successful paediatric clinical trials has also increased. however, there is still room for potential improvement, for example on financial rewards for paediatric drug development which are too often modest in number and size, with a rewards system that needs to be reviewed to give greater incentives to pharmaceutical companies to research and develop paediatric drugs, especially in the oncology field. we also need to promote much wider access to innovative therapies that can save the lives of children and adolescents with life-threatening diseases.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of the resolution in question, which offers valuable suggestions to the commission to improve the regulation on medicinal products for paediatric use. the paediatric medicines regulation has had a significant impact on the development of medicines for paediatric use. since its entry into force, many pharmaceutical companies have considered paediatric development as an integral part of their overall product development activity. the number of paediatric research projects has increased significantly and more high-quality information on the paediatric use of approved medicines is now available. however, this regulation has several shortcomings. financial mechanisms for rewards and incentives for the development of paediatric medicinal products, such as marketing authorisation for paediatric use, are late and have limited effect. the current system of rewards should be reviewed to determine how it could be improved to further stimulate research and development of paediatric medicines. in addition, paediatric investigation plans (pips) are too often impractical or started too late with the medicinal product. the resolution proposes a revision of the current pip system in order to improve it by limiting the speculation of pharmaceutical companies on the incentives offered.

in writing. ‒ the right to petition is a pillar of european citizenship. the 2015 annual report aims to provide an overview of the work of the committee on petitions, whose timetable does not correspond to the commission's legislative programme but is set by citizens who, in exercising their right to petition the european parliament, express their concerns about the different union policies and legislative measures. the data show that 36.3% of petitions were considered and 63.7% were archived because the signatories continue to confuse national competences with those of the european union, and the eu institutions with the council of europe or the court of human rights. this shows that more needs to be done to better inform citizens about the right to petition and what they can achieve by exercising this right before the european parliament.
in writing. ‒ today i voted in favour of approving the report of the peti committee on its activities in 2015. petitions are a valuable source of firsthand information based on citizens' experiences and help to identify possible violations and gaps in the implementation of eu legislation at national level. parliament's involvement in these procedures allows for additional control over the investigative activities of the relevant european institutions. however, the number of petitions received remains modest compared to the overall population of the european union, indicating that the vast majority of eu citizens and residents are still unaware of the existence of the right to petition and its potential benefits. the recent creation of an internet portal where people can register, petition and join petitions already declared admissible is an important simplification, but more needs to be done, especially to raise awareness of this right as a powerful tool for direct participation in democratic life. it is also essential to improve cooperation with national parliaments, their relevant committees and member state governments to ensure that petitions are dealt with by the authorities competent to take action.

on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you to the commissioner. we have been talking officially about a customs union since 1968, but i must say that today we are far from a customs union in the true sense of the word, because if it were a 'union' we should have the same tariffs, but also the same rules. unfortunately, this is not the case, customs clearance practices vary from one state to another and if we talk about sanctions we find absurdities, ranging from the payment of simple fines to even criminal consequences in some states. what is the practical consequence of this approach? that those countries which apply the rules more lightly, in fact, only attract more profits for themselves and this is to the detriment of all the member states and also of the citizens, because we are going to encourage unfair competition practices on the one hand, but we are not protecting consumers, because we are allowing the entry of counterfeit goods but also of bacteria, as in the case of xylella. but welcome this resolution in which we strongly call for uniform customs controls. we also call for the same computer system to be applied in all countries to facilitate controls and the exchange of information, which should also be interoperable with the health certification systems of the individual member states. if we can achieve this, a real union, where all goods entering the european territory are treated equally, then we can speak of consumer protection and a real advantage for all member states.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, different controls in different ports and a customs union which is only a customs union on paper. this is what you see when you go out of these buildings and talk to people who work in european ports. customs controls and anti-counterfeiting are not the same in italy or slovenia, spain or estonia, france or the netherlands, and there is a real war going on between european ports to seize more goods, with customs administrations often running on the border of legality and sometimes going beyond it in order to attract as much traffic as possible. many of the customs controls are derived from european legislation. i would therefore like the commission to investigate this phenomenon in depth, because, in addition to being dangerous for citizens, it distorts the internal market and penalizes those who, as in my country, do their job well. we must apply the law in the same way because with the free movement of goods once a product has entered europe it can end up in any country without any further controls, and knowing this situation there are those who take advantage of it. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this is what makes it so difficult to bring the phenomenon to light and for the same reason you cannot simply rely on local authorities to stop it. so, from my point of view, the solution is a commission inquiry at european level and i wonder whether there will be the courage and the will to carry it through.
